name: Gridright: an interconnection-rights fleet that buys retiring coal and steam plants for their grid rights and repowers them with gas
sector: Gas and steam power generation: brownfield repowering (steam turbines, boilers, HRSGs) and grid interconnection
one_liner: The scarcest permission in power is a grid connection, which takes about 5 years to get new. Buy mid-size retiring coal and old gas-steam plants for their capacity interconnection rights and existing steam turbines, repower them fast (boiler gas conversion first, then gas turbine plus HRSG to make combined cycle), and sell capacity and firm power to the grid and co-located loads.
what_it_owns: Capacity interconnection rights, which are portable to replacement generation under PJM's 2026 fast track and FERC surplus interconnection rules. The sites, water rights, rail and transmission yards. Existing steam turbine-generators and switchyards. An AI-built steam-plant parts and records library. And the repowered generating fleet with its capacity contracts. This is the 'own the permission' shape: the interconnection is the approval nobody can copy.
wedge_first_revenue: Target 50-400 MW units owned by co-ops, munis and small IPPs, which big PE ignores. Close before retirement and file as a PJM Replacement Generation Resource, or keep the 1-year surplus-interconnection clock alive. First repower is a coal-to-gas boiler conversion of the existing steam unit (about 12-18 months, est.) that clears the capacity auction. At the $333/MW-day cap, a 200 MW unit earns about $24M a year of capacity revenue alone, before energy (est. from PJM cap).
ladder: 1) Gas-convert existing boilers and sell capacity and energy. 2) Add aeroderivative or used frame gas turbines plus HRSGs feeding the existing steam turbine (repowered combined cycle). 3) Co-locate data centers or industrial loads behind the point of interconnection under surplus interconnection service (storage, solar). 4) A rollup of 20-40 sites, 5-10 GW, becoming a mid-cap IPP. 5) Later, advanced-nuclear or SMR replacement at the same rights, since coal-to-nuclear sites carry DOE and state support.
numbers: Queue: average about 5 years from proposal to grid connection (https://www.pew.org/de/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/02/09/to-harness-power-plants-unused-capacity-states-can-turn-to-surplus-interconnection-service). On Jan 29, 2026 FERC accepted PJM's fast-track for Replacement Generation Resources that assume capacity interconnection rights from retiring generators; surplus interconnection service may continue at most 1 year after retirement (https://www.troutmanenergyreport.com/?p=13304 ; https://www.iso-ne.com/static-assets/documents/100031/a03_tc_surplus_interconnection_service_presentation.pdf ; https://www.mcguirewoods.com/client-resources/alerts/2025/2/ferc-approves-expansion-of-pjms-surplus-interconnection-service-to-address-near-term-resource-adequacy-concerns). Prices: PJM capacity cleared at the $333.44/MW-day cap (would have been $529.80 uncapped), and the 2027/28 auction is about $16.4B (per P3). New CCGT costs about $2,000/kW (https://www.publicpower.org/periodical/article/new-report-finds-rising-cost-new-gas-plants-outpacing-planning-assumptions), and turbine slots extend to 2029-2031 (https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/steam-turbines-gas-turbine-bottleneck-siemens-energy). Precedent: Homer City (PA's largest coal plant) is being redeveloped as a 4.5 GW gas-powered data-center campus (https://abcnews.go.com/amp/Technology/wireStory/pennsylvanias-largest-coal-fired-power-plant-now-retired-120412657). Unit economics (est.): coal-to-gas boiler conversion about $50-200/kW; repowered combined cycle reusing the steam turbine and switchyard about $800-1,200/kW against $2,000/kW greenfield; site acquisition often $0-100/kW plus assumed decommissioning liabilities. Capital: $20-50M equity for first site plus project debt (est.). Time to $100M revenue: about 3 years at 2-3 sites (est.). Ceiling comparables: Vistra, NRG, Talen and Constellation (IPP market caps of tens of billions, est.).
ai_role: AI does four jobs. (1) Underwriting the long tail: it ingests EIA-860 data, ISO queue data, retirement notices, plant permits and transmission studies to rank every unit in the US by repower value and interconnection headroom. This is per-deal labour that today only big IPPs staff (P2, P7). (2) Reverse compilation of the plant: decades of paper drawings, P&IDs, turbine overhaul records and boiler inspection reports become a digital plant model in weeks, so repower engineering and permitting packages can be drafted for each site (P1, P4). (3) A steam-turbine parts library for 1960s-90s GE, Westinghouse and Allis-Chalmers units, reverse-engineered as in P12. (4) Control retrofits and fleet tuning: new controls on old units for ramp rate and minimum load (P8), with operating telemetry as the evidence for capacity accreditation (P9).
main_killer: First rungs are held by funded players and sellers price in hope. Vistra, NRG, Constellation, PE (Knighthead, LS Power) and hyperscalers are all hunting coal sites. DOE 202(c) orders and utilities keep some coal plants open. Sites carry environmental liabilities (ash ponds, CCR rules).
ai_answer_to_killer: Go where the big buyers cannot look economically: the hundreds of 50-400 MW co-op, muni and small-IPP units across PJM, MISO and SERC. AI makes per-site diligence close to zero marginal cost, so the startup can screen and bid on every one, beating PE's analyst throughput. Structure the deal as a rights purchase plus a liability-assumption contract where sellers (co-ops facing closure costs) value relief from ash-pond and decommissioning liabilities more than price. AI-driven environmental characterisation and remediation planning prices those liabilities better than the seller can. 202(c) is an upside: units kept running preserve their rights while the repower is prepared.
competitors: IPPs: Vistra, NRG, Constellation, Talen. PE and developers: LS Power, Knighthead (Homer City), Hull Street Energy, Earthrise Energy (coal-to-clean). Hyperscalers buying sites directly. Utilities self-repowering. Renewable developers using surplus interconnection at coal sites. Nuclear site developers (TerraPower's Kemmerer coal site).
principles_used: P6 and P12 (own the right to substitute: the interconnection is the interface), P14 (owner-operator is its own gate inside the fence), P8 (control-layer uplift on orphaned assets), P9 (operating history for capacity accreditation), P2 (an AI-built library for an orphaned steam fleet)

score.name: Gridright: an interconnection-rights fleet that buys retiring coal and steam plants for their grid rights and repowers them with gas
score.rationale: Web search budget was used up, so I could not run fresh checks. The cited facts (FERC acceptance of the PJM Replacement Generation fast track in Jan 2026, the capacity price cap of $333/MW-day, the Homer City redevelopment) match what was publicly reported. Arithmetic check: 200 MW x $333.44 x 365 = about $24.3M a year, which confirms the capacity claim. N: boiler gas conversion at $50-200/kW clearing a capped capacity price gives very high site IRRs, and project debt is standard. T: a conversion takes 12-18 months, and 2-3 sites reach $100M in about 3 years. C: IPP comparables (Vistra, Constellation, Talen) are tens of billions; a 5-10 GW rollup credibly passes $1B, and $10B+ would need much more scale, so 4. A: AI long-tail underwriting, digitising paper plant records and pricing liabilities is plausible lift on per-deal labour. But AI is not what makes the pain solvable; the FERC rule and capital are. AI only partly answers the killer (competition for sites), because sellers price in hope and co-ops now know their interconnection is valuable. D: interconnection rights are a permission that cannot be copied once owned. That fits the 'own the permission' law well, though each site must be won in competition first.
score.biggest_risk: Sellers price in hope. Since Homer City and the capacity prices at the cap, co-ops, munis and small IPPs know their rights are worth $100s/kW, and Vistra, NRG, LS Power, PE and hyperscalers bid aggressively. 202(c) orders, CCR ash-pond liabilities and capacity-price reform or cap changes could compress returns.

name: Orphan Silicon Works: the qualified foundry for obsolete military electronics
one_liner: An owned, trusted production line that decompiles obsolete circuit cards, ASICs and avionics boxes into modern form-fit-function replacements (re-synthesised onto current FPGAs and parts) and owns the resulting TDPs, approvals and the only qualified source.
sector: Defence and aerospace sustainment (DMSMS, obsolete electronics)
what_it_owns: A characterised, frozen manufacturing target: the 'PDK for legacy electronics', a qualified board-and-module line (IPC-A-610 Class 3, AS9100, DMEA Trusted Accreditation, ITAR). It also owns a growing library of FFF replacement designs with company-generated data rights, since they are clean-room re-implementations, not copies of OEM data. Over time it holds DLA source approvals and QPL/QML listings on those part numbers, plus last-time-buy die and component inventory. It sells the physical part, not engineering services.
wedge_first_revenue: Begin with buyers who can approve the replacement themselves, so the DLA queue is not on the critical path: (a) contractor-operated and civil-registered operators of ex-military types (including Ghost Wing-style fleets), (b) foreign military users of US-origin platforms, whose national airworthiness authority approves, (c) Navy and Army engineering support activities using emergency or Section 803-style FFF substitution for parts with zero bids, and (d) OEM primes with DMSMS line-stoppages, who buy a qualified replacement module for their own program. First revenue is a replacement CCA or LRU on a known-dead part with long backorders, at a fixed unit price.
ladder: 1) 20-50 high-pain FFF boards for operators who self-approve. 2) Submit the same designs as DLA alternate-source and SAR packages; AI-drafted packages let it file hundreds a year, so the queue runs in parallel. 3) An 'emulation core' family: a few qualified FPGA/SoC modules that emulate thousands of dead legacy chips (the Phoenix BIOS move for avionics), each a frozen, characterised target. 4) Program-level DMSMS sustainment contracts (performance-based logistics) for whole avionics suites. 5) The default second source for legacy US and allied electronics, the HEICO of defence electronics.
numbers: Pain: obsolescence costs the US military 'hundreds of millions of dollars each year' by older DoD-linked estimates (https://acqnotes.com/acqnote/careerfields/diminishing-manufacturing-sources-and-material-shortages), and that undercounts readiness loss. The F/A-22 alone ran about $100M/yr of DMS management (https://www.navsea.navy.mil/Portals/103/Documents/NSWC_Crane/SD-18/PDFs/Resources/ResourcesDMSMS.pdf). Virginia-class logged about 1,440 DMSMS issues since 2001 (https://www.dsp.dla.mil/Portals/26/Documents/Publications/Journal/140701-DSPJ-01.pdf). Sole-source pricing: DoD IG found TransDigm part profits from 17% to over 4,000%, with more than 75% of its net sales sole-source (https://fortune.com/2019/05/15/transdigm-pentagon-gouging ; https://www.bloombergquint.com/business/pentagon-rips-transdigm-for-gouging-with-4-361-half-inch-pin). Addressable market (est.): legacy defence electronics spares and repair at about $15-25B/yr globally. Unit economics (est.): an FFF board sells at $5-50k with 50-65% gross margin. AI cuts per-design engineering from about $150-500k to about $20-60k, so break-even falls to about 20-50 units per design. Capital: $15-30M for a trusted SMT and test line plus a reverse-engineering lab (est.). Time to $100M revenue: about 5-7 years with 1,000+ designs in the library (est.). Ceiling comparables: HEICO Electronic Technologies Group; Rochester Electronics (private, largest authorised EOL semi source); TransDigm's sole-source model.
ai_role: Reverse compilation is the core of the business. X-ray CT and delayering produce netlists. ML infers behaviour from in-circuit test captures. LLM and HDL agents re-synthesise legacy logic (TTL, PALs, dead ASICs) onto current FPGAs, and AI generates equivalence test benches that run the old box and the new box side by side over millions of vectors. Electronics is the one sustainment domain where software's cheap verification partly survives: the replacement can be checked by running it. AI also writes SAR, alternate-source and qualification packages at volume and ranks the 5M+ DLA NSNs by backorder pain and price gap. Laws used: P1 (own the frozen target), P4 (checking cheaper than changing), P6 and P12 (interface clone plus owned approval), P7 (signed equivalences).
main_killer: The gatekeeper queue: DLA source approval takes 12-18 months per part, and engineering support activities are understaffed. OEM primes defend data rights and may push programs to refuse non-OEM boards. Volume per part number is tiny.
ai_answer_to_killer: Don't wait on one queue. Sell first to buyers who are their own approver (contractor operators, foreign militaries, primes with line-down problems), and file AI-generated alternate-source packages in bulk so hundreds of approvals mature in parallel; the queue is a pipeline, not a wall. Solve the volume problem with emulation-core modules: one qualified hardware platform reconfigured in firmware for many dead parts, so qualification evidence on the platform carries over and each new part needs only a functional equivalence proof. Clean-room reimplementation from behaviour avoids OEM data rights, and the 2025-26 DoD push on right-to-repair and data rights in acquisition reform works in its favour.
competitors: Rochester Electronics (EOL semis), GDCA, Spectrum Control, Mercury Systems, Cyient/Teledyne repair, HEICO ETG, and the OEMs' own obsolescence groups. Government depots (NSWC Crane, Warner Robins) reverse-engineer in-house. Startups: Firestorm ($82M reported, unverified, additive), and Hadrian ($1.37B at $7.9B, Aug 2026) in metal parts, not electronics (https://thenextweb.com/news/hadrian-1-37bn-series-d-7-87bn-defence-factories).
principles_used: P1, P4, P6, P7, P12 (also P13 portable recipes)

score.name: Orphan Silicon Works: the qualified foundry for obsolete military electronics
score.rationale: Search budget exhausted, so this relies on the cited DoD IG/TransDigm, F-22 DMS and Virginia-class DMSMS sources plus prior knowledge. It owns the physical part, the clean-room TDP library and the approvals, which fits the 'permission + evidence' monopoly law. Capital is low ($15-30M), and AI cutting per-design NRE from about $150-500k to about $20-60k makes 20-50 unit break-evens viable (N4). Electronics is the one sustainment domain where equivalence can be checked by running old and new boxes side by side over millions of vectors, so AI really does both the reverse compilation and the verification evidence (A4). It sidesteps the DLA-queue law by selling first to self-approving buyers (foreign MAAs, contractor operators, primes with lines down) and running alternate-source filings as a parallel pipeline. T3: first revenue within 2 years is plausible, but $100M by year 7 needs about 1,000 designs and the DLA approvals to mature, which is tight. The ceiling uses HEICO ETG/TransDigm-style sole-source comparables, credibly $1B+ and arguably more (C4). D4: each approved part number becomes a sole-source annuity that compounds, and the emulation-core platform carries its evidence across parts. Incumbents (GDCA, Lansdale, Innovasic, Rochester) are fragmented and not AI-native.
score.biggest_risk: Revenue per part number is tiny and DLA/ESA approvals still gate the larger government market. If self-approving buyers prove too small, the ramp to $100M stalls behind the 12-18 month queue.

name: Keel Forge: an AI-characterised naval castings and forgings foundry, bought, not built
one_liner: Acquire PE-held or family-owned foundries and forge shops that already hold NAVSEA and prime approvals, turn each into an AI-characterised 'frozen target' with in-situ process signatures, and own the scarce capacity for the large castings and forgings that gate submarine, ship and ground-vehicle repair.
sector: Defence sustainment (naval and ground-vehicle hot-section and structural castings and forgings)
what_it_owns: The scarce physical capacity (melt shops, presses, heat-treat, NDT). The approvals and qualified-supplier status that come with the acquired plants (NAVSEA Level I/SUBSAFE-adjacent, ASME, prime AVLs). A process design kit per plant: published design rules and ML process signatures that make each line a characterised, compilable target. A library of patterns and recipes for out-of-production repair and spare castings.
wedge_first_revenue: Revenue starts on day one by buying a foundry or forge with an existing defence backlog. The AI wedge is yield and cycle time: solidification simulation, gating and risering design, and in-process sensing to cut scrap and rework on large steel, bronze and nickel-aluminium-bronze castings where first-pass yield is poor. That raises throughput from capacity already approved, so no new approval is needed.
ladder: 1) Acquire one approved foundry and raise yield and on-time delivery. 2) Roll up 3-6 more (hundreds of US foundries have closed and many are founder- or PE-owned), so pattern and recipe libraries move across plants under one quality system (P13 portable recipes). 3) Open a 'MOSIS for castings' service: the Navy's maintenance centres and primes send repair-part designs to a published design-rule target and get qualified castings in weeks. 4) Own spare and rotable inventory of long-lead castings and sell them on availability contracts to the public shipyards and depots. 5) The TSMC of large metal parts for defence.
numbers: Pain: submarine and ship maintenance is late largely because of long-lead castings and forgings; lead times of about 2-3+ years on large castings are reported (est.). Congress has put est. $10B+ into the submarine industrial base since about 2018. The Abrams fleet's maintenance cost rose $181.3M from FY2015 to FY2023 (https://www.gao.gov/products/GAO-26-108113 ; https://news.usni.org/2025/09/25/gao-report-on-weapon-system-sustainment). US foundries: about 1,700 operating, down from more than 3,000 decades ago (est.). Asset prices: small foundries often trade at about 4-7x EBITDA (est.). Unit economics (est.): defence castings sell at $20-80/lb against commodity at $3-10/lb, and AI-driven yield gains of 10-20 points flow almost directly to margin. Capital: $30-80M for the first acquisition plus sensors and simulation, with roll-up debt later (est.). Time to $100M revenue: 2-4 acquisitions, about 3-5 years (est.). Ceiling comparables: PCC (bought by Berkshire for $37B, est.); Hadrian ($1.37B at about $7.9B, Aug 2026, https://seekingalpha.com/news/4627869-defense-startup-hadrian-raises-1_37b-at-7_9b-valuation-amid-pentagon-demand) for machining, which shows the appetite; TSMC's model of owning the characterised process.
ai_role: AI is the process compiler and characteriser. Solidification and forging simulation with ML surrogates design gating and dies in hours. Multimodal in-process sensing (thermal, ultrasonic, X-ray CT reading) gives each part a signature and turns sampled inspection into 100% evidence. Craft capture records master moulders' and heat-treaters' know-how and trains new hires in months (P11). LLMs draft first-article, PQR/WPS and traceability packages at near-zero marginal cost. Scan-to-pattern recreates out-of-production castings from worn parts. Laws used: P1 (own the frozen target), P3 (own pooled scarce capacity), P11 (abundant builders need qualified cells), P13 (recipe plus envelope).
main_killer: New qualification takes years, and there is a labour shortage of skilled foundry workers. The business is capital-intensive with thin historical margins, and PE sellers price in hope. AI also helps incumbents such as PCC and Arconic-class players.
ai_answer_to_killer: Buy approvals instead of earning them: acquisition inherits the plant's existing qualifications, so the regulator queue does not apply to the base business; new approvals are only extensions. Thin margins come from scrap, rework and late delivery, which are the per-unit labour and yield problems AI does fix. Ten to twenty points of yield on a sold-out, approval-gated market is the margin. The labour shortage is answered by craft capture and robotic finishing (P11, the Hadrian 60-90 day ramp pattern). Against incumbents, roll up the long tail of small approved plants that large players ignore. Avoid hope-priced sellers by targeting distressed and succession-driven plants, where yield upside is largest.
competitors: PCC (Berkshire), Arconic/Howmet, Bradken, Ellwood Group, Lehigh Heavy Forge, ATI, Scot Forge, Navy-funded efforts such as the BlueForge Alliance, and AI-native machining/manufacturing startups (Hadrian, Divergent, Freeform, Foundry Lab) that mostly avoid large castings.
principles_used: P1, P3, P11, P13 (also P4 delta qualification)

score.name: Keel Forge: an AI-characterised naval castings and forgings foundry, bought, not built
score.rationale: Search budget exhausted. From prior knowledge, multi-year lead times on large naval castings, the BlueForge/submarine industrial base funding and the PCC ($37B Berkshire) comparable are all well supported. It fits the hardware-monopoly law directly: scarce physical capacity plus approvals, bought rather than earned, which also sidesteps the gatekeeper queue. Acquisition gives day-one revenue (T5), and $100M through 2-4 acquisitions within 3-5 years is believable. N3: the first acquisition needs $30-80M of equity or debt before product-market proof, which is awkward at YC stage. Sellers price in hope, and AI yield gains of 10-20 points are optimistic for large steel and NAB castings. A3: AI clearly addresses scrap, rework, gating design and paperwork (per-unit labour, per the laws). The skilled-labour shortage and requalifying extended approvals are only partly answered by craft capture. C4: the PCC/Howmet comparables make $10B conceivable, but a roll-up of small plants supports $1-5B more credibly. D4: approved melt and press capacity in a sold-out market is hard to copy, and recipes and patterns carry across plants. Re:Build-style roll-ups and PE are competing buyers.
score.biggest_risk: Execution is a PE-style industrial roll-up with heavy upfront acquisition capital and labour constraints. If AI yield gains come in at 3-5 points rather than 10-20, the business reverts to a thin-margin foundry purchased at hope prices.

name: Stampworks: an AI-native, code-stamped robotic fabrication foundry
sector: Robotics + heavy fabrication (energy and defence hardware)
one_liner: Build owned robotic welding and machining cells that hold the code stamps (ASME U/S/R, AWS D1.1, AISC, later NAVSEA/DLA approval) and run AI-compiled weld and process recipes. They produce the welded hardware the energy build-out is short of (pressure vessels, heat exchangers, transformer tanks, HRSG modules, skids, structural modules) and sell the stamped products, not the robots.
what_it_owns: The stamps and qualified procedures (WPS/PQRs, which under ASME Section IX belong to the qualifying organisation and cannot travel to another company). It also owns the robotic cells and plants, the per-weld sensor record (arc audio, thermal, weld-pool video, in-line NDE) that serves as the evidence for every joint, and its own product designs: standard skids and modules (the 'fabless product' layer on top of its own foundry).
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1: one plant with 6-10 robotic cells and an ASME U-stamp, building standard pressure vessels, air receivers and skids for data-centre cooling, gas-gen and battery-plant developers. The pitch is a 6-12 week lead time against est. 6-18 months at legacy shops, at equal or lower price, with a full digital weld record. First revenue is est. $5-10M; vessels and skids are high-ticket ($50k-1M each).
ladder: 1) ASME vessels and skids. 2) Transformer tanks and enclosures, where transformer lead times have run into years (est. 2-4 years for large units, per industry reports in 2024-25), as a supplier to transformer makers and later as an owned transformer product line. 3) Modular power and cooling packages for data centres as the company's own products. 4) Defence: NAVSEA-certified welding for shipbuilding and submarine-industrial-base modules, a severe shortage. 5) Nuclear: N-stamp and NQA-1 modules for SMR builders. Each rung adds a stamp, which is a permission moat.
numbers: US welder gap about 400,000 (https://seedtable.com/companies/path-robotics/funding-rounds/series-d-2024-10). Market (est.): US pressure vessel and heat exchanger fabrication $15-25B/yr, transformer market $60B+ globally, and US naval shipbuilding spend about $30-40B/yr (all est.). Unit economics (est.): a robotic cell at $0.5-1M producing the arc-on time of 3-5 welders across 3 shifts, with 25-35% EBITDA on stamped products versus 10-15% at legacy shops. Capital: est. $20-40M for plant 1 (could be an acquired, already-stamped shop for $5-15M, which also buys the stamp and history), $100-200M for 4-5 plants. To $100M revenue: est. 4-5 years with 3 plants. Ceiling comparables: Hadrian (AI-native defence machining, venture-funded; raised about $260M in 2025, est.), Protolabs (owns the factory and its design rules), and Chart Industries (about $4B revenue, est.) as the stamped-equipment product comparable.
ai_role: (1) Recipe compiler: AI generates weld procedures and robot paths from the drawing and the code, and predicts distortion, so each new part number needs hours rather than weeks of a welding engineer's time. (2) Craft capture: sensor-instrumented welding plus ML records master welders' technique and runs it on robots, and lets novices supervise cells (the Hadrian 60-90-day ramp: https://jobs.lever.co/hadrian/8ef79201-2683-4d46-831d-2887407e9ebb). (3) Per-weld evidence: in-line vision and ultrasonic inspection give 100% weld records instead of spot radiography, which cuts repair rates and, over time, gives the Authorized Inspector a documented basis for trusting the process. (4) AI drafts the quality-manual documentation, PQRs, MTR traceability and data reports per vessel.
main_killer: Stamps and customer approvals (utility approved-vendor lists, NAVSEA, N-stamp) take years and require history. Heavy fabrication is low-margin and capital intensive, buyers are conservative, and robotic welding of thick, heavy, low-volume weldments is hard because fit-up varies.
ai_answer_to_killer: Buy an already-stamped fabrication shop (many family-owned shops are for sale as owners retire), which gives day-one stamps, AVL listings and history. This is the 'buy your approvals' move, like buying an ODA. AI vision with adaptive seam tracking handles fit-up variation, which is what made low-volume heavy weldments resistant to robots. Margin comes from owning standard products and from lead-time scarcity: buyers pay for months saved when a data centre or power plant is waiting. Each acquired shop's AVL listings carry over to the AI cells, which keeps qualification time inside the acquisition timeline rather than the regulator's queue.
competitors: Legacy ASME fabricators (thousands of small shops; Chart, Alfa Laval for heat exchangers), Path Robotics and other AI-welding robot sellers (tool vendors), Hadrian and Re:Build Manufacturing (an acquisition-led roll-up of manufacturers), Machina Labs (robotic sheet forming), and shipyard and submarine supplier programmes. Funding figures not re-verified this run except Path.
principles_used: P11 (abundant builders; own the qualified cell and the stamp), P13 (portable recipes, certification bound to the organisation), P4 (per-weld evidence as delta qualification), P1 (frozen target with design rules), P14 (buy the gate)

score.name: Stampworks: an AI-native, code-stamped robotic fabrication foundry
score.rationale: Not searched this run (budget used up); figures recalled. The strongest of the five. Buying an already-stamped family shop for $5-15M gives day-one revenue, an ASME U/R stamp, AVL listings and history, so first revenue arrives in year 1 and the gatekeeper-queue law is avoided by acquisition. Lead-time scarcity is real for transformer tanks (recalled transformer lead times of 2-4+ years), HRSG modules and data-centre and gas-gen skids. Vessels and skids are high-ticket, which supports $100M by about year 5 with 3-4 plants. The ceiling is credible: Chart Industries was bought by Baker Hughes for about $13.6B in 2025 (recalled), naval shipbuilding pull is severe, and N-stamp modules for SMRs add an upside rung. AI answers the two killers that matter: adaptive seam tracking and recipe compilation for variable fit-up in low-volume heavy weldments, and acquisition for approvals. Defensibility is only a 3. The U-stamp itself is common (thousands of holders, obtainable in about a year), so the moat must come from the NAVSEA/N-stamp rungs, owned product designs and the per-weld evidence record. Re:Build and Hadrian-style funded roll-ups can copy the play. Heavy fabrication margins and the integration risk of acquired shops are real.
score.biggest_risk: It turns into a low-margin job-shop roll-up (the Re:Build pattern). The cheap lower-rung stamps give little moat until the NAVSEA and N-stamp rungs land.

name: Gridiron: a resurrection fleet for data-centre electrical gear
sector: Data-centre physical infrastructure: medium-voltage power train (transformers, switchgear, UPS, gensets)
one_liner: Buy decommissioned and stranded transformers, switchgear, UPS and gensets. Use AI to turn each unit back into a full test-and-design record, remanufacture it, put our own warranty and captive insurance behind it, and rent it out by the MW-month to AI builders stuck in 2-4 year equipment queues.
what_it_owns: The fleet itself: re-certified MV power blocks (transformer + switchgear + UPS skids, 2.5-10 MW each). Also the per-serial-number evidence record (test history, telemetry, remanufacture traceability), our own NRTL field-evaluation and warranty history, and the captive insurance cell that carries the risk. Customers rent, Gridiron keeps title. This is the United Rentals / Aggreko position for the scarcest iron in AI.
wedge_first_revenue: Bridge power-train rentals to neoclouds, crypto-to-AI conversions and second-tier colos that hold a utility feed but have no transformer or switchgear for 18-36 months. First deal: rent 2-4 re-certified 2.5-3 MVA pad-mount transformer + switchgear skids at a premium MW-month rate on 12-36 month terms. Supply comes from retired enterprise data centres, closed factories, crypto mines and utility surplus yards. First revenue in about 6-9 months: rewind and re-test is weeks, and a UL field label is per-unit labour, not an 18-month queue.
ladder: 1) Pad-mount and dry-type distribution transformers plus LV switchgear (easiest to test and field-label). 2) UPS and battery plant, and diesel/gas gensets (UL 2200 field evaluation). 3) MV switchgear and substation transformers up to 30-80 MVA, with an owned rewind and repair shop: the scarce physical capacity, and our 'foundry'. 4) A standard rentable '10 MW power block' API: any site gets a characterised, insured power train in weeks. 5) Asset-backed securitisation of the rental book once there are 24-36 months of availability history (P10). At that point the company is a lessor-operator of grid-edge iron with the lowest cost of capital in the category.
numbers: Lead times: distribution transformers about 2 years and large power transformers about 2-4 years (80-210 weeks); transformer prices up about 60-80% since 2020 (NREL, Major Drivers of Long-Term Distribution Transformer Demand, Feb 2024, https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87653.pdf; figures from prior knowledge, verify). Demand: hyperscaler capex about $400B in 2025 and est. $550-650B in 2026. Electrical M&E is est. 15-25% of the roughly $10-13M/MW all-in build cost, so about $2-3M/MW (est.). At est. 30-50 GW of US data-centre additions to 2030, the electrical-gear pool is roughly $60-150B (est.). Unit economics (est.): a used 2.5 MVA transformer plus switchgear skid costs about $80-150k to acquire, plus $60-120k to remanufacture and test, against roughly $400-700k new with a 2-year wait. Renting at est. $8-15k per MW-month gives a 12-24 month payback, and 3-5 rental cycles over a 30-year life. Capital: est. $15-30M seed/A for the first 100 MW of fleet plus a rewind shop. Asset debt after 24 months. Time to $100M revenue: est. 4-5 years (about 700-1,000 MW on rent). Ceiling comps: United Rentals ($16.1B 2025 revenue, $22.5B fleet at OEC, per project notes); Aggreko (taken private by TDR/I Squared for about GBP 2.3B in 2021, prior knowledge); Eaton bought Fibrebond, a modular power-enclosure maker, for about $1.4B in 2025 (prior knowledge, verify).
ai_role: AI does the decompiling (P1/P12). From nameplates, scanned drawings, dissolved-gas analysis, frequency-response analysis, power-factor/tan-delta tests, thermal imaging and the unit's history, it rebuilds a technical data package and a remaining-life model for each serial number. That is the same 'AI-built parts library' move as the turbine fleet, applied to the scarcest gear in AI. It also: (a) checks substitutions, so any customer's single-line diagram can be built from whatever units sit in inventory (the 'hardware lockfile', P7); (b) drafts the NRTL field-evaluation dossier, the arc-flash study and commissioning paperwork per unit, which is per-unit labour that AI does fix; (c) runs fleet telemetry that turns operating hours into evidence an insurer can price (P9/P14); (d) triages thousands of liquidation listings, auctions and utility surplus lists to find mispriced units.
main_killer: Two problems. First, supply: good used MV gear is thin, utilities hoard spares, and once the gear shortage is publicised, brokers 'price in hope' (law 2). Second, buyers: hyperscalers will not put refurbished gear in a Tier III critical path, and the shortage may ease by 2028-29 once Hitachi, Siemens Energy, Eaton and Hyundai capacity comes online.
ai_answer_to_killer: Supply: do not depend on finding used units. Use AI-designed rewinds and re-cores of failed and obsolete transformers (the core tank and steel are reusable, while windings, bushings and tap changers are the failure points), so failed units become feedstock. AI-based remanufacture design is what turns scrap transformers into fleet. Buyers: start with the many neoclouds, sovereign-AI builds and behind-the-meter projects that price speed over pedigree. Give our own availability guarantee backed by a captive insurer, priced from per-unit telemetry (the HSB 1866 model, P14), so the customer never carries refurbishment risk. Shortage ending: rental fleets earn more when demand is correlated and lumpy (P3, break 3). After the shortage the same fleet serves emergency replacement, bridge-to-grid, outage cover and utility storm reserves, which is the Aggreko business, and the owned rewind shop stays scarce capacity either way.
competitors: OEM service arms (Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, ABB, Eaton, Schneider). Transformer remanufacturers and dealers (SPX Transformer Solutions, Sunbelt Solomon (owned by Sunbelt Rentals / Ashtead), Maddox Transformer, ELSCO). Rental power (Aggreko, Sunbelt Rentals Power & HVAC, United Rentals Power, APR Energy). Modular power makers (Fibrebond/Eaton, Vertiv modular). Funding for each not verified in this run.
principles_used: P1 (decompiling hardware is now cheap), P3 (owned pooled capacity rented through an API: 'EC2 for iron'), P7 (substitution resolver), P9/P14 (fleet evidence plus captive risk makes us our own gate), P10 (securitisation sets cost of capital), P12 (break the OEM aftermarket lock).

score.name: Gridiron: a resurrection fleet for data-centre electrical gear
score.rationale: Search budget was exhausted, so this relies on prior knowledge. The NREL and Wood Mackenzie data on 2-4 year transformer lead times and roughly 60-80% price rises since 2020 are well established. This is the closest analogue to the 20/25 turbine resurrection fleet. N: buying at about $80-150k, remanufacturing for $60-120k and renting at about $8-15k per MW-month gives 12-24 month paybacks, and asset debt is available for rental fleets. That is strong. T: rewinding, re-testing and per-unit field labelling are labour, not regulator queues, so 6-12 months to first revenue is credible, and about 700-1,000 MW on rent by year 4-5 is aggressive but plausible. C: the United Rentals and Aggreko comparables support a credible $1B+ outcome, and $10B is a stretch. A: AI rebuilding test-and-design records and remaining-life models per serial number cuts per-unit labour (which the laws say AI fixes). AI-designed re-cores also answer the used-gear supply killer. But remanufacturers already do rewinds without AI, so the AI lift is efficiency, not enablement. D: the owned fleet, the rewind shop as scarce capacity and the captive insurance record compound. Sunbelt Solomon (Ashtead) already runs a large reman-and-rental transformer fleet, and OEM service arms can match it, so D is 3, not 4. Passes narrowly at 19 with no leg below 3.
score.biggest_risk: Sunbelt Solomon and the OEMs already own the reman-and-rental position with balance sheets far larger than Gridiron's. Hyperscalers also refuse refurbished gear in critical paths, so if the shortage eases by 2028-29 the fleet is left with low-margin emergency rentals.

name: RAID Power: a redundant array of inexpensive engines, an owned firm-power fleet built from mass-produced gas engine modules
sector: Gas and steam power generation: distributed firm power (reciprocating gas engines) for data centers and industry
one_liner: Do to the heavy-frame gas turbine what Google's commodity servers did to the mainframe. Own thousands of hot-swappable 0.5-2 MW natural-gas engine modules built on high-volume engine blocks, orchestrated by software into N+k firm-power plants, and sell guaranteed firm power, not boxes.
what_it_owns: The fleet: generating modules, sites, air permits and gas interconnects. A central robotic remanufacturing depot, the 'factory' that maintenance becomes. Long-term firm-power and capacity contracts. And the fleet's operating-history dataset, which sets its cost of debt (P10). Reliability is a property of the array and its software, not of any one machine, so the company is the approver of its own availability guarantee.
wedge_first_revenue: Bridge and behind-the-meter power for 20-100 MW data-center and industrial loads stuck in 5-7 year interconnection queues, billed as $/MW-month capacity plus a fuel pass-through. First 10-20 MW use bought-in gensets on modern heavy-duty natural-gas truck and industrial engine blocks with three-way-catalyst aftertreatment, deployed within 6-9 months against 12-18 months for large reciprocating engines and 5+ years for frames. Year-1 revenue is roughly $5-15M (est.).
ladder: 1) Bridge power fleets. 2) Permanent behind-the-meter firm power with heat recovery to absorption chillers. 3) Its own standardised 'frozen target' module design, sourcing blocks from automotive-scale lines so Wright's law applies (P5). 4) Grid capacity resource: aggregated arrays bid into PJM/ERCOT capacity and reserve markets. 5) Fuel-flexible modules (hydrogen blends, RNG) and export to emerging-market grids as 'power in a container'. 6) Securitised firm-power contract book at infrastructure spreads.
numbers: Shortage: global turbine orders of 110 GW against 60-70 GW of capacity, six-year lead times, equipment prices heading to about $600/kW (+195% since 2019) (https://www.power-eng.com/gas/turbines/gas-turbine-prices-climb-195-as-supply-crunch-reshapes-power-development/). Recent US combined-cycle projects cost about $2,000/kW (https://www.publicpower.org/periodical/article/new-report-finds-rising-cost-new-gas-plants-outpacing-planning-assumptions). Large reciprocating engines quote 12-18 months against 5+ years for heavy frame (https://www.marketsandmarkets.com/Market-Reports/data-center-onsite-behind-the-meter-power-market-129738654.html). Caterpillar's backlog is about $63B, its large-engine backlog is up 3.5x since January 2024, and it plans to triple capacity (https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/08/03/caterpillars-order-backlog-hit-a-record-63-billion/ ; https://www.manufacturingdive.com/news/caterpillar-triple-power-generation-capacity-raises-2030-targets-q1-2026-earnings/). Hyperscale orders for engine-based power are now 400-800 MW each, e.g. Wärtsilä 412 MW in Ohio and 790 MW in Texas, and Everllence 480 MW (https://pgjonline.com/news/2026/april/waertsilae-to-supply-412-mw-of-gas-fired-power-for-us-data-center ; https://www.modernpowersystems.com/news/everllence-secures-480-mw-gas-engine-contract-for-us-hyperscale-data-centre/). Grid interconnection averages about 5 years (https://www.pew.org/de/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/02/09/to-harness-power-plants-unused-capacity-states-can-turn-to-surplus-interconnection-service). Unit economics (all est.): installed cost $600-900/kW for an array of volume modules against $1,200-2,000/kW for large reciprocating engines or CCGT. Contract price $25-40/kW-month for firm capacity plus fuel; about 25-35% unlevered project IRR in a supply-short market, converging to 12-15%. Capital: $1M-ish per MW (est.); project debt after 24-36 months of history. Time to $100M revenue: about 3-4 years (est.) at roughly 150-250 MW contracted. Ceiling comparables: Bloom Energy (owned and leased firm power for data centers, market cap tens of billions in 2026, est.), Enchanted Rock, United Rentals, Aggreko (bought for about £2.3B in 2021).
ai_role: AI does four jobs. (1) Fleet orchestration as the 'scheduler', the RAID controller: it dispatches modules for load-following, keeps N+k redundancy and rotates wear so the array delivers higher availability than any single unit (P3, P8). (2) Per-module self-models: ML on vibration, exhaust and oil analysis predicts failures and triggers a hot swap before an outage, turning maintenance from field labour into a scheduled swap plus depot remanufacture (P9). (3) Craft capture in the depot: AI-guided teardown, inspection and rebuild at line speed (P11). (4) Evidence and finance: telemetry becomes the availability record that lenders and insurers price, compressing the cost of capital (P10, P14). It also automates air-permit modelling and paperwork across many sites.
main_killer: Physics and permits. Small engines run at about 35-40% electrical efficiency against about 45-50% for large reciprocating engines and about 60% for CCGT, so fuel cost per MWh is higher. Many small stacks complicate air permits in nonattainment areas. Maintenance hours per MW scale with module count. Wärtsilä, Caterpillar, Bloom and well-funded developers may out-scale the startup.
ai_answer_to_killer: (a) Efficiency: in data-center behind-the-meter use the comparison is not CCGT but no power for 5 years. Firm power is priced on capacity, and heat recovery to absorption cooling replaces chiller electricity, taking effective efficiency to 60-70% (est.). AI dispatch keeps modules at their best-efficiency point instead of part-loading a big machine. (b) Emissions: rich-burn plus three-way catalyst, truck-style, reaches very low NOx, and AI closed-loop air-fuel control holds it per module. That turns the permit into an advantage, and AI can generate permit modelling for each site in days. (c) Maintenance: the hot-swap plus central robotic remanufacture model converts linear field labour into factory throughput, which is exactly the per-unit labour AI collapses. (d) Incumbents sell boxes with 12-18 month lead times. The startup sells owned output and buys blocks from automotive-scale supply that is not sold out.
competitors: Engine OEMs selling equipment: Caterpillar, Wärtsilä, INNIO Jenbacher, Cummins, Everllence, Rolls-Royce mtu, Generac. Owned and operated firm power: Bloom Energy (fuel cells), Enchanted Rock (gas microgrids), VoltaGrid (Jenbacher-based mobile power), Aggreko, APR Energy, ProEnergy, FTAI Power (CFM56-derived 25 MW units, https://distributionstrategy.com/2026/01/ftai-aviation-moves-into-data-center-power-leveraging-engine-distribution-and-mro-platform/), Mainspring (linear generators).
principles_used: P3 (pooled, owned capacity behind an API), P5 (Wright's law on a standard module), P8 (software-defined fleet performance), P9 (fleet telemetry as evidence), P10 (output-as-a-service as a financing technology), P13 (the module is a container: certify once, deploy anywhere)

score.name: RAID Power: a redundant array of inexpensive engines, an owned firm-power fleet built from mass-produced gas engine modules
score.rationale: Web search budget was used up, so I could not run fresh checks. I judged against the cited figures (Caterpillar's $63B backlog, Wärtsilä/Everllence orders of 400-800 MW, interconnection queues of about 5 years) and prior knowledge of VoltaGrid and Enchanted Rock. N: $600-900/kW installed against capacity at $25-40/kW-month gives fast payback in a market short of supply. The book is project-financeable once it has history. T: bridge power can earn in 6-9 months, and $100M at 150-250 MW in 3-4 years is realistic. C: Bloom, Aggreko and United Rentals make $1B+ credible; $10B+ is less clear, so 4. A: AI orchestration, predictive hot-swap and permit automation are useful, but the pain (no power for 5 years) is solved by any gensets plus capital, not by AI. AI also does not answer the real killer, which is crowded competition and the short life of truck engine blocks on continuous duty. D: this is the weak leg. VoltaGrid (Jenbacher, with large hyperscaler contracts), Enchanted Rock, FTAI Power, ProEnergy, APR and Caterpillar dealers already run owned fleets that sell output. A fleet of commodity modules on short contracts is easy for funded players to copy, and once grid or turbine supply eases the bridge contracts roll off. Fails on D below 3.
score.biggest_risk: There is no moat. Well-funded owned-power players (VoltaGrid, Enchanted Rock, FTAI, Bloom) already sell the same thing at hyperscale. Truck-derived blocks may wear out under 8,000+ hr/yr baseload with high maintenance and fuel cost, and the margin collapses as the turbine and grid shortage eases after 2029-30.

name: Rewound: an owned fleet of resurrected large power transformers, leased by the MVA-year
sector: Electric grid hardware: large power transformers and generator step-up (GSU) units
one_liner: Buy retired, surplus and failed large power transformers and GSUs (coal-plant retirements, failed utility units, cancelled projects). Re-rate and rewind them in an owned, AI-characterised rebuild plant. Keep them as an owned fleet of spares and bridge units that data centres, IPPs, renewables developers and utilities lease by the MVA-month, available in weeks rather than 128+ weeks.
what_it_owns: (1) The fleet: tanks, cores and rebuilt units, owned and leased, never sold by default. (2) The 'transformer PDK', a characterised rebuild process with published design rules, so the AI design compiler can turn any measured core and tank into a valid new rating. (3) The evidence record: factory acceptance tests to IEEE C57, plus dissolved-gas, thermal and partial-discharge telemetry for every unit in service, which lowers the fleet's cost of debt over time. (4) The rebuild plant itself, which is scarce capacity.
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1: buy 5-10 retired GSUs from announced coal or gas retirements, usually priced near scrap or salvage, because operators pay to remove them (est.). Rewind them to the ratings data centres and solar/storage developers need (typically 34.5/138 kV, 50-200 MVA). Lease the first units as bridge transformers to developers whose interconnection depends on a GSU on a 144-160 week lead time. Large-load buyers and IPPs are less conservative than utilities and will pay a premium to save time. First revenue is a reservation fee plus a monthly lease, est. 1.5-2% of the new-unit price per month for bridge terms.
ladder: Rung 1: bridge leases of rewound GSUs to developers and data centres. Rung 2: subscriptions to an owned spare pool for utilities and IPPs, a Grid Assurance-style pool that rents rather than sells at cost. Rung 3: long-term 'firm MVA' leases with availability guarantees and HSB-style insured performance, securitised once there are 24-36 months of fleet history. Rung 4: new-build units made on the same characterised line, using standard frozen designs ('generic' LPTs). Rung 5: own and operate transformation capacity at customer substations (see the Substrate idea). The loop: every unit in service adds telemetry and evidence, which cuts cost of capital, which lets the company buy more cores.
numbers: Shortage: Wood Mackenzie puts average power transformer lead time at 128 weeks and GSUs at 144 weeks (Q2 2025), with GSUs above 160 weeks by early 2026. US 2025 supply deficit is about 30% for power transformers. Prices are up about 77% since 2019. About 80% of LPTs are imported (https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/05/11/u-s-transformer-market/). Remanufactured units ship in about a third of new-unit lead time at about 60-70% of new cost, per RESA, a vendor claim (https://resapower.com/systems/transformers). The installed base is about 12k-30k LPTs, average age 38-40 years on a weak DOE estimate (https://reliamag.com/topics/guides/aging-transformer-fleet-statistics). Ceiling comparable: GE Vernova paid about $5.3B for the 50% of Prolec GE it did not own. Prolec has about $3B revenue at about 25% EBITDA margin, which implies roughly $10.6B EV and about 14x EBITDA (https://isimarkets.com/insights/ge-vernova-to-take-full-control-of-mexico-rooted-prolec-ge-in-usd-5-28bn-deal/). MacLean Power Systems (Blackstone-backed) is acquiring Delta Star for transformers and mobile substations (https://pulse2.com/maclean-power-systems-to-acquire-delta-star-to-expand-power-transformer-and-substation-portfolio). Unit economics (est.): rewinding a 100-200 MVA unit costs about $1.5-3M against a new price of $5-8M. A bridge lease earns about $0.8-1.5M a year per unit. Capital (est.): $30-60M for the rebuild plant and test bay; the fleet is financed with asset-backed debt. Time to $100M revenue (est.): about 100-120 units leased, or a mix of leases and sales, in 5-6 years.
ai_role: Compiler stack (P1). Scan, core-loss and frequency-response tests, and AI forensic teardown characterise each salvaged core and tank. An AI design compiler generates a new winding design, cooling and rating for that specific core against the plant's own characterised rules, work that used to take weeks of senior engineer time per unit. AI drafts FAT plans and test reports. Fleet DGA, thermal and PD telemetry plus learned failure models turn heterogeneous old units into a statistically priced fleet (P9, P10). The resurrection analogue to the gas-turbine idea, applied to a part with no FAA- or NRC-style approver.
main_killer: Utility conservatism and approved-vendor lists. Utilities will not put a 'used' transformer on the bulk grid. Supply of salvageable cores may also be lumpy and mismatched to the ratings in demand (voltage class and impedance are site-specific).
ai_answer_to_killer: Escape the gatekeeper law. Transformers have no federal pre-market approver: acceptance is a witnessed IEEE C57 factory test plus a buyer's specification. So the company is its own approver in the P14 sense, and evidence arrives at test-bay speed. Start with non-utility buyers who pay for time (data centres, IPPs, GSUs for solar and storage). Offer a lease with availability guarantees and insurance-backed performance (P14, HSB model) so the buyer carries no technical risk. On mismatch, the AI re-rating compiler makes each core flexible: it rewinds to the needed voltage and impedance within the core's flux limits, and a large inventory of characterised cores plus fast design makes matching a solvable search problem. Each unit's DGA history is the evidence that eventually gets onto utility vendor lists.
competitors: Remanufacturers selling a service, not owning a fleet: RESA Power, SPX/Waukesha service, Hitachi Energy and Siemens Energy service shops, Northern Transformer, and regional rewinders. Utility spare pools that sell at cost: Grid Assurance (https://kleinmanenergy.upenn.edu/commentary/blog/grid-assurance-llc-to-offer-resiliency-subscriptions-to-major-utilities/) and EEI STEP. Rental fleets of small mobile units: Zeppelin Rentals (bought BEFRA with about 70 mobile transformers, https://transformer-technology.com/zeppelin-rentals-expands-fleet-with-mobile-transformer-acquisition/) and United Rentals. New-build OEMs expanding: Hitachi Energy (more than $1B US investment), Siemens Energy ($421M Charlotte), HD Hyundai, Hyosung, Prolec/GE Vernova.
principles_used: P1 (own the characterised rebuild target), P5 (value goes to the qualified copy plus the installed base), P9 (fleet telemetry becomes evidence), P10 (recurring revenue is a financing technology), P12 (break the OEM lead-time monopoly by clone-and-own), P14 (no external gate, so the company is its own approver).

score.name: Rewound: an owned fleet of resurrected large power transformers, leased by the MVA-year
score.rationale: Web search budget was used up, so I could not run fresh checks. The cited Wood Mackenzie figures (128-week average lead time, 144-160+ weeks for GSUs, a supply deficit of about 30%) and the Prolec deal at $5.3B for 50% match public reporting. N: a $1.5-3M rewind against a $5-8M new unit, leased at $0.8-1.5M a year, pays back in about 2-3 years, and the fleet can carry asset-backed debt. The $30-60M plant is raisable. T: rewinds take months, so lease revenue can start in year 1-2, and 100-120 units in 5-6 years is plausible. C: transformer and mobile-substation businesses (Prolec at about $10.6B EV, United Rentals-style fleets) make $1B+ credible. A: the AI re-rating compiler and forensic characterisation are plausible ways to cut senior-engineer time per unit and make core-to-rating matching a search problem. But rewinding is an established craft, so the AI lift is incremental. The killer is utility approved-vendor lists and the supply of usable cores, which AI only partly addresses. D: the fleet plus test-bay evidence compounds, but RESA, the OEM service shops and the rental fleets (Zeppelin, United Rentals, MacLean/Delta Star) can lease the same rebuilt units. Supply of salvage cores will become competitive once it is seen as valuable. It misses the pass line by 1 point.
score.biggest_risk: Core supply. Retiring coal GSUs are increasingly kept for repowering at the same interconnection (the Gridright thesis), so salvage cores will not be priced at scrap. Mismatches in voltage and impedance limit reuse. New-build capacity from Hitachi, Siemens, Hyundai and Hyosung arriving in 2027-29 may shrink the bridge-lease premium before the fleet history is long enough to get onto utility vendor lists.

name: Isotope Equivalents (the 'HEICO + spares bank' of the nuclear fleet)
sector: Nuclear: operating fleet sustainment
one_liner: An NQA-1 / 10 CFR 50 Appendix B supplier that owns a growing library of commercially dedicated, reverse-engineered equivalents for obsolete safety-related and important-to-safety parts. It holds them as a pooled, fleet-wide spares bank and sells availability, not drawings.
what_it_owns: (1) Its own Appendix B quality program and 10 CFR Part 21 reporting status, which makes it the legally accountable dedicating entity (P14: the gate moves inside the company). (2) The equivalence library: critical-characteristic analyses, test records and TDPs for each part number, per plant application (P7, the 'hardware lockfile'). (3) Physical pooled inventory placed across the fleet (P3, multiplexing rare failures across about 94 US reactors). (4) Operating-history evidence for every installed part (P9).
wedge_first_revenue: Obsolete Class 1E relays, breakers, transmitters, valve and pump internals and I&C cards whose OEM line is gone or quoted at 2-3 year lead times. An Emerson exec says a nuclear-grade valve can take up to 3 years. Reverse-engineer and dedicate on spec in 8-16 weeks, at 30-50% below OEM/replacement-mod cost. First customers are single-unit and merchant owners under SLR (subsequent licence renewal to 80 years), who face 'no-source' parts on emergent outages where a forced-outage day costs about $1M+ (est., 1 GW x 24h x ~$45/MWh). First revenue is per-part sales; the second product is a subscription to the spares bank (guaranteed delivery within X days for a covered part list).
ladder: 1) Dedicated piece parts, sold. 2) Pooled spares-bank subscriptions per unit (recurring revenue, insurance-like). 3) Owned sub-assemblies: valve and actuator rebuild kits, digital replacements for analog modules (Phoenix-BIOS move, P12). 4) Life-of-plant parts agreements for SLR plants to 80 years, plus restarts (Palisades, Duane Arnold, Crane), which need thousands of no-source items. 5) The supply-chain backbone for SMR fleets: reuse the library and dedication machinery to dedicate commercial industrial parts for new builds. This is the largest rung, since every new design hits the shrinking N-stamp/NQA-1 supplier base.
numbers: US nuclear operating cost: $19.38/MWh (of a $31.76/MWh total) in 2023 (NEI, https://www.nei.org/getContentAsset/47fa8caa-9b0d-4029-932c-07f902e82f4f/8d8ff8d6-b2ae-401b-a63c-f6b108e809d2/2024-Costs-in-Context-final.pdf). At ~780 TWh/yr that is ~$15B/yr of US operating spend (est.). Materials and parts at ~15-20% is ~$2.3-3B/yr US (est.) and ~$8-10B globally (est.). Supplier base is shrinking: 'declining number of NQA-1 and ASME N-stamped suppliers' is flagged as a critical constraint (https://opportunityiowa.gov/media/8333/download). Valve lead times up to 3 years (https://emersonautomationexperts.com/?p=44236). Unit economics (est.): AI cuts reverse-engineering plus dedication from about $50-150k to about $10-25k per part number; gross margin ~50-60% on dedicated parts, as HEICO earns on PMA. Capital: ~$15-30M to set up the Appendix B program, a test lab (seismic, EQ, environmental) and initial inventory (est.). Time to $100M revenue: ~5-6 years (about 30% share of no-source and obsolete demand at 10-15 US plants plus spares subscriptions) (est.). Ceiling comparables: HEICO (11,500+ PMAs, market cap well above $16B, https://www.ramapo.edu/rfg/wp-content/uploads/sites/370/2022/06/Heico-Pitch.pdf) and Curtiss-Wright's nuclear segment (est.).
ai_role: AI collapses the per-part labour that kept the long tail undedicated. It does scan/CT-to-CAD, material ID from spectroscopy and microstructure, critical-characteristic selection from failure-mode and application data (EQ, seismic, EMI), drafting of CGD plans and Part 21 evaluations, and active-learning test selection, so the fewest physical tests are run. LLMs mine LERs, OE databases, work orders and obsolescence notices to rank which part numbers to dedicate first. Fleet telemetry and failure data price the spares bank. This takes break-even from the top few percent of part numbers to most of the tail.
main_killer: Ceiling and incumbency. Curtiss-Wright, Framatome, Westinghouse, AtkinsRéalis/Candu, Paragon, NuSource and Park Nuclear already do CGD. Utilities are very conservative and run NUPIC audits. The US market alone may cap near a few hundred million in revenue.
ai_answer_to_killer: This idea escapes the gatekeeper-queue law: individual part dedications do not go through an NRC queue. The licensee accepts them through audit (a joint NUPIC audit is accepted by all utilities), so AI speed turns straight into lead-time advantage. Incumbents dedicate parts as a high-cost project service. AI lets this company dedicate parts speculatively, ahead of demand, and own them as inventory, which incumbents' cost structure cannot match. The ceiling breaks on the SMR rung: every advanced reactor vendor needs thousands of dedicated commercial items and no qualified supply base exists. The same library and dedication engine becomes their supply chain, globally (est. >$1B/yr by the 2030s).
competitors: Curtiss-Wright Nuclear (RAPID database, https://cwnuclear.com/products-and-services/obsolescencesolutions); Framatome; Westinghouse; AtkinsRéalis spare parts (https://www.atkinsrealis.com/~/media/Files/A/atkinsrealis/download-centre/en/brochure/spare-parts-en.pdf); Paragon Energy Solutions (PE-backed); NuSource/Swagelok (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20200227005047/en); Park Nuclear (https://parknuclear.com/?p=937). No AI-native, inventory-owning entrant found.
principles_used: P2 (own the approved equivalent, not the open design), P7 (signed equivalence as a reusable artifact), P12 (break OEM aftermarket locks part by part), P14 (be the accountable dedicating entity), P3/P10 (pooled spares bank as a utility), P9 (operating evidence).

score.name: Isotope Equivalents (the 'HEICO + spares bank' of the nuclear fleet)
score.rationale: Closest match to the one shape that has survived so far, 'be your own approver'. As the dedicating entity under Appendix B and Part 21, the gate sits inside the company, and acceptance runs through a NUPIC audit, not an NRC queue, so AI speed does turn into lead-time advantage. AI cutting per-part reverse-engineering and dedication cost is a plausible per-unit labour fix, and it lets the company dedicate parts ahead of demand and hold them as inventory, which answers the incumbents' cost structure. Time is good: an Appendix B program plus a NUPIC audit takes about 12-18 months, and forced-outage urgency drives early sales. Ceiling is the weak leg. The US parts pool (~$2-3B, est.) is shared with Curtiss-Wright, Framatome, Westinghouse and PE-backed Paragon, and the SMR rung that breaks the ceiling is speculative and timed to new-build schedules. N is fine at part level but needs many SKUs per plant to reach $100M. Defensibility (quality program, audit status, operating evidence, pooled inventory) compounds, but incumbents already hold the same permissions. One point short of a pass. Note: the shared web-search budget ran out before I could run any search, so the key numbers (NEI $19.38/MWh operating cost, valve lead times) were taken from the idea's own citations and were not independently checked.
score.biggest_risk: The ceiling. US fleet sustainment alone caps near a few hundred million in revenue against entrenched CGD incumbents, and the SMR supply-chain rung that makes it $1B+ depends on advanced reactors reaching serial build in the 2030s.

name: HotHour (an engine-hour utility for orphaned mid-life engines)
sector: Commercial aerospace: engines and aftermarket
one_liner: Buy out-of-production engine types cheaply (V2500-A5, CF34-8/10, PW127, later CFM56-5B), keep them flying with a library of PMA parts and DER repairs that AI helps build, and sell engine-hours (power by the hour) to airlines and lessors rather than parts.
what_it_owns: The engine pool and its spare modules (the asset). A Part 145 repair station holding in-house DER delegations, and later an acquired PMA/ODA holder, which makes HotHour its own approver for repairs. A library of PMA parts and DER repairs. A per-serial-number operating-history dataset that lowers its borrowing cost against the pool.
wedge_first_revenue: Year 0-1: buy 10-20 run-out V2500 and CF34 engines and feedstock at teardown prices (est. $1-4M each vs $8-15M for green-time, est.). Part out and sell used serviceable material for cash, then put the best units back together as green-time lease engines. First revenue is USM sales plus short-term engine leases (est. $2-5M ARR within 12 months). DER repairs come before PMAs because a DER-approved repair goes through the repair station's own authority, not the FAA PMA queue.
ladder: 1) USM and green-time engine leasing on 2-3 types. 2) DER repairs (blades, vanes, cases) done in-house, which lowers cost per shop visit. 3) Acquire a small PMA holder or ODA and file PMA parts in volume for the hot section. 4) Power-by-the-hour contracts with regional and low-cost airlines on those types, with HotHour carrying the time-on-wing risk. 5) Securitise the engine pool once it has 24-36 months of telemetry. 6) Expand to more orphaned types (PW4000, CF6-80, military derivatives such as TF33/F108).
numbers: Comparable ceiling: FTAI Aviation Aerospace Products revenue was $1.60B in 2025, up from $1.08B in 2024. Q1 2025 segment adj. EBITDA was about $131M (36% margin), and Q2 2025 was $164.9M on $420.7M. FTAI built 184 CFM56 modules in Q2 2025 and estimates about 9% annualised market share (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1590364/000162828026012940/ftai-20251231.htm ; https://www.itiger.com/news/2555810074). That is one company on essentially one engine family (CFM56/V2500) reaching about $1.6B. HEICO PMA pricing runs at about 70% of OEM list or less (P2 source). Engine MRO market est. $40B+/yr (est.), and the CF34 and V2500 aftermarkets are each est. $3-6B/yr. Capital: est. $30-60M for the first 20-engine pool plus a repair station, then debt-funded. Time to $100M revenue: est. 4-5 years (USM plus leasing alone can reach $100M on about 60-80 engines, est.). Margin target: 30-40% EBITDA, as at FTAI.
ai_role: Reverse compilation (P1, P12): CT/scan to TDP, material ID from metallography, and DER substantiation drafts, so per-repair engineering falls from about $50-200k to about $5-20k (est.) and a long tail of 500+ repairs on niche types becomes economic. Fleet telemetry and borescope vision models predict each serial number's remaining life, which reduces variance in shop-visit cost. Lower variance lets HotHour price power-by-the-hour profitably and borrow more cheaply (P9, P10). Teardown-yield prediction tells it which run-out engines to buy and which to part out.
main_killer: FTAI, AerCap, Willis Lease, HEICO and the OEMs (GE/CFM branded service, P&W) already hold the first rungs. Sellers of run-out engines price in hope. PMA and ODA approvals sit in FAA queues of 6-18 months.
ai_answer_to_killer: Pick the engine types FTAI does not prioritise: CF34 regional, PW127 turboprop, and late military derivatives. HEICO covers those types thinly because PMA volume per part is small. With AI, the per-part engineering cost falls about 10x, so those long-tail parts become worth doing. Use DER repairs (repair-station authority, no PMA queue) for the first 2-3 years, then buy an existing PMA holder or ODA instead of waiting in the queue. AI ranks which run-out engines to buy, so the bid is driven by teardown yield, not hope.
competitors: FTAI Aviation (CFM56/V2500 modules, $1.6B), Willis Lease Finance, AerCap Engines, Kellstrom, AAR, GA Telesis, HEICO (PMA), Chromalloy (repairs), and OEM service networks (GE, P&W, Safran). Several of these are funded or PE-backed.
principles_used: P2, P5, P7, P10, P12, P14 (own the asset, be your own approver via DER and an acquired PMA/ODA, and finance cheaply on fleet history)

score.name: HotHour (an engine-hour utility for orphaned mid-life engines)
score.rationale: Web search budget for this turn was used up, so no number was re-checked live. Scores rest on the cited SEC filing and prior knowledge: FTAI Aerospace Products at about $1.1B in 2024 and about $1.6B in 2025 at roughly 35% margins is consistent with what I know. N4: USM part-out plus green-time leasing is a proven cash-generating model with asset-backed debt, so the part-level IRR closes. T4: USM sales and leases can bring revenue within 12 months, and FTAI shows $100M is reachable on about 60-80 engines. C4: FTAI's own scale makes $1B+ credible; $10B+ needs multiple engine families plus PBH. A3: AI-cheapened DER substantiation and teardown-yield bidding are plausible answers to sellers pricing in hope and to the PMA queue (DER repairs avoid it, and buying an ODA is a known route). But the main killer is capital competition for feedstock against FTAI, AerSale, GA Telesis and the lessors, and AI only partly answers that. V2500 and CFM56-5B are not truly orphaned (large active fleets, hot feedstock market during the GTF groundings), so the claim of a gap that FTAI ignores holds mainly for CF34 and PW127. D3: the pool, the DER/PMA library and per-serial data compound, but incumbents already hold the same kinds of asset and approvals with more capital. Strong, but it falls one point short of 19 because AI is not decisive against the incumbent capital moat.
score.biggest_risk: Feedstock bidding wars with well-capitalised FTAI, AerSale and lessors on the same engine types erase the teardown-price arbitrage before the DER/PMA library has scale.

name: Mainline Silicon: the HEICO of dead control electronics
sector: Semiconductors / electronics: legacy ICs and control-system modules in power plants, refineries, rail and defence-adjacent industrial fleets
one_liner: Own the largest approved library of form-fit-function replacement circuit cards and chips for obsolete control systems (GE Mark IV/V, Westinghouse WDPF, Bailey Infi90, Foxboro I/A, old PLC racks). AI turns each dead card back into a technical data package and an FPGA- or modern-silicon re-implementation, and the company holds the commercial-grade dedication or approval for each part number.
what_it_owns: A library of signed equivalence packages: one per card or chip part number, each carrying its own nuclear 10 CFR 21 commercial-grade dedication, utility approved-vendor listing or IEC 61508 safety case. Also the re-implemented designs, test fixtures (the hardware 'unit tests'), and the field-return and operating-hour record across every installed card. Customers buy the physical card; the company owns the right to substitute it (P2, P6, P7, P12).
wedge_first_revenue: Start with the 50-100 highest-failure cards in GE Mark V and Bailey Infi90 DCS racks still running in US coal, gas and nuclear plants and refineries. Today these are bought from brokers on eBay-grade supply at 5-20x their original price, with no traceability. Sell dedicated, warrantied, traceable drop-ins at roughly 50-70% of the broker price. Non-nuclear industrial buyers need no regulator, only the plant engineer's approval, so first revenue can come in months 6-12 (est.). Nuclear CGD packages follow in year 2, at a higher margin.
ladder: 1) Non-safety industrial DCS and turbine-control cards, about 100 part numbers. 2) Nuclear non-safety, then safety-related cards via in-house CGD, the company acting as its own dedicating entity. 3) Legacy ICs inside those cards (obsolete ASICs, PALs, 5V logic) re-implemented as company-owned 'emulation silicon' on a mature-node shuttle. 4) Rail signalling, water utilities, oil and gas SCADA. 5) Defence DMSMS via DLA source approval, accepting the 12-18 month queue. 6) Long-term supply agreements with fleet owners, the HEICO-style annuity.
numbers: Comparables: HEICO Electronic Technologies Group revenue is about $1.2B+ (FY2024, est. from HEICO 10-K, https://www.heico.com/investors), on a niche-electronics model with 20%+ margins. Rochester Electronics, the authorised aftermarket for discontinued chips, is privately held with an est. $500M+ in revenue (est.). The installed base of legacy DCS and turbine controls in the US is est. tens of thousands of racks. The industrial control-system obsolescence and migration spend is often cited at about $65B globally (ARC Advisory, est.). Unit economics (est.): AI-assisted reverse engineering plus re-implementation at about $20-60k per card part number, against $200k+ manually. Cards sell for about $3-25k each, and one part number typically recovers its engineering cost after 20-50 units. Capital (est.): $8-15M to a 300-part library and first nuclear CGD program, and $40-80M to 3,000 parts. Time to $100M revenue (est.): 6-8 years. Ceiling: HEICO's market cap is above $30B (https://www.heico.com/investors). Note: the web search budget ran out during this run, so figures not taken from the brief are marked est. and need checking.
ai_role: Do in electronics what has been 'decompiling hardware' elsewhere (P1, P12): X-ray/CT and board scans to a netlist; firmware and PAL/GAL fuse-map extraction to behavioural models; LLM-built test benches from OEM manuals; equivalence checking of the old card against the new one on automated test rigs (the hardware CI loop, P4); automatic drafting of CGD critical-characteristic packages and IEC 61508 evidence. AI also ranks which part numbers to build next by failure rate, broker price and installed base. Inside the company this lets one engineer handle about 50 part numbers a year instead of 3-5 (est.).
main_killer: Plant engineers and nuclear QA will not trust a startup card in a control loop that can trip a 1 GW unit. Incumbent migration vendors (Emerson, ABB, GE Vernova) pitch full replacement, and a broker-and-repair long tail (e.g. Radwell, IDS, Spectrum Controls-style shops) already serves the cheap end.
ai_answer_to_killer: Make trust cheap to check, as software did. Every shipped card comes with a bit-for-bit behavioural equivalence record from an AI-built test bench that replays years of the plant's own historian I/O against the old and new cards, plus a burn-in log. Start with non-safety cards, where the plant engineer is the approver. Rather than waiting on a regulator, the company becomes the dedicating entity under 10 CFR 21 and carries the liability, backed by a captive insurance policy priced on its field-return data (P14). The field record across thousands of installed cards becomes the moat. Full DCS migration costs $5-50M per unit and 2-4 years of outages (est.), while a card swap is overnight, so the wedge never has to beat Emerson on a whole system.
competitors: Rochester Electronics (chips, authorised aftermarket, not cards or dedication); Radwell, PLC Center and gray-market brokers (no evidence); Emerson Ovation, ABB, GE Vernova (rip-and-replace migration); Spectrum Controls and Westinghouse/Curtiss-Wright nuclear I&C (dedicated parts, slow); NuclearLogistics/Paragon Energy Solutions (CGD house; Paragon is PE-owned); HEICO ETG (aerospace and defence, not plant controls).
principles_used: P2, P6, P7 (signed equivalence as the asset), P12 (clean-room clone with value moving to the approval holder), P4 (cheap verification via test benches), P14 (be your own gate via CGD plus a captive insurer)

score.name: Mainline Silicon: the HEICO of dead control electronics
score.rationale: Not searched this run (budget used up); figures recalled. HEICO ETG did about $1.2B in FY2024-25 and HEICO's market cap is about $35-40B, which matches the brief. The shape is strong: it owns signed equivalence packages and CGD approvals, it is its own dedicating entity, and it can sell to non-safety industrial plants with no regulator, where broker prices for GE Mark V and Infi90 cards run at many times the original.
