name: Old Interconnect: buy orphaned solar and storage plants for their grid connection
sector: Power electronics (PV inverters, battery PCS, plant controllers) plus energy assets
one_liner: Buy distressed and orphaned utility- and commercial-scale solar plants whose inverter OEM has exited or dropped support (a large share of 2010-2017 builds). Keep them alive with AI-reverse-engineered inverter power stages and controller firmware. Then use the scarce existing grid interconnection to add storage and repower, and sell the firm output.
what_it_owns: The plants and, crucially, their interconnection rights. Existing points of interconnection are the scarcest physical capacity in US power (P3) while new projects sit in years-long queues. It also owns update authority over an orphaned inverter fleet (P8) and an AI-built library of replacement inverter boards, firmware and power modules (P2, P12).
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1: buy 5-20 MW of distressed commercial and small utility PV with dead or orphaned central inverters at a deep discount (est. $0.10-0.30/W against $1.0-1.5/W new-build). Restore availability with AI-diagnosed repairs and re-implemented control boards, and earn existing PPA or merchant revenue immediately. Because the company owns the asset, it is its own approver (P14). There is no regulator gate for inverter repairs behind an existing interconnect agreement, provided the plant stays inside its IEEE 1547 or utility-agreed settings.
ladder: 1) Distressed PV rescue for cash yield. 2) Fleet-wide firmware and control upgrades for +2-5% energy and grid-services capability (P8). 3) Add batteries behind the existing point of interconnection (surplus interconnection service in FERC-jurisdictional markets lets new resources use spare capacity at an existing POI without a full queue study), turning solar into firm capacity paid at PJM and ERCOT scarcity prices. 4) Repower with new modules on the same interconnect. 5) Own-design, generic and repairable inverters and PCS built on the parts library, deployed across the fleet. 6) Securitise the fleet cash flows (P10).
numbers: The LBNL Queued Up report counted about 2,600 GW of generation and storage in US interconnection queues at end-2023, with median time from request to operation of about 5 years (https://emp.lbl.gov/queues, recalled, verify). PJM capacity cleared at the $329-333/MW-day cap for 2026/27 and 2027/28 (from the brief, P3). Inverters are widely reported as the leading cause of PV downtime, often cited at about 40%+ of lost energy or tickets (kWh Analytics Solar Risk Assessment and Raptor Maps reports, est.). Unit economics (est.): a plant bought at $0.2/W restored to 98% availability yields 15-25% unlevered. Adding a 4-hour battery behind an existing POI avoids a 4-5 year queue and network-upgrade costs, worth est. $50-150/kW of interconnection value. Capital: $30-60M of equity for 100 MW, and project debt thereafter. Time to $100M revenue (est.): about 5-7 years with about 700-1,000 MW plus storage. Ceiling comparables: Brookfield Renewable and Clearway-style yieldcos at $5-30B (est.). Note: the web search budget ran out during this run, so numbers are marked est. or recalled.
ai_role: (1) Decompiling dead inverters: board scans to schematic, firmware extraction, and re-implementing control loops and gate-driver boards on modern parts. (2) Per-unit ML tuning from SCADA (P8). (3) Fleet anomaly detection that turns string, IGBT and capacitor failures into predicted swaps (P9). (4) Diligence: AI reads thousands of distressed-asset data rooms, PPAs and interconnection agreements to find plants where surplus POI capacity has the highest value. (5) Automated grid-code compliance evidence for each control change.
main_killer: Is solar too cheap to bother rescuing? New modules cost $0.10-0.25/W and new inverters are cheap, so the repair library may not beat replacement. Sellers of distressed assets also 'price in hope', and funded players (Greenbacker, Altus, PE secondary buyers) hold the first rungs.
ai_answer_to_killer: The asset is not the panels. It is the energised interconnection plus site control, and that is what is underpriced in distressed sales, because sellers value the plant on its legacy PPA cash flow, not on the option to add storage behind its point of interconnection. AI diligence screens thousands of small distressed plants (under 20 MW, too small for PE to diligence manually) for surplus interconnection value: the long tail that funded players skip, like HEICO's niche parts. The inverter library is a cost lever that makes the cheap first rung (keep it alive for $0.02/W instead of a $0.10/W inverter swap) positive while the storage add-on is developed.
competitors: Distressed renewables buyers (Greenbacker, Altus Power, Excelsior, PE secondaries), O&M providers (NovaSource, Clearway O&M), inverter repair shops (Power Electronics service, Ampt, independent central-inverter refurbishers), storage developers using surplus interconnection (e.g. Plus Power, Key Capture-style developers).

A: AI diligence on sub-20 MW long-tail plants and cheap inverter keep-alive are plausible per-unit-labour wins, but the real killer is competition for existing POIs, and AI screening is copyable. D: owned POIs are scarce capacity, but interconnection arbitrage is already a crowded hunt (coal-retirement POIs, PE secondaries); the inverter library is a cost lever, not a moat.

name: Nuclear Generics: a 10 CFR 21 dedicated-equivalents company for valves, pumps and their parts, with an ASME N-stamp line
sector: Industrial machinery and fluid systems: nuclear safety-related valves, pumps, seals, actuators
one_liner: The HEICO/Hatch-Waxman of nuclear fluid systems. It owns a growing library of dedicated, form-fit-function-equivalent valve and pump parts and whole assemblies that it approves itself through commercial-grade dedication. Later it adds an ASME Section III N-stamp line that becomes the frozen 'PDK' for SMR fluid-system modules.
what_it_owns: (1) A library of thousands of commercial-grade dedication (CGD) packages, each tied to a specific application, plus the stocked dedicated parts. (2) Its own 10 CFR 50 Appendix B / NQA-1 quality program and a NUPIC-audited approved-supplier status, so one audit covers every US utility. (3) ASME N/NPT certificates on an owned machining, welding and test line. (4) The operating-evidence record for every part it installs. Under Part 21 the dedicating entity takes on the safety obligation, so the company is legally its own approver.
wedge_first_revenue: Obsolete safety-related and augmented-quality valve and pump spares at the 94 operating US reactors (https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=207): valve internals (discs, seats, stems, packing sets), pump wear rings, mechanical seals, actuator parts. The original OEMs (for example Copes-Vulcan, Anchor/Darling, Pacific Pumps lines) often no longer support these parts, or quote lead times of 40-70+ weeks with large premiums (est.). First revenue comes from selling reverse-engineered, dedicated parts on emergent outage-critical orders at about 60-70% of the OEM quote, with a 2-6 week turn. Target: about $2-5M in year 1 from 3-5 utilities (est.).
ladder: 1) Dedicated spares for the existing fleet. 2) Whole dedicated replacement assemblies (valves, pump rotating assemblies) and life-extension kits for the 80-year subsequent licence renewals. 3) An owned ASME N-stamp line that builds 'standard' safety-class valves and pump skids with published design rules, the nuclear fluid-system PDK. SMR and microreactor developers (who need hundreds of Class 1-3 valves each and face the same N-stamp vendor scarcity) design to it instead of qualifying a new supplier. 4) Exchange pools of rotables for long-life valves and pumps, sold per refuelling cycle. 5) Export of the same library to CANDU, Korean and European fleets.
numbers: Market: about 94 US reactors and about 415 worldwide (EIA/IAEA). Annual nuclear O&M plus capital-parts spend on valves and pumps is about $1.5-3B in the US and $6-10B globally (est.). New build adds more: an SMR needs thousands of valves (est.), and the US targets 400 GW of nuclear by 2050 under the 2025 executive order (est. from memory). Unit economics: an AI-built reverse-engineering plus CGD package plausibly costs $5-20k against $50-200k today (P6 figure). A part sells at $5k-$500k with 40-60% gross margin (HEICO PMA-like; HEICO operating margin about 22-24%, https://www.heico.com investor reports). Capital: $8-15M seed/A for the QA program, NUPIC audit, a lab (CT, OES, hardness, flow test) and an initial machining cell. $40-80M for an N-stamp line. Time to $100M revenue: 6-8 years (est.). Ceiling comparables: Curtiss-Wright nuclear segment (several $B revenue, est.), HEICO (~$4B revenue, ~$40B market cap, est.), Framatome/Westinghouse parts businesses. Note: the search budget ran out in this run, so most figures come from prior knowledge and are marked est.
ai_role: AI cuts the per-part labour that limits a dedication library. It goes from CT or 3D scan and metallurgy (OES, microstructure) to drawing and material spec; infers critical characteristics from the application envelope (pressure, temperature, cycles, seismic and EQ class), pulled from plant FSARs, OEM manuals and Part 21 reports; drafts the dedication plan, the technical evaluation and the acceptance-test matrix; and uses surrogate FEA plus active test selection to choose the fewest physical tests. It also mines INPO/NRC operating-experience and LER databases to rank which obsolete parts to do first, by price gap and outage risk. Engineers then handle hundreds of part numbers a year instead of tens.
main_killer: Utility conservatism and procurement gatekeeping. Utility procurement engineering has to accept the supplier (NUPIC audit, Appendix B program). Utilities fear that a startup's dedication error triggers a Part 21 report or an NRC violation. And OEMs (Curtiss-Wright, Flowserve, Framatome) already do CGD and can price-match.
ai_answer_to_killer: Shrink the gate instead of fighting it. A NUPIC joint audit is done once and shared by all members, so one pass opens about 90% of the US fleet. AI makes the QA program audit-ready from day one, with complete traceability, every dedication record cross-referenced, and automatic Part 21 evaluation workflows. Start with augmented-quality and non-safety parts, which have a lower bar, to build history, then move up to safety-related. Offer a 'shadow dedication': give the utility the full package to review and sign for its own in-house dedication, so it holds the liability the first time and the company earns trust without carrying the first-failure risk. Against OEM price-matching: HEICO's rule of staying under ~30% share per part and the long tail (thousands of SKUs no OEM wants to support) keep the incumbents' incentive to respond low.
competitors: OEMs and authorised vendors: Curtiss-Wright (nuclear division), Flowserve Nuclear, Framatome, Westinghouse, Crane Nuclear, Emerson. Independent dedicators and third-party parts suppliers: Nuclear Logistics Inc (AZZ, est.), Paragon Energy Solutions, Ultra Electronics NSPI (est.), GE-Hitachi parts. None is AI-native, and all are capacity-constrained (est.). Venture-backed nuclear supply-chain startups (for example Fermi-adjacent and SMR supply-chain plays) mostly build components for new reactors rather than owning an equivalence library (est.).
principles_used: P2 (approved equivalent, not the open drawing), P6 and P7 (signed form-fit-function equivalence as the asset), P12 (breaking the OEM aftermarket lock part by part), P14 (Part 21 dedication: the dedicator becomes the gate), P1 (the N-stamp line as the frozen target/PDK for SMRs), P4 (delta qualification)

T: an Appendix B program plus NUPIC audit acceptance takes 12-24 months, and utilities are slow to adopt, so first safety-related revenue near year 2 is tight (augmented-quality parts first helps). About 94 US and ~415 global reactors is a far smaller base than aviation's ~28,000 aircraft that powers HEICO; the $1B+ case rests on SMR new build and the N-stamp PDK rung, which is credible but speculative. A: AI answers both the pain (dedication labour) and the main killer (audit-ready traceability, shadow dedication shifts first-failure risk). name: Orphan Compression: an owner-operated fleet of rebuilt legacy gas compressors for gas-to-power, RNG, hydrogen and CO2
sector: Industrial machinery: reciprocating and integral gas compressors and their engines
one_liner: Buy discontinued and orphaned compressor packages and integral engine-compressors cheaply (Cooper-Bessemer, Clark, Dresser-Rand legacy frames, older Ajax). Keep them alive with an AI-built parts and controls library, and rent the compression horsepower to the new gas buildout: behind-the-meter data-centre gas plants, pipeline laterals, RNG and landfill gas, CO2 capture and storage, and hydrogen blending. No drilling or production.
what_it_owns: (1) The fleet of compressor packages (horsepower as a financeable asset, like Archrock and Kodiak, but bought at a fraction of new cost). (2) The reverse-engineered parts library for orphaned frames: valves, piston rings, rider bands, packing, crossheads, cylinder liners, governors. (3) Its own retrofit control layer (update authority, P8) that cuts emissions and lifts efficiency on legacy units. (4) The fleet operating and emissions-compliance evidence (EPA OOOOb methane monitoring) that both the regulator and lenders price.
wedge_first_revenue: New gas compression lead times are long because engines (Caterpillar G3500/G3600, Waukesha) and frames are backlogged by data-centre gas demand. Packages are quoted at 50-80+ weeks (est.). Wedge: rebuild idle or stacked legacy units bought at about 10-30% of new (est.) and rent them at monthly rates of about $20-30/hp-month (est.) to RNG, landfill-gas and midstream customers who need horsepower now. First revenue comes from 5-15 units on 12-36 month contracts.
ladder: 1) Rental of rebuilt legacy units in short-lead-time niches. 2) Re-engineered 'generic' compressor cylinders and valves made by the company, now sold into third-party fleets as an approved-equivalent parts line (P2/P7), plus its own controls retrofit kits. 3) Purpose-built service lines for CO2 (Class VI sequestration hubs under 45Q) and hydrogen-blend compression, which need materials and seal changes the library already characterises. 4) Own the compression stations themselves on new laterals feeding behind-the-meter power, selling compression as a utility (per MMcf). 5) International stacked fleets (Middle East, Latin America).
numbers: Comparables: Archrock about $1.1-1.3B revenue (2024-25) on about 4.6M operating hp, Kodiak about $1.1-1.2B revenue on about 4.4M hp, USA Compression about $950M (est.; https://ir.archrock.com, https://ir.kodiakgas.com). Their adjusted gross margins are about 65-70% (est.), the best evidence that owned horsepower is a high-margin utility. Contract compression market about $8-10B US and $15B+ global (est.). Unit economics: a 1,500 hp unit acquired and rebuilt for about $0.3-0.6M against $2-3M+ new (est.) and rented at about $25/hp-month earns about $450k/yr revenue at about 60% margin, a 1-2 year payback (est.). Capital: $10-20M seed and first fleet, then ABL and fleet debt (Archrock and Kodiak borrow against horsepower). About 300-400k hp gives about $100M revenue in 5-6 years (est.). Ceiling: Kodiak market cap about $3-4B and Archrock about $4-5B (est.). Note: the search budget ran out in this run, so all figures are est.
ai_role: (1) Reverse-engineering out-of-production compressor and engine parts from scans, wear patterns and old manuals, plus metallurgy; the per-SKU cost falls so a whole orphaned frame family becomes supportable. (2) Valve and ring material redesign for new gases (H2, CO2, sour RNG) using surrogate models. (3) Fleet condition monitoring (pressure-volume, vibration, valve temperature) with time-series models to cut unplanned downtime, the variable that prices rental contracts. (4) Controls retrofit: legacy pneumatic or relay controls translated into a modern PLC with AI combustion and load tuning, cutting methane slip and NOx so old units pass OOOOb and state rules. (5) Automated emissions-compliance reporting.
main_killer: Funded incumbents and fit risk. Archrock and Kodiak have scale, cheap capital and customer relationships. Midstream customers also prefer new standardised packages, and orphaned legacy frames are a heterogeneous, emissions-heavy fleet that may not pass methane rules. This is a 'first rungs held by funded players' case.
ai_answer_to_killer: Do not compete for the core midstream horsepower that incumbents serve with new Caterpillar-Ariel packages. Serve the lead-time gap and the non-standard niches they avoid (RNG and landfill gas, CO2 hubs, behind-the-meter power laterals, short-term rentals) where speed beats price. The AI retrofit and parts library is exactly what turns a heterogeneous orphaned fleet into a standardised one: one emissions-compliant control layer and one parts library across frames. Fleet telemetry then builds the history to get incumbent-level debt costs within 24-36 months. Incumbents can be an exit path (they acquire fleets: Archrock bought TOPS, Kodiak bought CSI) if the library proves out.
competitors: Archrock, Kodiak Gas Services, USA Compression, Enerflex (Exterran), CSI (now Kodiak), J-W Power, Flogistix (methane-focused), plus OEMs and packagers (Ariel, Caterpillar, Exterran, Natural Gas Services Group ~$150M revenue, est.). Parts: Hoerbiger (valves), Cook Compression (Dover). No one owns a reverse-engineered library for orphaned frames sold as owned horsepower (est.).
principles_used: P3 (owned pooled capacity, not marketplace), P8 (update authority on an orphaned fleet via retrofit controls), P10 (horsepower subscription as financing), P12 (breaking orphaned OEM parts locks), P2/P7 (approved-equivalent parts library feeding own fleet first, then others), P9 (asset plus data plus risk). A materially new angle relative to the gas-turbine resurrection fleet: different asset class (reciprocating compression), different buyer (gas-to-power, RNG, CO2, H2), and it complements the turbine fleet.

score.name: Orphan Compression: an owner-operated fleet of rebuilt legacy gas compressors for gas-to-power, RNG, hydrogen and CO2
score.rationale: No search was possible because the shared search budget for this turn ran out. These figures come from prior knowledge: Archrock about $1.3B revenue (2025) on about 4.7M operating hp with adjusted gross margin near 70%; Kodiak about $1.2B. Owned horsepower is a proven, debt-financeable, high-margin asset. Rental revenue can start within months of buying and rebuilding stacked units, and incumbent market caps of $3-5B support a $1B+ ceiling. It is not a drilling or prospecting idea: it serves RNG, CO2 and power. The ML story is the weak part. Ariel frames make up most of the rental fleet and are fully supported. Legacy Cooper, Clark and Ajax units already have a deep aftermarket of rebuild shops, so a parts library is not the bottleneck. Converting units to electric drive matters more. Defensibility rests on the fleet, which Archrock and Kodiak can copy with cheaper capital, or by buying the same stacked units.

name: Breakerbank: the HEICO and rotable pool for building switchgear
sector: Construction and buildings hardware: building electrical service (switchgear, breakers, unit substations)
one_liner: Own the largest library of IEEE C37.59-qualified conversion and retrofill designs, plus an owned rotable pool of remanufactured breakers and switchgear lineups. Lease and exchange them to buildings, factories and data centres stuck in 1-2 year OEM lead times.
what_it_owns: (1) Signed equivalence. A library of conversion and retrofill designs (vacuum-breaker retrofills for obsolete air-magnetic and oil breakers, drop-in cells, relay upgrades), each design-tested to IEEE C37.59 and C37.09/C37.20.x and UL/NRTL field-labelled. This is the hardware analogue of a PMA library. (2) A rotable pool of thousands of remanufactured, tested breakers and complete lineups, owned and moved through exchange and lease contracts, as aviation rotable lessors do. (3) A test-lab record with per-unit test data, which makes its exchange units insurable.
wedge_first_revenue: Emergency and planned exchange of obsolete low- and medium-voltage breakers in existing commercial buildings, hospitals, universities and industrial plants. The OEM's answer there is either 'no longer supported' or 'new lineup in 60-100 weeks'. First revenue is (a) exchange sales of remanufactured retrofill breakers at roughly 40-60% of new, shipped in days, and (b) month-to-month and multi-year leases of temporary or bridge switchgear and unit substations to data-centre, EV-depot and industrial-expansion projects waiting on new gear. Leases are billed per kVA-month, with buyouts.
ladder: 1) Retrofill exchange for the top 200 obsolete breaker families (Westinghouse DHP, GE AM/AKR, ITE, Federal Pacific, etc.). 2) Own the C37.59 design library for about 2,000+ part families, a long tail that only becomes economic because AI cuts the engineering per family. 3) An owned rotable pool plus a bridge-power lease fleet: skid-mounted switchgear and unit substations, the 'United Rentals of switchgear', priced at shortage rents. 4) Long-term 'electrical-service-as-a-service': own the building's main switchgear and sell capacity and uptime over 15-20 years under a captive insurance programme. 5) Own a qualified remanufacturing line, scarce capacity, that OEMs and utilities subcontract to.
numbers: Web search budget was exhausted, so these are recalled or estimated figures. MV switchgear and transformer lead times stretched to about 1-2+ years in 2023-2025 (Wood Mackenzie and NREL reported large power transformer lead times of 120-210 weeks, https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/88165.pdf; switchgear 50-100 weeks is est. from industry reports). Global switchgear market about $100-110B/yr (est.). US installed base of breakers older than 30 years: several million units (est.). Comparables: HEICO FY2024 revenue about $3.9B, about 22-23% operating margin, market cap about $30-40B (https://www.heico.com/investors). United Rentals 2025 revenue $16.1B on $22.5B of fleet at original cost (per brief). AAR Corp rotable and parts-supply businesses (https://www.aarcorp.com). Unit economics (est.): a remanufactured MV vacuum retrofill costs $8-15k to produce and sells for $25-45k versus $50-90k OEM new with a 40+ week lead time. Bridge-lineup lease at $15-40k/month per 2-5 MVA lineup (est.), so a $600k asset pays back in about 2 years at shortage rents. Capital: $10-20M for test lab, initial pool and NRTL programme; inventory then financed with ABL. Time to $100M revenue (est.): 5-7 years (about 3,000 exchanges/yr plus a lease fleet of about 300 lineups). Ceiling: HEICO-style multiple on a $1-3B revenue electrical aftermarket; Schneider and Eaton aftermarket and service are each multi-billion businesses.
ai_role: (a) Decompilation: AI turns OEM instruction books, drawings, photos and 3D scans of legacy cells and breakers into interface specs (racking geometry, primary and secondary disconnects, interlocks, bus ratings) for each family. This is the cost that made long-tail C37.59 designs uneconomic (P6, P12). (b) Generative design of adapter and retrofill hardware for each family against that spec (P1). (c) AI selects the minimum design-test matrix (momentary, short-time, temperature rise) by sharing evidence across similar families, then drafts the C37.59 design-test reports and field-label packages (P4, P7). (d) Vision plus ML on per-unit test signatures (contact resistance, timing, insulation, partial discharge) gives every rotable a machine-generated evidence record and grades it automatically (P13). (e) Fleet and pool optimisation sizes pool depth by breaker family against failure and demand forecasts, the airline rotables model (P3, P10).
main_killer: OEMs and incumbent retrofill shops (Eaton, Schneider, ABB and Siemens retrofill groups, plus PEARL-member reconditioners) already hold the top families. Third-party conversion carries real arc-flash and fire liability, and insurers, AHJs and engineers of record default to 'OEM or new'. Funded players and PE roll-ups hold the first rungs.
ai_answer_to_killer: Breakerbank competes on the long tail and on time, not on the top 50 families. AI cuts per-family engineering from est. $100-250k to $10-30k, so it can certify 10x more families than incumbents bother to. Shortage rents beat brand: a hospital or data centre facing an 80-week wait pays for the 'days, not years' option. The liability gate is internalised in three ways: every design gets independent C37.59 design tests at a third-party high-power lab, every unit carries an NRTL field label and its own test record, and a captive plus reinsurance programme is priced on that per-unit evidence (the HSB/UL lineage, P14). Owning the rotable pool means Breakerbank is the approver of what goes into exchange, and the lease fleet earns money even when OEM lead times normalise, because bridge power is always needed during construction.
competitors: OEM retrofill and aftermarket arms: Eaton, Schneider Electric, ABB, Siemens, GE Vernova (Industrial Solutions, now ABB). Independent reconditioners and resellers: Group CBS, Southern States, regional PEARL-member shops (est.). Equipment renters with temporary power fleets: Aggreko, Sunbelt, United Rentals Power & HVAC. None owns a design-tested long-tail conversion library together with a leased rotable pool.
principles_used: P7 (signed equivalence certificate as the hardware lockfile), P2 (abbreviated-equivalence pathway, C37.59, as the 'ANDA'), P12 (break the obsolescence lock part by part, HEICO-style), P3 (owned pooled capacity rented per month), P13 (per-unit evidence signature), P14 (insurer as gate).

score.name: Breakerbank: the HEICO and rotable pool for building switchgear
score.rationale: Not search-verified because the search budget ran out. From prior knowledge: MV switchgear lead times of roughly 40-100+ weeks through 2024-25 are widely reported, driven by data-centre demand, and transformer lead times of 120-210 weeks appear in NREL and Wood Mackenzie reports. Reconditioning and retrofill margins are high, because cores are cheap and the gear is sold at 40-60% of the new price. Exchange and bridge-lease revenue can start within about 12-18 months, and the owned rotable pool and lease fleet satisfy the 'own the asset' rule. AI cutting per-family decompilation and adapter design is a real per-unit engineering saving, which fits law 1. The killer is only partly answered. C37.59 design tests run at a few high-power labs (KEMA, Powertech, etc.) whose capacity is scarce and queued, and AI cannot shorten that. AHJ, engineer-of-record and insurer acceptance of third-party retrofills is slow to change. Retrofill is also already a crowded field: OEM retrofill arms, Group CBS, and PEARL shops. name: Jones Act Resurrection Fleet (life-extension owner-operator with its own parts library)
sector: Maritime shipping hardware (US-flag coastwise fleet)
one_liner: Buy the ageing, protected Jones Act fleet (tankers, ATBs, tugs, barges, ro-ros) at near-scrap prices, keep it alive 15+ extra years with an AI-built non-OEM parts and repair library approved by the owner and class surveyor rather than a federal queue, and sell the scarce protected capacity on time charter.
what_it_owns: The vessels and their Jones Act coastwise trading rights (a legally scarce supply that cannot be replaced cheaply, because a new US-built hull costs 3-5x the world price). It also owns a library of reverse-engineered, class-accepted equivalent parts and repair procedures for orphaned engines, pumps, steering gear and cargo systems (P2/P7 'signed equivalences'), plus the fleet's condition and operating record, which lowers its financing spread (P10).
wedge_first_revenue: Buy 2-4 Jones Act ATB units or tug/barge combinations, est. $5-25M each against new-build costs of est. $60-120M. Use AI to build a parts library for orphaned components, and put them on time charter to refiners and chemical shippers at day rates of est. $25-60k. Revenue starts on day one of ownership, since the assets are trading or are re-activated within months. This is the maritime analogue of the turbine resurrection fleet, with one materially new angle: the approval gate is the owner plus the class surveyor (ABS) rather than the FAA/DLA/NRC, so the gatekeeper law bites much less.
ladder: 1) Acquire and life-extend small coastwise units (ATBs, tank barges, tugs). 2) Expand to Jones Act product tankers and ro-ros, which are the most capital-scarce. 3) Turn the parts library into an in-house remanufacturing cell, with class-approved WPS/PQR, an additive/casting cell and an engine re-man line, that also serves the US Navy/MSC reserve fleet (the RRF is ancient) as owned parts sold under its own approvals. 4) Become the dominant protected-capacity owner, with lower cost of capital from the cleanest fleet reliability record, then build new hulls when that pays (the foundry idea).
numbers: Search budget was exhausted in this run, so these are prior-knowledge figures marked est. Hanwha bought Philly Shipyard for $100M (closed Dec 2024; https://www.hanwha.com/newsroom). US shipyards deliver well under 1% of world commercial tonnage, against China's est. 50%+ (UNCTAD Review of Maritime Transport, https://unctad.org/topic/transport-and-trade-logistics/review-of-maritime-transport). A US-built MR product tanker costs est. $150-250M against est. $45-55M in Korea. The Jones Act ocean-going self-propelled fleet is est. ~90-100 ships, many 20-40+ years old, plus thousands of tugs and barges (MARAD, https://www.maritime.dot.gov/data-reports/data-statistics/data-statistics). Jones Act tanker time charters run est. $55-80k/day against est. $25-35k/day for world MRs. The domestic US maritime freight market is est. $15-25B/yr. Unit economics: a life-extended ATB costs est. $15-25M all-in, earns est. $35k/day x 340 days = $12M/yr revenue at est. 40-50% EBITDA, and pays back in about 3 years. $100M revenue needs about 8-10 units, est. $150-250M capex, debt-financed against charters, in est. 4-6 years. Ceiling comparables: Kirby Corp (inland/coastal barge owner, est. $3.2B revenue, est. $6-7B market cap); Matson (est. $3.4B revenue); Crowley (private, est. $3B+); Overseas Shipholding Group (bought by Saltchuk for est. $950M in 2024).
ai_role: AI cuts the per-part cost of reverse engineering. It scans worn parts, identifies materials, infers drawings and tolerances, and runs surrogate FEA and fatigue checks. It drafts class-acceptable substantiation for non-OEM spares and repair procedures, so long-tail orphaned parts (discontinued Colt-Pielstick, EMD, old MaK and Wärtsilä marks) become economic to supply. It mines engine and hull telemetry and survey histories to predict failures and plan drydock scopes, cutting off-hire days. It packages condition data for lenders and charterers (P10).
main_killer: Sellers price in hope, because Jones Act scarcity is well known. Incumbents (Kirby, Crowley, Saltchuk/OSG, Seacor/AIP) and PE hold the first rungs, and old hulls face steel-renewal and ballast/emissions retrofit costs that may sink the life-extension maths. Jones Act repeal risk is a political tail.
ai_answer_to_killer: Buy what incumbents cannot underwrite: hulls whose blocker is orphaned machinery, not steel. AI-generated parts libraries turn 'scrap because no spares' into 'trading', so the seller's price reflects the scrap value of a dead engine, not the hope value of the trade. AI condition assessment, applied at scale to class survey records and thickness gauging, screens the hundreds of candidate hulls quickly and prices steel renewal exactly, so the company bids only where the life-extension maths clears. On repeal risk: protected capacity becomes more valuable as USTR port fees on Chinese-built ships (2025) and the SHIPS Act push the other way, and the parts library and re-man cell keep value under any regime because they also serve Navy/MSC reserve fleets.
competitors: Kirby, Crowley, Saltchuk (OSG, TOTE), Matson, Seacor/AIP, Harley Marine/Centerline, Hornbeck; non-OEM marine spare suppliers (Wärtsilä/Everllence pattern-part competitors such as est. Engine Parts Group); OEM service arms Wärtsilä and Everllence (ex-MAN Energy Solutions).
principles_used: P2/P7 owning signed equivalences rather than publishing a library; P12 breaking the OEM aftermarket lock with the owner-operator capturing it; P14 the gate inside the company (owner plus class surveyor); P10 lower cost of capital from fleet history; P8 update authority over orphaned machinery.

score.name: Jones Act Resurrection Fleet (life-extension owner-operator with its own parts library)
score.rationale: The web search budget was exhausted, so these figures are from prior knowledge. The Jones Act premium is real: US-built tankers cost 3-4x Korean builds, coastwise rates are well above world MR rates, and Saltchuk did buy OSG for about $950M. A life-extended ATB at $15-25M earning $30-40k/day is plausible and pays back in about 3 years, so N is 4 and capital is debt-financeable against charters. T is 4 because revenue starts on acquisition. C is 4: Kirby at roughly $6B market cap is the ceiling comparable, and $10B+ would need the Navy/MSC re-man rung. The A leg is the weak point. The real killers of old Jones Act tank tonnage are oil-major vetting age limits (SIRE/OCIMF practice; many charterers reject tank vessels over 20-25 years) and steel and ballast-water renewal, not orphaned spares. An AI parts library and condition scoring answer only part of that. Condition data could plausibly argue for vetting exceptions, which is why A gets 3 and not 2. D is 3: the protected trading right is shared with well-capitalised incumbents who also know the scarcity value, so sellers will price it in.
score.biggest_risk: Charterer vetting age caps and steel-renewal costs, not missing parts, are what retire old Jones Act hulls. So the 'scrap price because of dead machinery' arbitrage may only exist on a thin slice of the fleet, and sellers price in the scarcity of the trading right.

name: Exchange: resurrecting copper-era telecom central offices and stranded enterprise halls as owned AI-inference capacity
sector: Data-centre real assets: stranded powered shells, retiring telecom central offices, legacy enterprise data centres
one_liner: Buy or long-lease the thousands of 1-20 MW powered buildings that the AI era is stranding: telecom central offices being emptied by copper retirement, and enterprise and colo halls too air-cooled for 130 kW racks. Use AI to reverse-engineer and retrofit each one in weeks with owned liquid cooling and power, and run them as a distributed, owned inference fleet in the metros where grid queues run 3-7 years.
what_it_owns: The scarcest permission in AI infrastructure: existing, energised utility interconnections and zoning in dense metros. Under the laws, monopolies are held by permission, and an interconnect is one, but here it is already granted. Also the buildings or long leases, the owned retrofit plant (CDUs, dry coolers, 800 VDC/UPS), and a fleet-wide operating record. It sells inference capacity (GPU-hours or kW-months to neoclouds and model labs), not a retrofit service.
wedge_first_revenue: Telecom central offices: AT&T has said it plans to exit most of its copper network by end-2029, and Verizon and Lumen are retiring copper as well (prior knowledge). That frees urban buildings that already have multi-MW feeds, -48 VDC plant, diesel backup, fibre to every carrier, and hardened structures. First deal: a sale-leaseback or master lease of 5-10 COs from one telco or tower/real-estate holder. Retrofit 1-3 MW each, pre-let to an inference neocloud that needs low-latency metro capacity. First revenue in about 9-12 months, because each building's power is already permitted.
ladder: 1) Central-office pilots, 1-3 MW each. 2) Roll up stranded enterprise data centres (banks, insurers and manufacturers moving to cloud dump 2-10 MW sites), often at land value. 3) Software-defined capacity (P8): AI power-capping and UPS/genset-backed oversubscription raise each building's usable IT load by est. 20-40% on the same utility feed. 4) A metro inference grid of 1-2 GW across hundreds of sites, billed as a single pool (P3 multiplexing across sites). 5) Securitise the leases and capacity contracts like a data-centre REIT, and use the operating record to win flexible-interconnection upgrades at each site.
numbers: Supply (est.): the US has est. 19,000-25,000 telephone wire centres / central offices (prior knowledge). Even 5% with 1-5 MW feeds is about 1,000+ sites and est. 2-4 GW. Legacy enterprise DC stock is est. more than 10 GW in the US, a large share being vacated. Valuation (est.): a powered urban shell trades well below a new build. New AI-ready capacity costs about $10-13M/MW plus 3-7 years of grid wait, versus est. $1-3M/MW to acquire and $3-5M/MW to retrofit for liquid cooling, so roughly half the capital and 1/4 the time. Revenue (est.): wholesale AI colocation leases at about $150-200/kW-month in constrained metros. A 2 MW CO earns about $4M/yr against est. $8-14M of all-in capex, a 3-4 year payback. Time to $100M revenue: est. 4 years (about 45-55 MW leased across about 25-40 sites). Capital: est. $20M equity for the pilot, then project and REIT-style debt. Ceiling comps: Digital Realty and Equinix (market caps est. $50-90B, prior knowledge); DataBank and EdgeConneX (PE-owned edge/regional platforms); Core Scientific, a converted crypto host, which CoreWeave agreed to buy for about $9B in 2025 (prior knowledge; the deal was later voted down by shareholders, verify), proving that stranded powered sites become very valuable.
ai_role: (a) Decompiling the building (P1/P12): many COs and enterprise halls have no accurate as-builts. AI turns LiDAR scans, utility bills, legacy single-line diagrams, BMS logs and photos into a verified digital twin (structure, power path, cooling capacity) in days, not months of engineering. (b) A retrofit compiler: per-site liquid-cooling and power designs generated against a fixed kit of owned standard modules (P5 standard modules, Wright's law). (c) Site triage: models over public utility, zoning, permit and telco filings rank thousands of candidate buildings by usable MW and conversion cost, finding the long tail PE does not price. (d) Fleet operation: AI power and thermal control oversubscribes each feed safely and pools workloads across sites, and fleet telemetry builds the operating record that lowers cost of capital (P9/P10).
main_killer: Law 2, sellers and PE: as soon as 'powered shell' becomes the theme, telcos and owners price in hope, and data-centre PE (Blackstone, Digital Bridge, Brookfield) already holds the first rungs. COs are also small and awkward: low floor loads, multi-tenant telco equipment that stays in place, and some feeds below 1 MW.
ai_answer_to_killer: Go where PE cannot underwrite: the long tail of 1-5 MW sites, where diligence and design cost per MW kills a fund's economics. AI collapses per-site diligence and design labour (scan-to-twin, auto-retrofit design, automated permit and NRTL paperwork) from est. $300-500k per site to est. $30-50k. That makes 1-3 MW sites investable for us and uneconomic for funds, the HEICO long-tail logic applied to buildings. Offer telcos a structure, not a price: a master lease or JV across hundreds of COs, so they keep their remaining equipment and share upside. On small or under-powered feeds, use software-defined oversubscription plus on-site batteries to lift usable MW. Floor-load limits are met with rear-door or in-row liquid cooling designed per building.
competitors: Edge/regional platforms: DataBank, EdgeConneX (EQT), Flexential, Cologix, Vapor IO, American Tower/CoreSite edge. Stranded-site converters: Core Scientific, Applied Digital, IREN, TeraWulf (crypto-to-AI). Telco real-estate monetisers and PE (Blackstone/QTS, DigitalBridge/Vantage, Brookfield). Funding not verified in this run.
principles_used: P3 (multiplex an owned pool across many sites), P8 (software-defined capacity on an existing grid feed), P12 (decompile undocumented buildings), P5 (standard retrofit modules), P10 (operating record lowers cost of capital). Escapes the gatekeeper law because the interconnect permission already exists.

score.name: Exchange: resurrecting copper-era telecom central offices and stranded enterprise halls as owned AI-inference capacity
score.rationale: Search budget was exhausted, so this relies on prior knowledge. AT&T's copper exit by about 2029 and the large US stock of wire centres are real, and existing energised interconnects in queue-constrained metros are a genuine permission. N: about $8-14M of all-in capex per 2 MW site earning about $4M/yr at $150-200/kW-month is a 3-4 year payback. The lease rate may be high for small sites, but data-centre debt is readily available, so N is 4. T: power is already permitted, so first revenue in 9-12 months is plausible. But reaching about 50 MW across 25-40 awkward sites in 4 years means many site-level permits and retrofits, so T is 4. C: an owned 1-2 GW metro fleet supports $1B+, and Equinix and Digital Realty show the upside, but demand for small-site metro inference is unproven. A: scan-to-twin plus auto-retrofit design that cuts per-site diligence from about $300-500k to $30-50k does answer the long-tail economics killer, since it lowers per-unit labour. It does not stop telcos pricing in hope or fix low floor loads and sub-1 MW feeds. D: owned interconnects compound as a portfolio. But DataBank, EdgeConneX, the crypto converters and PE all target powered shells, and telcos can run JVs themselves.
score.biggest_risk: Telcos and data-centre PE price central-office real estate in hope once the theme is public, while the actual sites prove too small, under-powered and structurally weak for liquid-cooled AI racks.

name: Flexgrid: own the backup power at data centres and trade flexibility for fast grid connections
sector: Data-centre backup generation, batteries and grid interconnection
one_liner: Replace each AI campus's idle diesel backup with Flexgrid-owned batteries and gas generation. In return Flexgrid gets dispatch rights, signs as the flexible resource on the interconnection, gets the campus connected years sooner, and sells capacity and ancillary services from a fleet that otherwise sits idle 99% of the time.
what_it_owns: The behind-the-meter generation and storage fleet at host data centres, on Flexgrid's balance sheet. Also the dispatch rights and the 'flexible load' interconnection or capacity-market positions those assets earn, the reliability guarantee (with a captive insurer), and the fleet's dispatch-and-reliability history, which is the evidence utilities and insurers price.
wedge_first_revenue: Duke's Nicholas Institute estimated that about 76-126 GW of new large load could connect to the existing US grid if it curtailed 0.25-1% of the year (Norris et al., Rethinking Load Growth, Feb 2025, https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/publications/rethinking-load-growth, prior knowledge). First customer: a 50-200 MW AI campus in PJM, ERCOT or SPP waiting on the grid. Flexgrid installs and owns 20-50 MW of batteries plus gas generation, is the reason the utility can grant a non-firm/flexible interconnection early, and charges the campus a monthly backup-and-speed fee. It also earns capacity revenue (PJM cleared about $329-333/MW-day for 2026/27-2027/28) and energy arbitrage. First revenue est. 12-18 months.
ladder: 1) Backup-as-a-service at 1-3 neocloud campuses (battery-first to avoid diesel permit limits). 2) Register the fleet as capacity and demand response in PJM and ERCOT. 3) Build a utility-accepted 'flexible interconnection' track record and become the standard counterparty utilities name in large-load tariffs. 4) Expand to GW scale across campuses, pooled and dispatched as one virtual power plant (P3). 5) Securitise the contracted fee and capacity cash flows, and add owned firm generation (recips, fuel cells, or resurrected turbines) where the campus needs islanding.
numbers: Market (est.): US data-centre load est. about 25-45 GW in 2025 and rising to est. 80-130 GW by 2030. Each MW of IT carries est. 1.0-1.3 MW of diesel backup costing about $600-1,000/kW installed (est.), so about $50-100B of backup capital that sits idle (est.). Revenue stack per MW of owned battery/gas (est.): PJM capacity at about $330/MW-day is about $120k/MW-yr. The campus fee for backup plus faster connection is est. $60-150k/MW-yr (one year of earlier operation on a GPU campus is worth est. $10-20M/MW of revenue, so speed is cheap to sell). Arbitrage and ancillary services add est. $20-60k/MW-yr. On est. $0.8-1.3M/MW capex (4-hour battery or recip mix), payback is about 4-6 years. Time to $100M revenue: est. 4-5 years (about 400-600 MW owned). Capital: est. $30M equity plus project debt and tax-credit transfer (storage ITC). Ceiling comps: Enchanted Rock (gas microgrids, raised hundreds of $M from Ares and others, prior knowledge); Bloom Energy's 2025 deal with Brookfield for up to $5B of fuel-cell deployments (prior knowledge, verify); Fluence and Stem show that battery tool and integrator margins are thin, so ownership is the point.
ai_role: (a) Joint dispatch and risk modelling: a model co-optimises GPU workload flexibility, battery state of charge, gas start probability and grid stress forecasts so the campus's own SLA is never breached while it earns from flexibility. This replaces a human-in-the-loop decision with a priced, provable guarantee. (b) Evidence (P9/P14): every grid event, test start and curtailment becomes a measured record of 'promised curtailment delivered'. That is the ETOPS-style operating history that lets utilities grant flexible interconnections and lets an insurer price the backup guarantee. (c) Interconnection paperwork and studies: AI drafts load-flexibility studies, tariff filings and ISO registrations per site, which is per-unit labour. (d) Fleet health telemetry and predictive maintenance give lenders low-variance cash flows (P10).
main_killer: Data-centre operators will not hand over control of their backup (the last line of defence for uptime). Utilities move slowly on non-firm and flexible interconnection tariffs, so this is a gatekeeper queue AI does not shorten. Diesel run-hour and air-permit limits also cap non-emergency use.
ai_answer_to_killer: Control: Flexgrid owns the risk, not just the asset. It guarantees backup availability with liquidated damages and a captive insurance cell priced from its telemetry (HSB model), and AI models prove to the operator in advance, through replay against historical grid events, that a flexible dispatch never cuts into the reserve needed for an outage. Permits: go battery-first and gas-recip-first so diesel limits do not bind. Utility queue: do not wait for a tariff. Use existing mechanisms (ERCOT CLR/controllable load resources, PJM demand response, and the large-load flexible-connection tariffs utilities have been filing in 2025-2026), and build the evidence record in the most permissive ISO first. Once Flexgrid has 2-3 years of delivered-curtailment data across hundreds of MW, it is the default counterparty: the operator that is its own gate (P14), because the risk sits on its balance sheet.
competitors: Enchanted Rock, Bloom Energy, VoltaGrid (gas bridge power for xAI/Oracle-type campuses), ProEnergy, Generac/Cummins/Caterpillar (genset OEMs), Emerald AI (Nvidia-backed software for flexible data-centre load, seed about $24.5M 2025, prior knowledge), Verrus (Sidewalk Infrastructure Partners' flexible data-centre developer), battery IPPs (Jupiter Power, Plus Power), Fluence/Tesla Megapack integrators.
principles_used: P3 (an owned, pooled fleet under correlated scarcity), P8 (update authority over owned backup assets), P9 (fleet operating hours become accepted evidence, ETOPS-style), P10 (contracted cash flows plus low variance mean cheap capital), P14 (own the risk and you become the gate). Partly escapes the gatekeeper law by using existing ISO programmes rather than waiting for new tariffs.

score.name: Flexgrid: own the backup power at data centres and trade flexibility for fast grid connections
score.rationale: Search budget for this run was used up, so I checked the key numbers against what I already knew rather than a live search. From memory, PJM capacity cleared at the cap: about $329/MW-day for 2026/27 and $333.44/MW-day for 2027/28. That makes about $120k/MW-yr believable, and with a campus fee and arbitrage on top, $0.8-1.3M/MW of capex pays back in 4-6 years, which works for project finance. Selling speed-to-power to GPU campuses is a strong pull, and first revenue in 12-18 months is plausible. The weak legs are A and D. The things that kill it are operator control and utility tariffs, and those are answered mostly by contracts, liquidated damages and a captive insurer, not by AI. AI dispatch and replay modelling help, but they do not change which way the decision goes. Copying is the problem: hyperscalers and well-funded players (VoltaGrid, Enchanted Rock, Bloom/Brookfield, Verrus, Emerald AI) are already in this space and have cheaper capital. Hyperscalers can also own their own backup and sign their own flexible-load agreements. There is also a double-counting risk: backup reserved for outages conflicts with capacity-performance obligations.
score.biggest_risk: Hyperscalers and capital-rich bridge-power players keep the backup and the flexibility value in-house, so a third-party owner is not needed. Capacity-performance penalties also clash with keeping a reserve for outages.

name: Lazarus Storage: an owner-operated fleet of orphaned grid batteries
sector: Energy storage (grid BESS)
one_liner: Buy grid battery plants whose integrator, BMS or inverter vendor has died or been cut off (Powin's Chapter 11 in 2025, FEOC-hit Chinese integrators, 2015-2020 systems running dead EMS software). Re-arm them with an AI-built control stack and a cell/module equivalence library, then sell capacity and energy as owner-operator.
what_it_owns: The batteries themselves (MW/MWh, interconnection positions, offtake contracts), the right to update them (its own EMS/BMS firmware on assets it owns), a library of signed module, PCS and spare-part equivalences, and a fleet-wide safety and degradation record that insurers and lenders can price.
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1: buy 50-150 MWh of stranded or under-performing BESS from developers or bankruptcy estates at an est. 30-50% of replacement cost. Wedge customers are owners whose warranty died with the integrator. They sell the asset outright, or pay Lazarus a share of recovered revenue while Lazarus takes over operation and holds an option to buy. First revenue comes from wholesale arbitrage, ancillary services and resource-adequacy payments on the first acquired site, within 6-9 months of close.
ladder: 1) Take over orphaned sites and restore availability with a reverse-compiled EMS/BMS layer (P8 update authority on owned assets). 2) Build a second-source equivalence library for modules, racks, PCS boards and HVAC/fire systems, so spares stop being sole-source (P7, P12). 3) Augment capacity with re-qualified non-FEOC cells under its own equivalence evidence. 4) Pool 24-36 months of fleet telemetry into a degradation and thermal-runaway risk record for a captive insurer and cheaper debt (P9, P10, P14). 5) At about 1-3 GW, securitise the fleet's cash flows and become the low-cost owner of the 'used storage' asset class, the role United Rentals or AerCap plays for theirs.
numbers: Market: US utility-scale battery capacity about 26 GW at end-2024, adding roughly 15-19 GW a year (est., EIA trend; searches were unavailable for this run). Global stationary storage is several hundred GWh installed (est.). Distress supply: Powin filed Chapter 11 in mid-2025 and its assets went to FlexGen (est., from memory). Many owners of Powin, early Chinese-integrator and 2016-2020 systems face expired warranties and obsolete EMS (est.). Unit economics: new US 4-hour BESS installed about $200-300/kWh (est.); distressed or used assets at an est. $60-150/kWh. Capacity value is where money concentrates: PJM 2027/28 cleared at its $333.44/MW-day cap, about $122/kW-yr (prompt data), and CAISO resource-adequacy prices run about $5-15/kW-month (est.). A 1 GW / 4 GWh fleet earning a blended $100-140/kW-yr gives about $100-140M/yr revenue at an est. 50-60% EBITDA margin. Capital: about $0.4-0.8B for 1 GW, mostly asset-level debt after the first 2-3 sites; equity need is about $15-40M to reach a financeable proof. Time to $100M revenue: est. 4-5 years. Ceiling comps: Fluence (integrator, about $2-3B revenue, est.); Plus Power, Jupiter Power and Key Capture (owner-operators, private, est.); AES and Vistra storage fleets. Battery pack price fell 20% to $115/kWh in 2024 (https://about.bnef.com/blog/lithium-ion-battery-pack-prices-see-largest-drop-since-2017-falling-to-115-per-kilowatt-hour-bloombergnef/), so cells are cheap while integration and control are now the scarce layer.
ai_role: AI does five jobs here. (a) It reverse-compiles proprietary BMS/EMS behaviour from logs, firmware dumps and Modbus maps into a new owner-controlled control stack, which used to need specialist embedded teams per vendor. (b) It builds per-cell and per-rack degradation and anomaly models from messy SCADA data, so an orphaned site's real state of health is known before purchase; this is the underwriting edge when buying cheap. (c) It runs equivalence matching and drafts dossiers for replacement modules, PCS boards and fire-suppression parts against UL 9540/9540A test data. (d) It runs dispatch and bidding across ISOs. (e) It drafts evidence for authorities having jurisdiction (AHJs), insurers and lenders. AI fixes the per-site labour that makes an orphan a write-off for anyone without a fleet.
main_killer: Safety and the gatekeeper after Moss Landing. Fire marshals (AHJs), insurers and interconnecting utilities may refuse or slow approval for re-controlled, mixed-component sites. One thermal event on a re-armed site could end the model. Incumbents (FlexGen, Fluence services, Wärtsilä) also bid for the same distressed assets.
ai_answer_to_killer: Be your own gate where the law allows, and make the evidence better than the OEM's. Lazarus operates only behind its own fence (owned sites, own staff). It keeps NFPA 855 and UL 9540A configurations unchanged at the cell, module and rack level where possible, and changes the software and second-sources the balance of plant. Changes roll out canary-style, one site first, to avoid a common-mode failure (P14 break 3). Continuous AI thermal and gas anomaly detection produces a per-rack telemetry record an insurer can price (the HSB inspection-plus-insurance model), backed by a captive insurer once the record exists. Against funded bidders: AI health scoring prices distressed sites more accurately than generalist buyers can, so Lazarus can bid where the remaining value is real and walk away where it is not.
competitors: FlexGen (bought Powin assets, est.), Fluence and Wärtsilä services, Tesla Megapack services, independent O&M firms (est.), storage owner-operators Plus Power, Jupiter Power, Key Capture, esVolta (est.), and PE secondary buyers such as Arevon and Excelsior (est.). None of them is centred on orphan re-control as owner.
principles_used: P8 (update authority on owned, orphaned assets), P7 and P12 (signed equivalences break integrator spare-part locks), P9 and P14 (fleet telemetry as insurer-grade evidence; own the gate behind the fence), P10 (lower variance means cheaper debt), P3 (owned pooled capacity sold as output).

score.name: Lazarus Storage: an owner-operated fleet of orphaned grid batteries
score.rationale: Search budget was used up, so I checked from memory: Powin filed Chapter 11 in June 2025, and FlexGen bought its assets and service contracts later in 2025. Buying at $60-150/kWh, which is about $240-600/kW for 4-hour systems, against $100-140/kW-yr of capacity and RA revenue pays back in roughly 2-5 years, so the asset-level numbers are good. AI is central here. Reverse-engineering the BMS/EMS, scoring state of health before purchase, and thermal anomaly detection are exactly the per-site labour that turns an orphan into a buy. The same telemetry partly answers the safety and insurer killer. T is held back by supply: the FlexGen deal shows that orphaned fleets do get picked up by service consolidators. Real distressed supply in 2026-28 may come to hundreds of MW, not the roughly 1 GW needed for $100M, and sellers price in hope. D is moderate. Owned assets and an equivalence library compound, but FlexGen, Fluence and PE secondary buyers can bid for the same sites with cheaper capital. The ceiling grows as the roughly 100 GW of 2020s storage builds age out of warranty, so C=4.
score.biggest_risk: There are not enough truly orphaned assets at distressed prices. Consolidators like FlexGen absorb the bankruptcies, and one thermal event on a re-armed site ends the AHJ and insurer path.

name: Nucleon Foundry (the TSMC of nuclear-grade components, with a published PDK)
sector: Nuclear: new build and SMR/microreactor supply chain hardware
one_liner: An owned, ASME Section III / NQA-1 qualified manufacturing line (PM-HIP near-net shapes, wire-arc and laser powder-bed AM, precision machining, in-house NDE) that publishes nuclear 'design rules'. Any reactor developer can 'compile' a valve body, pump casing, reactor internal or heat-exchanger header to it and receive a code-stamped, evidence-carrying part.
what_it_owns: The frozen, characterised target (P1/P13): its ASME N/NPT/MO certificates and NQA-1 program; a qualified process envelope for each alloy and process (PQRs, allowables, in-situ signature limits); the PDK (design rules plus a DFM checker trained on its own yield data); the scarce physical capacity (HIP vessels, AM cells, test stands); and a per-part digital traveler record that is the qualification evidence.
wedge_first_revenue: Long-lead, small-quantity components for advanced reactor first-of-a-kind and demo units (Kairos, X-energy, TerraPower, Oklo, Natura, Aalo, Radiant, the DOE pilot program reactors). These developers currently wait 18-38 months for forged valves and nozzles. Start with non-code / Appendix B augmented-quality parts and Section III Class 2-3 items made by PM-HIP, which has an earlier ASME acceptance trajectory than AM (status of code cases: verify, est.). Charge a premium for weeks-to-months delivery. Also sell replacement castings for fleet valves where the original foundry has gone.
ladder: 1) Prototype and demo-unit parts for SMR developers (cash, high price). 2) Recurring production slots ('wafer starts') for serial SMR builds, taken on capacity reservation with deposits, as TSMC does. 3) Class 1 pressure-boundary parts as AM/PM-HIP code cases mature, using the line's own signature history as the evidence base. 4) Large near-net components (RPV nozzles, heads, steam-generator parts) by assembling HIP/AM segments, attacking the forging chokepoint where only JSW and Doosan anchor supply and the US has none. 5) Own the standard modules: catalogue 'standard cells' (valves, pumps, HX headers) that every design reuses, so Wright's law accrues to the foundry.
numbers: Forging chokepoint: large Gen III+ presses manage about 4 pressure vessels per year each (https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/nuclear-fuel-cycle/nuclear-power-reactors/heavy-manufacturing-of-power-plants). JSW and Doosan anchor a small qualified pool, with no US firm on the list (Aug 2026, https://neutronbytes.com/2026/08/24/the-reactor-isnt-the-bottleneck-the-forge-is/). N-stamp valve lead times reported up to 38 months, and 18-24 month forged-valve delays (unverified, https://pmarketresearch.com/auto/nuclear-industry-valves-market/). Nuclear valve market estimates range from $2.1B to $12.5B, conflicting (same source). AM code status: Argonne submitted the first draft ASME Code Case for PBF-LB high-temperature reactor components in Apr 2026 (https://3dprintingindustry.com/news/argonnes-asme-submission-aims-to-open-a-formal-pathway-for-lpbf-in-nuclear-reactor-manufacturing-250479/); the NRC/ASME AM roadmap is at https://ww2.nrc.gov/docs/ML2332/ML23324A268.pdf. Unit economics (est.): $2-10M per cell; ~45-55% gross margin at high utilisation on qualified parts that sell at 3-10x commodity cost. Capital: $40-80M to the first stamped production line, plus DOE/DoD manufacturing grants (est.). Time to $100M revenue: ~6-7 years, tied to SMR serial builds (est.). Ceiling: if 10-20 GW/yr of advanced reactors are built globally in the 2030s, at ~$300-600/kW of code components, the pool is $3-12B/yr (est.). Comparables: TSMC as the model; BWXT (~$15B+ market cap, est.); Doosan Enerbility.
ai_role: AI is the internal compiler. A text/spec-to-part DFM checker runs against the foundry's characterised envelope. AI does automatic process planning, HIP-can design and toolpaths. In-situ ML monitoring (melt-pool, acoustic, thermal) gives each part a defect-probability signature, so per-part evidence replaces lot destructive tests where the code allows it. Physics-informed transfer models move a recipe to new machines with few coupons. LLMs draft the code-required package: PQR/WPS, design reports, Certified Material Test Reports, data reports (N-1/NPP-1). Active learning reduces coupon matrices for new code cases.
main_killer: ASME code acceptance and the N-stamp audit set the clock (code cases take years, NRC endorsement via RG 1.84 lags). Capital-heavy facilities have to be built before SMR demand is firm, and many SMR developers may fail or slip.
ai_answer_to_killer: Sequence by what the code already permits. PM-HIP and conventional machining plus welding are the first stamped products, and AM starts on non-pressure-boundary and augmented-quality parts that need no code case. AI makes the evidence for new code cases cheap and fast: dense in-situ datasets plus targeted coupons. Being the line that generates the data behind the code case (with Argonne, ORNL and EPRI) makes the foundry the reference process, the way MOSIS/TSMC rules became the standard. Demand risk is diversified across 10+ reactor developers plus fleet replacement castings (no single-customer bet), with capacity reservation deposits and DOE/DoD industrial-base funding paying for the cells.
competitors: Japan Steel Works and Doosan Enerbility (heavy forgings); BWXT, Curtiss-Wright, Flowserve, Velan, Framatome components; North American Forgemasters; Sheffield Forgemasters (UK, state-owned); AM-for-nuclear players: Westinghouse (AM thimble plugs), ORNL TCR program, Hadrian and Machina Labs (adjacent, aerospace/defence focus). No US 'nuclear PDK foundry' found.
principles_used: P1 (own the frozen target, not the compiler), P13 (certify the recipe plus envelope), P11 (abundant builders need a qualified cell), P3 (pooled, owned capacity), P5 (standard modules and Wright's law).

score.name: Nucleon Foundry (the TSMC of nuclear-grade components, with a published PDK)
score.rationale: A strong ceiling story: the heavy-forging chokepoint (JSW and Doosan, no US firm), BWXT-scale comparables, and a $3-12B/yr pool if advanced reactors scale. Defensibility is real once earned: N/NPT stamps, qualified process envelopes, a PQR library and per-part signature history are permission plus evidence, the moats that hold. From memory, PM-HIP 316L already has an ASME Section III code case (N-834), which supports the 'sequence by what the code permits' plan; I could not check this because the search budget was used up. But AI mostly speeds evidence generation, while the clocks that gate the business (ASME code cases, NRC endorsement via RG 1.84, N-stamp surveys) are gatekeeper queues that AI does not shorten. That is a direct hit from the first law, so A stays at 3. Numbers: $40-80M of cells built ahead of firm demand, with utilisation risk across SMR developers that may slip or fail. Time: early non-code and augmented-quality revenue is plausible within 2 years, but $100M by year 7 depends on SMR serial builds, which are not assured.

name: Second Holston: the AI-native energetics foundry (the 'TSMC of explosives and propellants')
sector: Defence munitions / energetics: upstream energetic materials (nitramines, nitrocellulose, oxidizers)
one_liner: Own the second US source of the few energetic materials every warhead and motor depends on: a continuous-flow, sensor-dense plant whose per-batch evidence stream lets it qualify its process, not each lot. It publishes a frozen 'materials PDK' that the new motor and warhead startups design against.
what_it_owns: The qualified plant: a COCO facility, or one on an Army Enhanced Use Lease site. It also owns the sited and permitted explosive-safety footprint, the per-batch process-signature evidence library, the source approvals and qualification records held with each prime, and the published, characterised formulation and design-rule set (the 'ISA' customers build to). It sells kilograms of qualified material on take-or-pay contracts. It does not sell the process technology.
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1-2: small, fast-turn lots of qualified energetic material and pressed or cast subassemblies for venture-backed motor and warhead makers. Anduril targets 6,000 SRMs a year at McHenry, and Ursa Major, X-Bow, Mach Industries' in-house motor arm and Castelion are others. These buyers today queue behind legacy primes for Holston and Radford output. They are also their own qualifiers for their own products, which shortens the acceptance loop. Revenue in parallel from DPA Title III and OTA capacity awards: FY26 includes $650M for SRM capacity expansion, and DoD put $192.5M into reshoring precursor chemicals in 2024. First $5-20M of revenue at premium prices (est.) for 'second source' insurance.
ladder: 1) Fast-turn pilot lots for new entrants under OTA and Title III. 2) Second-source qualification at one legacy program office (Army JPEO A&A, or the Navy at Indian Head) for a single material. 3) Multi-year take-or-pay contracts with primes for surge capacity, which Holston cannot supply because GMLRS and PrSM already compete for its expansion. 4) A second and third plant (a regional 'fleet' of energetics fabs, including an allied site in Europe or Australia). 5) Become the merchant energetics backbone, with the PDK as the standard new munitions are designed to. The Intel/TSMC position.
numbers: Bottleneck: Holston AAP is the only US producer of RDX/HMX, the Army goal is to only 'more than double' RDX output by July 2028, and Plant X (a second complex) was studied but not built (https://www.intellinews.com/us-running-out-of-explosives-due-to-tennessee-plant-bottleneck-430363/). Radford is the only domestic nitrocellulose producer (https://dsm.forecastinternational.com/2026/06/24/the-energetics-bottleneck-threatening-u-s-munitions-production/). AP is made at scale by only AMPAC, and Northrop's $100M+ AP line is slowed by certification (https://techcrunch.com/2025/08/12/anduril-opens-solid-rocket-motor-factory-amidst-ongoing-chemical-chokepoint/). Precedent for capital and siting: Hanwha's ~$1.3B Enhanced Use Lease energetics plant at Pine Bluff Arsenal (https://www.executivegov.com/?p=280570). 155mm output was 36k/month against a 100k goal as of March 2026, with $4.5B spent Feb 2022 to Sep 2025 (https://www.defensenews.com/news/your-military/2026/07/14/manufacturing-woes-hamper-us-155-mm-ammo-production/). The PAC-3 objective was raised from 3,376 to 13,773 interceptors, and multiyear procurement covers 8 munitions (https://breakingdefense.com/2026/01/fy26-defense-bill-boosts-budget-by-8b-largely-bypassing-last-minute-28b-munitions-request/). Market: US military energetics materials at ~$3-6B/yr, growing with munitions surge (est.). Unit economics: a continuous-flow modular line at $50-150M capex per module (est.), 40-60% gross margins on take-or-pay surge pricing (est.). Capital: $300-800M to first full-rate module, much of it from Title III, EUL land, and DOE/OSC-style loans (est.; the Office of Strategic Capital is the relevant lender). Time to $100M revenue: 4-6 years (est.). Ceiling comparables: TSMC ($122.5B 2025 revenue) as the analogue; in-sector, BAE's operation of Holston and Radford, Nammo, Chemring (~GBP 0.5B revenue), Eurenco. Valuation signals: Castelion at $13B (https://www.orrick.com/en/News/2026/08/Castelion-Raises-1B-Series-C-to-Scale-Production-of-Low-Cost-Hypersonic-Weapons) and Mach at $3.7B (https://tectonicdefense.com/mach-industries-raises-an-additional-600m-boosts-valuation-to-3-7b) show investors pay for owned munitions capacity.
ai_role: AI is the internal compiler (P1, P11, P13). (a) Process ML on in-line spectroscopy, thermal, rheology and particle-size sensors gives every batch a signature, and 'inside the qualified envelope' becomes the acceptance claim. That is the container checksum for energetics, and it cuts lot-acceptance destructive testing. (b) Physics-informed surrogates of reaction kinetics and crystallization let a small team characterise the frozen 'PDK' (particle size, sensitivity, aging behaviour) for customers. (c) AI drafts qualification packages, hazard analyses and site explosive-safety submissions (per-unit paperwork, which AI does fix). (d) Captured tacit operator craft from retiring Holston-era chemists shortens operator ramp from years to months. (e) Predictive control raises yield and safety margins in a hazard-dense process.
main_killer: Qualification and siting time. A new source of a legacy energetic must be requalified program by program. Northrop's own AP line is proof it takes years. Explosive-safety siting, environmental permits and capex are also slow and large, and Holston's own expansion plus Hanwha's $1.3B plant are funded players holding the first rungs.
ai_answer_to_killer: 1) Sell first to customers who are their own approvers. New-entrant motor and warhead makers qualify their own products and only need your material inside their evidence package, so the gate moves inside the customer (P14). 2) Qualify the process family once with per-batch digital evidence and use it as a 'delta qualification' basis for each new program (P4, P13). 10 USC 148 already directs DoD to expedite energetics qualification and remove timeline barriers, which gives a statutory hook for accepting process-signature evidence. 3) Avoid siting delay by taking an EUL on an existing arsenal or AAP footprint already sited for explosives (the Hanwha precedent). 4) Hanwha and Holston target bulk legacy volume. Win the long tail of specialty grades, small lots and fast-turn work that they do not want, the way TSMC started with work the IDMs did not want.
competitors: BAE Systems (operator of Holston and Radford), Hanwha Defense USA (Pine Bluff EUL), Nammo, Eurenco, Chemring, AMPAC (AP), Northrop Grumman (captive AP), General Dynamics OTS, Rheinmetall (expanding in Europe), and Resodyn and other acoustic-mixing tool makers (the tool layer). Vertically integrated startups (Anduril, Mach) may try to make their own energetics.
principles_used: P1 (own the frozen target and its PDK), P3 (owned pooled qualified capacity), P11 (craft capture as an internal compiler), P13 (certify the process, not the plant or lot), P14 (sell to customers who are their own gate)

name: Generic Ordnance: the HEICO/ANDA of sole-source munitions components
sector: Defence munitions: fuzes, initiators, igniters, safe-and-arm devices, cartridge- and propellant-actuated devices (CAD/PAD), energetic subcomponents
one_liner: Use AI reverse-compilation to build a library of hundreds to thousands of approved second-source energetic components, then own the source approvals and the qualified lines that make them. This covers the single-bid fuzes, squibs and ejection-seat cartridges that hold up every munition and aircraft.
what_it_owns: A portfolio of government source approvals and qualified-product listings (DLA/Army/Navy source approval, QPL entries, first-article and lot-acceptance history) across many part numbers. It also owns the qualified small-lot energetic-component lines, the AI-built TDP and equivalence library, and long-term supply agreements. It sells parts; the approvals are the moat.
wedge_first_revenue: Bid the components where the government already owns the TDP and competition is thin. One example: M739A1 fuzes, a $712.5M IDIQ that drew a single bid. The Army is formally seeking second sources at 14,000/mo for M762A1/M767A1, 4,000/mo for M782A1 and 20,000/mo for M734A1/M783. Start with build-to-print on government TDPs, so there is no data-rights fight, plus DLA long-tail CAD/PAD and igniter NSNs flagged DMSMS or single-source. First revenue $5-15M on first-article plus initial lots (est.).
ladder: 1) Build-to-print fuzes and CAD/PAD on government-owned TDPs. 2) A library of 100-300 approved NSNs, worked in parallel so the 12-18 month approval queue is pipelined, not serial (HEICO adds 300-500 PMAs a year). 3) Form-fit-function improved replacements (electronic S&A, insensitive variants) under engineering change proposals. 4) Allied NATO-standard versions (STANAG fuzes) for European and Asian ammo makers. 5) Become the component 'Intel inside' for new-entrant munitions makers (drone and loitering munitions makers need fuzes and S&A devices they cannot source).
numbers: Single-bid M739A1 fuze IDIQ up to $712.5M through 2031 (https://www.armyrecognition.com/news/army-news/2026/u-s-army-awards-712m-contract-to-sustain-m739a1-artillery-fuze-production-through-2031). Army second-source market research at 14k, 4k and 20k units per month (https://defence-blog.com/?p=100328). L3Harris delivered nearly 500k fuzes in 2025, +80%, under an $872.4M M762A1/M767A1 order (https://thedefensepost.com/2026/02/05/l3harris-fuze-deliveries-2025/amp/). Sole-source FMU-139D/B ceiling increase to Northrop in 2026 (https://samsearch.co/gov-explore/federal/fmu-139d-b-fuze-production-ceiling-increase/N00019-26-NORFP-WPM201-0096). Market: US plus allied fuzes, initiators and CAD/PAD at $4-7B/yr (est.). Unit economics: 30-45% gross margin on approved components at prices 20-40% below incumbent (est., HEICO PMA analogue at about 70% of OEM: https://www.ramapo.edu/rfg/wp-content/uploads/sites/370/2022/06/Heico-Pitch.pdf). Capital: $60-150M for 2-3 qualified energetic-component lines and test capacity (est.). Time to $100M revenue: 4-6 years (est.). Ceiling comparable: HEICO (11,500+ PMAs, ~24% operating margin, one of the most valued aerospace compounders).
ai_role: (a) Reverse compilation: CT, metallography and electronics teardown of legacy fuzes and CAD/PAD to an AI-written TDP and critical characteristics in days instead of months (P12, P7). (b) AI reads decades of drawings, ECPs, lot-acceptance failure records and DMSMS notices to rank which NSNs to attack by price gap and sole-source risk. (c) Surrogate models plus active test selection minimise the first-article test matrix. (d) AI drafts first-article reports, source-approval requests and lot-acceptance documentation (per-unit paperwork). (e) Vision and sensor inspection on every unit cuts lot-acceptance rejects, which are the hidden cost in fuze production. Engineers handle hundreds of part numbers instead of tens, which makes a HEICO-scale library feasible for a startup.
main_killer: The source-approval queue (DLA/Army 12-18 months per item) and lot-acceptance testing. Incumbents also hold data rights on newer fuzes, and a startup with 20 approvals is too small to matter.
ai_answer_to_killer: 1) Pipeline the queue. AI makes the per-NSN package cheap, so submit 100+ in parallel; the queue sets latency, not throughput, and a library of thousands becomes reachable in 3-4 years (the HEICO cadence compressed). 2) Choose government-owned TDP items first (no data-rights fight), where the Army is explicitly asking for second sources. Demand-pull shortens review because the program office wants the second source. 3) Pair with new-entrant munitions makers who qualify their own systems (P14), so components get approved inside their programs. 4) Per-unit sensor evidence lowers lot-acceptance failure risk, the single biggest reason program offices fear new sources.
competitors: L3Harris (fuzes), Northrop Grumman (FMU-139 and others), Action Manufacturing, Kaman (fuzing), Chemring (CAD/PAD, initiators), PacSci EMC / Ensign-Bickford (initiators), Day & Zimmermann, Junghans/Diehl (Europe), Reutech, and Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head (organic CAD/PAD).
principles_used: P2 (ANDA/HEICO approved-equivalent library), P7 (signed equivalence certificates as the asset), P12 (clean-room reverse-engineering of sole-source interfaces), P4 (delta qualification)

Build-to-print on government-owned TDPs avoids data-rights fights, and first-article plus initial lots within ~2 years is plausible (T4). The HEICO comparable is credible for the ceiling, and drone/loitering-munition fuzes and safe-and-arm (S&A) devices add a new-entrant market (C4).
