name: Standard Motor Architecture: the 'x86 of rocket motors' made in volume
sector: Defence munitions: tactical solid rocket motors and gas generators for interceptors, drones, loitering munitions, rockets and allied missiles
one_liner: Freeze and fully characterise a catalogue of about 10 standard, modular, qualified solid motors (diameters and impulse classes, with published interface, aging and performance data). Build them in volume on AI-controlled lines so Wright's law drives the cost down, and let fabless missile and drone makers design to them the way chipmakers design to TSMC's PDK.
what_it_owns: The qualified motor family: its qualification and aging evidence across temperature and age envelopes, the published interface spec and design rules, and the volume production and static-test capacity. It also owns the operating dataset from every test-fired and fielded motor, which drives continuous delta qualification. It sells motors (units), not designs.
wedge_first_revenue: The long tail the integrated players do not serve. Anduril, Mach, Castelion and Ursa Major build motors mainly for their own missiles or prime contracts, which leaves dozens of drone, interceptor-drone, counter-UAS, target-drone, sounding-rocket and allied integrators who cannot get motors at all. Sell one or two standard boost motors (counter-UAS interceptors, launch boosters for one-way drones) off the shelf at fixed catalogue prices and 8-12 week lead times. First revenue $3-10M (est.).
ladder: 1) Catalogue boosters for drones and counter-UAS. 2) Qualified 'standard' motors adopted as baselines in DoD rapid-prototype programs and allied programs. Once a design uses your interface, switching means requalification (P13 lock-in). 3) Volume of 10k-100k motors a year, with cost falling about 20% per doubling. 4) Second-source qualification on a legacy interceptor or rocket motor via delta qualification against your evidence family. 5) Become the merchant motor standard every new fabless munition is designed around, the Intel/TSMC position for propulsion.
numbers: Demand pull: SRMs are named the key constraint on US missile production for five years (https://www.wicker.senate.gov/2026/2/chairman-wicker-issues-statement-on-additional-funding-for-anduril-solid-rocket-motor-facility). FY26 adds $650M for SRM capacity plus $200M in reconciliation for the SRM base (https://breakingdefense.com/2026/02/reconciliation-revealed-how-the-pentagon-plans-to-spend-all-152-billion-in-fy26/). Anduril targets 6,000 motors a year by end-2026 from 600 in early 2024, on $75M own capital plus $58M DPA, and has test-fired 700+ motors (https://www.defenseone.com/business/2025/08/anduril-becomes-third-us-supplier-rocket-motors-company-says/407227/ ; https://thedefensepost.com/2026/02/24/anduril-solid-rocket-motor-production/amp/). Ursa Major raised a $100M Series E plus $50M debt (https://www.voxelmatters.com/ursa-major-secures-100m-series-e-to-target-advanced-propulsion-applications/). Mach is at a $3.7B valuation with an in-house motor arm (https://siliconcanals.com/s-mach-industries-raised-300m-at-a-1-8b-valuation-and-its-new-in-house-rocket-motor-arm-targets-a-u-s-supply-bottleneck/). The PAC-3 objective is 13,773 (https://breakingdefense.com/2026/01/fy26-defense-bill-boosts-budget-by-8b-largely-bypassing-last-minute-28b-munitions-request/). Market: US plus allied tactical SRMs at $5-10B/yr, with drone and counter-UAS boosters a new, fast-growing tail (est.). Unit economics: standard boosters at $2-20k each for drone and counter-UAS and $50-300k for tactical missiles, at 35-50% gross margin at volume (est.). Capital: $150-400M to two lines plus test capacity (est.). Time to $100M revenue: 3-5 years (est.). Comparable ceilings: L3Harris/Aerojet Rocketdyne (acquired for about $4.7B), Northrop's propulsion segment, TSMC as the structural analogue.
ai_role: (a) Design compiler: surrogate internal-ballistics and structural models let one small team characterise a whole frozen family across temperature, age and vibration envelopes, the 'PDK' customers design to (P1). (b) Process signatures: ML on mix, cast and cure sensors, plus automated CT of every grain, give each motor a digital traveler, so acceptance is 'inside the envelope' rather than sampled destruction (P13, P5). (c) AI-planned active test campaigns pick the fewest static fires and aging tests to prove each envelope. Every fired motor feeds the fleet evidence (P9). (d) AI writes integration documents, interface control documents and qualification packages for each customer, so serving hundreds of small integrators is cheap. (e) Craft capture shortens the cast-and-cure technician ramp.
main_killer: The first rungs are held by funded players (Anduril, Ursa Major, X-Bow, Mach, Northrop, L3Harris), and each program qualifies its own motor. Standardising across programs has historically failed, because every missile wants a bespoke motor, and qualification is per-program.
ai_answer_to_killer: 1) The bespoke-motor norm existed because characterising a motor was expensive. AI surrogates plus per-unit evidence make a fully characterised standard family cheap to publish, and lower integrator design cost more than a custom motor would (P1: the frozen target creates abundance). 2) Target integrators below the funded players' interest: hundreds of drone and counter-UAS makers, plus allies under DoD's MOSA and modular-open-systems push, who have no motor team and accept a catalogue part. 3) Qualification is per program, but a motor that already carries a large envelope dataset needs only a delta test for each new integration (P4). 4) Volume across many small customers gives Wright's-law cost advantages that vertically integrated single-program makers do not get.
competitors: Northrop Grumman (propulsion), L3Harris/Aerojet Rocketdyne, Anduril (McHenry SRM), Ursa Major, X-Bow Systems, Firehawk Aerospace, Mach Industries (in-house motors), Nammo, Roxel/MBDA, Rafael, and Hanwha Aerospace.
principles_used: P1 (frozen characterised target as the scarce thing), P5 (standard modules plus Wright's law), P13 (portable qualified envelope locks in customers), P6 (published interface), P9 (each firing becomes evidence)

name: Gridiron Rental: the United Rentals of high-voltage transformers
sector: Power electronics and grid hardware (large power transformers, GSU transformers, mobile substations, later solid-state transformers)
one_liner: Own a pooled fleet of large and mobile power transformers: new standardised designs bought in volume plus remanufactured units rescued from retirements. Rent or lease them to data centres, IPPs and utilities that face 2-4 year waits, with an AI condition record on every unit that makes the fleet financeable and insurable.
what_it_owns: The fleet itself, the scarce physical capacity in a correlated shortage (P3), plus the evidence on each unit: AI-interpreted dissolved-gas analysis, frequency response and partial-discharge history, which insurers and lenders price. Wood Mackenzie projected 2025 US supply deficits of about 30% for power transformers and 10% for distribution transformers (https://www.woodmac.com/press-releases/power-transformers-and-distribution-transformers-will-face-supply-deficits-of-30-and-10-in-2025/, recalled, verify). ai_role: (1) Condition evidence: ML on DGA, FRA, bushing and thermal data yields a remaining-life estimate and a risk score per unit, which turns an unknown used transformer into a priceable asset (P9, P10). (2) Remanufacture compiler: AI designs the rewind or retrofit (winding redesign, cooling upgrade, re-rating) from scan data and old nameplates, cutting engineering from weeks to days (P1). (3) Fleet matching and dispatch, bin-packing units to sites by voltage class and impedance (P3, P13). (4) It drafts insurer and lender data rooms and interconnection documents.

ai_answer_to_killer: Sell first only to buyers who are their own gate: data centres, IPPs and industrials behind the fence. Every unit ships with a full factory-acceptance-equivalent test on an owned mobile test rig plus a continuous AI health record, accepted by a partner insurer (the HSB model, P14). name: Shuttle Foundry: an AI-run, open-PDK foundry for power and legacy chips on rescued fabs
sector: Semiconductors: mature-node (150/200mm) silicon, SiC and GaN power devices, analog/mixed-signal, rad-tolerant legacy
one_liner: Buy distressed or closing 150/200mm fabs cheaply, run them with AI process control and very few staff, and sell a frozen, published PDK plus multi-project-wafer shuttles for power and legacy chips. This is the MOSIS-plus-TSMC move for the long tail of power electronics that has no accessible onshore foundry.
what_it_owns: The fabs and tools (scarce physical capacity, P3, P11), the characterised, frozen process and its PDK (the 'ISA' in P1), qualification evidence (AEC-Q101, JEDEC, later DMEA Trusted Foundry accreditation), and the yield and process-signature data that makes its line the target others compile to. It also owns a growing catalogue of its own drop-in replacement power and legacy parts built on that process (the product-owner layer).
wedge_first_revenue: 1) Sell shuttle runs and small-lot production of SiC and GaN power devices and legacy analog to the fast-growing pool of fabless power startups (EV chargers, data-centre power, drones, defence), which today wait months for MPW slots at X-Fab, SkyWater and overseas foundries. 2) Re-fab obsolete power and analog parts as authorised or form-fit-function replacements (pulls through Idea 1's library). First revenue: buy a tooled 150mm fab from a bankrupt or consolidating owner (est. tens of millions, versus $1B+ greenfield), and run qualification lots within 12-18 months.
ladder: 1) MPW shuttles plus small-lot production for fabless power startups and universities (the MOSIS rung). 2) An own-brand catalogue of FFF replacements for discontinued power and analog parts. 3) DMEA Trusted Foundry accreditation and defence work (12-24 month queue, accepted). 4) Automotive qualification. 5) A second and third rescued fab; a regional 'availability zone' model (P3). 6) An AI-native lights-out 200mm SiC line designed from the fleet data.
numbers: Fabless share of IC sales rose from about 24% (2010) to about 50% (2024) (from the brief, P1). TSMC: 2025 revenue $122.5B, about 70% foundry share (from the brief). The SiC power device market is est. about $3-4B in 2025, growing 20%+ a year (est., Yole). GaN power is est. under $1B, growing 40%+ (est.). Distress: Wolfspeed entered Chapter 11 in mid-2025 and emerged later in 2025 (recalled, verify), and several European and US 150/200mm lines were closed or sold (est.). SkyWater bought Infineon's Fab 25 in Austin (2025, recalled, verify), proving the used-fab-acquisition path. Unit economics (est.): a 150mm fab at 10-20k wafers/month at $1-3k per processed SiC/GaN wafer gives $150-500M a year of capacity revenue. AI process control and automated metrology aim for 30-50% fewer engineers per wafer start (est.). Capital: $50-150M to acquire and requalify the first fab (CHIPS Act-style and DoD funding plausible), and $500M+ by fab 3. Time to $100M revenue: est. 4-6 years. Ceiling comparables: X-Fab (about EUR 0.8-0.9B revenue, est.), Tower Semiconductor (about $1.4B revenue, est.), TSMC as the platonic ceiling. Note: the web search budget ran out during this run, so all non-brief figures are est. or recalled.
ai_role: (1) Building the PDK: ML on in-line metrology and electrical test turns a messy legacy line into a characterised, frozen target much faster, which is exactly what P1 says creates abundance. (2) Run-to-run and virtual-metrology control, cutting the expert-engineer headcount that makes old fabs uneconomic (P11). (3) AI design-rule checking and DFM for customer designs, so a 5-person fabless startup can tape out to the PDK (the Mead-Conway move). (4) Reverse-compiling obsolete power and analog parts into the company's process (P12). (5) Auto-drafted qualification and reliability reports (AEC-Q, JEDEC HTRB/HTGB evidence packages).
main_killer: Capital intensity plus Chinese mature-node overcapacity: China is adding large 150/200mm and SiC capacity with state support, pushing wafer prices down. Old fabs also lose money for real reasons (staff, tool obsolescence, yield). Automotive and defence qualification takes years, and funded players (SkyWater, X-Fab, Tower) hold the first rungs.

Buying rescued fabs at cents on the dollar (distressed sellers, not hopeful ones) cuts capex per wafer-start by an est. 5-10x against greenfield. The product catalogue (own replacement parts) puts the highest margin on the company's own capacity, as Protolabs owns its design rules and machines.
competitors: SkyWater Technology (US trusted foundry, acquired Fab 25), X-Fab (SiC/GaN specialty foundry), Tower Semiconductor, GlobalFoundries (mature nodes), Polar Semiconductor (US 200mm, CHIPS-funded), Wolfspeed and onsemi (captive SiC), Chinese SiC fabs (SICC, SanAn), efabless (open-PDK shuttles, wound down in 2025, recalled), MOSIS (nonprofit, small).
principles_used: P1 (frozen characterised target, the PDK), P3 and P11 (own scarce qualified capacity, AI as internal compiler), P13 (portable recipes, value to capacity owner), P5 (Wright's law on the own-part catalogue), P12 (re-fab obsolete parts)

name: Ghost Fleet Autonomy (cold-stacked hulls to an owned unmanned logistics fleet)
sector: Shipbuilding / maritime defence hardware
one_liner: Buy cold-stacked and end-of-charter offshore supply vessels, tugs and small tankers for cents on the dollar, refit them with an AI-generated autonomy and control stack, and own and operate the result as an unmanned logistics and auxiliary fleet that the Navy, MSC and allies charter by the day.
what_it_owns: The hulls (the fleet itself), the update authority over every control system on them (P8), the fleet's operating-hour and incident record, which becomes the evidence for autonomy and insurance (P9, P14), and the refit design library for each hull class, which works like a PDK (P1).
wedge_first_revenue: Buy 3-5 cold-stacked US-flag OSVs, the 200-280 ft platform supply vessels left idle after the 2015 offshore crash and coming back onto the market in the 2025-26 Gulf of Mexico slowdown. Refit them to optionally-crewed operation: reduced crew first, so there is no autonomy-certification queue on day one. Charter them as commercial-standard logistics, target-towing, and sensor/USV motherships to Navy/MSC programmes and to allied navies (Taiwan, Philippines, Japan) under existing commercial charter vehicles. First revenue comes from day-rate charters, est. $15-35k/day per vessel, in 12-18 months.
ladder: 1) Optionally-crewed charters on refitted OSVs and tugs, with a crewed safety master aboard. 2) Collect 100k+ autonomous operating hours, turn them into an insurer-priced and class-noted record (ABS/DNV autonomy notations), and remove the crew. 3) Expand to small product tankers and ro-ros as unmanned contested-logistics ships (the Navy's distributed/contested logistics gap). 4) Build new standard hulls on the refit design rules once the evidence exists (see the block-foundry idea), then become the 'AWS of maritime logistics capacity': a large owned fleet sold as vessel-days.
numbers: Search budget was exhausted in this run, so figures come from prior knowledge and are marked est. Saronic raised $600M Series C at a $4B valuation (Feb 2025) and is building its 'Port Alpha' shipyard (https://www.saronic.com/blog/saronic-raises-600m-series-c). That shows investors will fund owned maritime-autonomy capacity at scale. A new US-built OSV costs est. $40-70M; cold-stacked US OSVs have traded at est. $1-6M (5-15% of new). An autonomy refit costs est. $3-8M per hull. All-in cost is roughly 15-25% of a newbuild, at in-service speed (6-9 months against 3-5 years for a newbuild). Navy unmanned and auxiliary budget lines run at est. $1-3B/yr and are growing, and MSC's charter budget is est. several $B/yr. At 40 vessels x $25k/day x 300 days = $300M/yr revenue. A $100M revenue run-rate needs about 15 vessels at est. $100-150M capex, about 4-5 years. Ceiling comparables: Saronic $4B+ private; MSC charter book; Tidewater (OSV owner) market cap est. $3-5B; Bollinger/Austal USA as builders.
ai_role: AI collapses the per-hull engineering labour of refitting heterogeneous, orphaned hulls. It reverse-engineers legacy propulsion and DP control logic from manuals, wiring and PLC dumps, and generates a per-hull autonomy integration (a 'compiler' from hull class to control stack, P1/P8). It learns a model of each vessel's dynamics from sea-trial and AIS data. It handles perception, collision avoidance and remote supervision, so one operator supervises many hulls. It drafts the class/flag safety cases, FMEAs and insurer submissions (the paperwork law). Fleet telemetry becomes evidence that compounds for removing crew (P9).
main_killer: The gatekeeper and the first rung. Uncrewed operation of large vessels lacks a settled IMO/USCG regime: the MASS Code is not mandatory until about 2032. Navy acquisition is slow, and incumbents plus heavily funded new entrants (Saronic, HavocAI, Blue Water Autonomy, Leidos Sea Hunter lineage) hold the programme relationships.
ai_answer_to_killer: Escape the queue by being your own gate (P14). Start optionally-crewed: a licensed master stays aboard, so the ships are ordinary US-flag commercial vessels under existing rules and no new certification is needed. Sell commercial charters, not developmental programmes, so the buyer pays for capacity now. Bodies are taken off the ship only as the AI-generated fleet evidence record (hours, near misses, interventions) builds a case that class and insurers price, as in the Waymo/Swiss Re pattern. Against funded entrants, the hulls are differentiated: they buy small new USVs, while this company resurrects large-displacement capacity that already exists, at 15-25% of newbuild cost. Navy studies say large autonomous logistics is the scarce piece.
competitors: Saronic (new-build small/medium ASVs, $4B, own shipyard); Blue Water Autonomy (new-build long-range USV, est. ~$64M raised 2025); HavocAI (small USVs); Sea Machines (autonomy kits sold as tools, a service model); Leidos/Sea Hunter; Saildrone; OSV owners Tidewater/Hornbeck (crewed); MSC charter incumbents (Crowley, Matson, TOTE).
principles_used: P8 update authority over orphaned assets; P9 operating hours as owned evidence; P14 owner-operator as its own gate; P3 owned pooled capacity sold by the day; P10 output-as-a-service financed on fleet history.

name: Hull PDK Foundry (the TSMC of steel ship blocks, building its own standard vessels)
sector: Shipbuilding (commercial and naval auxiliary)
one_liner: Build the first 'process design kit' for ships: an AI-native, robotically welded block foundry with frozen, class-qualified design rules (welding procedures, plate and stiffener catalogue, outfitting modules), and use it first to build and own a fleet of standard US-built vessels, then to fab blocks for anyone who designs to its rules.
what_it_owns: The characterised and qualified target (P1/P13): the yard's WPS/PQR set, design rules and statistical weld-quality evidence accepted by ABS/DNV and NAVSEA. It owns the scarce qualified capacity of block fab and outfitting (P3/P11), the vessels it builds for its own fleet (Jones Act barges, ATBs, naval auxiliaries, USV motherships), and the yield and inspection data that keeps improving the rules.
wedge_first_revenue: Start with the simplest hulls a regulator already understands: Jones Act tank and deck barges and harbour tugs. Use robotic panel lines, AI weld planning and in-process vision/ultrasonic inspection. Build them for the company's own fleet (or the resurrection fleet's charterers), and sell surplus barges. First revenue comes from barge charters or sales in est. 18-24 months, from a leased existing waterfront site (many dormant US Gulf yards exist).
ladder: 1) Barges and tugs for its own and others' use. 2) Freeze the design rules (block catalogue, standard midbody) and win ABS type approval for its process, not per ship, which is the 'qualify the process, not the part' move (P13). 3) Build ATBs, OSV-class hulls and Navy/MSC auxiliaries (T-AGOS-style, MASC USV motherships, sealift replacements); the Navy's own shipbuilding plan says capacity is the bottleneck. 4) Open the foundry to fabless ship designers (autonomy startups, allied navies, offshore wind installers) who design to its PDK, the MOSIS/TSMC split. Own the scarce qualified capacity and keep owning a fleet on top.
numbers: Search budget was exhausted in this run, so these figures are marked est. US shipbuilding productivity is est. 2-4x worse in labour-hours per CGT than Korea/Japan, and US yards report persistent welder shortages; Path Robotics raised $100M (Series D, Oct 2024) against a projected gap of about 400k welders (https://seedtable.com/companies/path-robotics/funding-rounds/series-d-2024-10). Navy shipbuilding spending is est. $30-35B/yr, and GAO and CBO report most programmes years late. Saronic's $4B valuation rests partly on its own Port Alpha yard (https://www.saronic.com/blog/saronic-raises-600m-series-c). Hanwha has committed est. $5B to expand Philly Shipyard (2025). A barge yard needs est. $50-150M capex. A 30,000-bbl tank barge sells for est. $8-15M, and an ATB for est. $60-120M. $100M revenue = est. 8-12 barges plus 1 ATB per year, or a share of one auxiliary programme, in est. 4-6 years. Ceiling comparables: HII (est. $11.5B revenue), Austal USA, Bollinger (private), Hanwha Ocean, HD Hyundai (est. $30B+ market cap), and TSMC as the structural analogue.
ai_role: AI is the internal compiler stack. It goes from spec to class-compliant structural design via generative scantling, to block breakdown and nesting, to robot weld paths and process plans, to an evidence compiler: per-weld sensor signatures plus automated UT/vision inspection turned into class reports. It captures craft from master welders and fitters into robot programmes and novice coaching (P11). It also runs schedule optimisation across the block flow, which is where US yards lose most labour-hours.
main_killer: Capital intensity and the 'first rung held by funded players': Hanwha/Philly, HD Hyundai partnerships with US yards, Saronic, Austal USA and Bollinger hold the government-backed expansion. Navy programmes go to established primes through long acquisition queues, and a new yard has no delivery history.
ai_answer_to_killer: Do not start on the Navy rung. Start on barges and tugs, where the gate is ABS rules plus USCG inspection on human but short timescales, the buyer is commercial, and the company can be its own customer through an owned fleet, so it gets delivery history without a procurement queue. AI makes a small yard productive enough that capex per delivered tonne is competitive at small scale: robotic cells instead of a 3,000-person workforce. The machine-generated weld-evidence record is what lets ABS approve the process rather than inspect every ship by hand. Against Korean entrants, the moat is a domestic, frozen, open PDK that fabless US and allied designers can target. Hanwha and HD Hyundai bring their own designs and do not sell their rules.
competitors: HII, General Dynamics (NASSCO, Electric Boat, Bath), Fincantieri Marinette, Austal USA, Bollinger, Eastern Shipbuilding, Philly Shipyard/Hanwha, HD Hyundai-US yard partnerships, Saronic (Port Alpha, small hulls), Hadrian (precision parts, not hulls), Path Robotics (welding tool vendor).
principles_used: P1 freeze the target (a ship PDK); P13 certify the process, not the plant or the part; P3/P11 own the scarce qualified capacity; P5 standard modules for Wright's-law learning; P4 delta-qualification evidence as a by-product of production.

name: Breakwater Power (shipbreaking feedstock into an owned floating firm-power fleet)
sector: Maritime hardware / energy (floating power)
one_liner: Intercept end-of-life ships before the breakers' beach, at scrap price, keep their large medium- and low-speed engines and hulls, convert them with AI-designed dual-fuel/LNG and control retrofits into floating power plants, and own and operate them, selling firm power to islands, ports, defence bases and data-centre sites that cannot wait 5+ years for turbines or interconnection.
what_it_owns: The floating power fleet: hulls, engines and their update authority (P8). It also owns the AI-built parts and conversion library for orphaned marine engine models, the operating and reliability record that sets its cost of capital (P10), and long-term PPAs and capacity contracts.
wedge_first_revenue: Buy 1-2 large vessels (bulkers, container ships, ro-paxes with multi-engine diesel-electric plants, or cruise ships, whose diesel-electric plants of 40-80 MW are already power stations) at scrap value. Convert them in a cheap repair yard (Turkey, the Middle East, Southeast Asia) and moor them under an emergency or bridging PPA at an island grid, a mining port or a military base. First revenue comes from capacity plus energy payments in est. 12-18 months. The materially new angle against the gas-turbine resurrection fleet: feedstock comes from the global shipbreaking stream (hundreds of large ships a year) with mobility built in. The asset moves to wherever the price spikes, which software-style statistical multiplexing cannot do on land (P3 'capacity that moves').
ladder: 1) Bridging power for islands and emerging-market grids (Karpowership's proven market). 2) Defence and allied basing: mobile, hardened, islandable power for Pacific bases and forward ports. 3) Data-centre bridging power at coastal sites in the US and allied nations, sold as firm MW-months while grid interconnection waits. 4) Convert to LNG, ammonia or methanol dual-fuel and pair with batteries, and securitise the fleet's PPA book (P10) to become the largest owner of mobile firm capacity.
numbers: Search budget was exhausted in this run, so these are prior-knowledge figures marked est. Karpowership (Turkey) operates est. 40+ powerships with est. 6+ GW of capacity across about 14 countries (https://www.karpowership.com/en/about-us). That proves demand and the conversion model, though it mostly builds on second-hand bulker hulls with new Wärtsilä/MAN engines. Ship scrap prices on the Indian subcontinent ran est. $450-560/LDT in 2024-25, so a 20,000-LDT cruise or large ro-pax costs est. $9-12M with 40-70 MW of installed diesel-electric power, roughly $150-300/kW. New reciprocating-engine plants cost est. $1,000-1,500/kW, and new gas turbines $790-1,800/kW with 4-7 year slot waits (project figure). Conversion and LNG retrofit cost est. $150-400/kW, so all-in is est. $300-700/kW. Emergency and bridging tariffs run est. $100-250/MWh on islands, and capacity pricing hit PJM's cap of $333.44/MW-day (project figure). A 50 MW ship at 70% capacity factor x $150/MWh = est. $46M/yr revenue. $100M revenue = 2-3 ships in est. 3-4 years. Ceiling comparables: Karpowership (private, est. multi-$B revenue), Wärtsilä Energy (est. EUR 1.5-2B segment revenue), APR Energy (mobile turbines, bought by Atlas Corp for est. $750M in 2020), Aggreko (bought by TDR/I Squared for est. GBP 2.3B in 2021).
ai_role: AI cuts the per-ship engineering of heterogeneous conversions. It reverse-engineers each vessel's power management system, switchboards and engine controls, and generates retrofit control logic for grid-forming operation (P8). It builds the parts and equivalence library for out-of-production engine marks (P2/P7/P12) from scans, manuals and wear data. It runs per-engine condition models and dispatch optimisation across a moving fleet. It drafts the environmental, class and PPA technical packages (the per-unit paperwork law).
main_killer: Emissions and permitting at the destination: old marine diesels burning HFO or MGO will not pass US air permits, and host-country politics have expelled powerships (Karpowership's disputes in South Africa, Lebanon and Pakistan). Engine life and parts are another risk: very old hulls may be too far gone. Karpowership, the first mover, holds the emerging-market relationships.
ai_answer_to_killer: Select and redesign for the permit, not the hull. An AI screening pass over the global scrap queue (IHS/Clarksons data, class records) picks ships with modern medium-speed, LNG-capable or dual-fuel engines: post-2010 cruise ships, ro-paxes and LNG carriers increasingly go to scrap young, and their 4-stroke engines can be converted. AI-designed SCR plus dual-fuel retrofit packages are built from a reusable library, so each conversion is a recompile, not a bespoke project. Aim first at regimes where the buyer is its own gate (P14): military bases, mining ports, island utilities under emergency orders, and data-centre behind-the-meter sites offshore of strict airsheds. Defence and allied buyers are a market Karpowership's Turkish ownership cannot easily serve, which lets the company take a different rung.
competitors: Karpowership (dominant powership owner), Wärtsilä and Everllence (engine OEMs who sell new engine plants), Siemens Energy and GE Vernova mobile/trailer turbines, APR Energy, Aggreko, ProEnergy, Seaboard Marine-style barge-mounted plants, and new entrants in floating nuclear (Core Power) as the long-term threat.

name: Fenceline Rail: autonomous behind-the-fence rail operator
sector: Rail - industrial, port, plant and terminal switching
one_liner: Take over and own the rail operations inside plants, ports, ag terminals, refineries and mines (outside FRA's general-system jurisdiction) with a fleet of autonomous battery-electric switching locomotives and railcar movers, and sell 'car moves' per car under a long-term contract, then roll up adjacent short lines.
what_it_owns: The switching fleet (autonomous, battery or hybrid; partly resurrected frames). The operating contracts and often the in-plant track assets bought from the host (sale-leaseback of rail infrastructure). The autonomy stack and its safety case, accepted by insurers. A growing car-move and incident record that serves as its own gate (P14). Eventually, short-line railroads with STB operating authority.
wedge_first_revenue: Inside a plant's fence, rail is behind an ownership boundary: FRA treats plant railroads that do not operate on the general system as outside most of its rules (FRA policy statement, 49 CFR Part 209 App. A, est. interpretation; verify). So the operator plus its insurer is the gate, and autonomy can ship without a federal type approval. First customer: a grain elevator, steel mill, chemical plant or port that now runs its own diesel switcher with 2-3 crews per shift. Offer a fixed per-car-move price about 20-30% below its current all-in cost, plus diesel elimination (an ESG and permit win).
ladder: 1) One plant with 2-3 owned autonomous switchers, paid per car. 2) Standard site package: 50-200 industrial sites (about 10,000+ US industries with rail sidings, est.). Each site gets an AI-built digital twin of its track, the autonomy stack, and a remote supervision centre. 3) Buy the in-plant track and car-storage assets, becoming the infrastructure owner that collects storage and demurrage-style fees. 4) Buy small short lines that serve these plants, and use the accumulated safety record to seek FRA waivers or pilot programmes for autonomy on low-speed general-system track. 5) Become the 'last-mile rail utility' for re-industrialising America (fabs, battery plants, data-centre transformer yards), owning the first and last mile that the Class Is have neglected.
numbers: Market: industrial switching and terminal rail services in the US, est. $3-5B/yr (est., based on about 10k+ rail-served facilities and crew costs of $300k-$1M+/site/yr). The short-line sector has about 600 railroads, about 47,500 route miles, and est. $5-6B revenue (ASLRRA; est.). Unit economics (est.): a manned diesel switcher operation costs a site $0.8-1.5M/yr including crews, fuel and maintenance. An autonomous battery switcher plus remote supervision costs est. $250-400k/yr to run on a $1-1.5M owned asset, so a contract at $700k-1M/yr gives 50%+ gross margins. Time to $100M revenue: est. 5-7 years, about 120 sites at $800k. Capital: est. $5M seed for the first 3 sites, then equipment ABS. Ceiling comparables: Genesee & Wyoming (about $8.4B take-private, 2019), Watco (private; industrial switching plus short lines, est. $1B+ revenue), OmniTRAX/Broe, Patriot Rail. Autonomy comparable: Parallel Systems (est. $100M+ raised). Note: live search was unavailable this run; figures are marked est. and should be verified.
ai_role: (1) Autonomy: perception and planning for low-speed (under 10 mph) switching in fenced yards, a far easier domain than roads. (2) AI turns each site's track maps, switch lists and car-ordering history into a digital twin and automatic switch plans (the compiler from customer intent to moves, P1). (3) Fleet telemetry from every car move becomes an insurer-grade safety record (P9, P14). (4) AI drafts the site safety plans, OSHA/MSHA documentation and insurer submissions. (5) It reverse-engineers and resurrects old switcher frames into battery units.
main_killer: Sales cycle and liability fear. Plant managers are conservative, a derailment or crush injury inside a chemical plant is catastrophic, and site-by-site variation (track condition, switches, crossings) makes each deployment custom. Class I and union politics may also fight autonomy at the interface with the general system.
ai_answer_to_killer: Sell an outcome under a performance contract with a captive-insurance-backed guarantee and remote human supervision during ramp-up. Start on sites with no public crossings, low speed and dedicated track. AI makes per-site onboarding cheap (a scan-to-twin within days) and turns heterogeneity into many site-specific models rather than one fragile generic one. Staged rollout (canary sites) and an operating record priced by an insurer replace the absent regulator approval. Union exposure is lower because many target sites use non-union plant crews or contractors; any expansion onto the general system waits until the record supports a waiver.
competitors: Watco, OmniTRAX, RailServe/Savage, Genesee & Wyoming industrial services, Trackmobile (railcar movers, owned by Wabtec? est.; verify), Shuttlewagon. Autonomy: Parallel Systems, Intramotev (autonomous battery railcars for mines and industry, est. funding $20M+), Rail Vision, Wabtec Trip Optimizer. Most either sell equipment or provide manned services, not owned autonomous capacity paid per car move.

score.name: Fenceline Rail: autonomous behind-the-fence rail operator
score.rationale: This one escapes the gatekeeper law best. Plant railroads that never run on the general system sit largely outside FRA rules (49 CFR 209 App. A, which I know from memory). So the operator plus its insurer is the gate, and low-speed autonomy in a fenced yard is a plausible ML problem. It owns a fleet, contracts and, later, track and short lines, so it is not a service. Comparables are real: G&W sold for about $8.4B, and Watco and OmniTRAX are large. Numbers: a 50% gross margin on $700k-1M per site is plausible. But reaching $100M takes about 120 custom site deployments at under $1M each, sold on slow industrial cycles. Many rail-served plants are switched by their serving Class I or by contractors such as RailServe, not by their own crews, so the real pool of displaceable in-house operations is probably 1-3k sites, not 10k. Defensibility rests on the per-site operating record and long contracts. It is moderate: Intramotev, Parallel and Watco could copy it, and the record compounds only slowly. The short-line rung keeps the ceiling but brings back the FRA/STB queue.
score.biggest_risk: Fragmented, slow per-site enterprise sales of under $1M per year each, with catastrophic-liability fear at chemical and steel plants. Getting to $100M in 7 years needs 120+ conservative plant managers to sign, and the serving Class I or an incumbent contract switcher can match on price.

name: Second Life Pipeline Co.: buying idle steel pipelines and requalifying them with AI for water, CO2 and hydrogen
sector: Pipelines: transmission pipe and rights-of-way repurposed for water conveyance, CO2 and hydrogen
one_liner: Buy idle, underused or abandoned steel pipelines and their rights-of-way for cents on the replacement dollar, requalify them with ML on in-line-inspection and material data under PHMSA's existing integrity pathways, and run them as an owned fleet carrying water, CO2 or hydrogen blends under long-term transport contracts.
what_it_owns: The pipe in the ground and the rights-of-way, which take a decade and eminent-domain fights to recreate. It also owns requalification evidence for each line (MAOP reconfirmation and material verification records, ILI history, integrity models) and long-term take-or-pay transport contracts. Permission plus installed base, the moat that knowledge cannot copy.
wedge_first_revenue: Buy one idle 50-300 mile crude, products or gas line in Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas or the Permian, where midstream companies carry idled lines as liabilities (abandonment cost, ongoing integrity obligations). First revenue options: (a) brackish or produced-water and reclaimed-water conveyance to data centres, industrial users or municipalities in water-short regions; (b) CO2 transport for ethanol and industrial capture with 45Q credits, following Tallgrass's conversion of its Trailblazer gas line to CO2. Transport tariffs start once the line is requalified, about 12-24 months after purchase.
ladder: 1) First line: acquire, requalify, sign one anchor shipper. 2) Build the 'reverse compiler' for pipe: ILI, records and metallurgy turned into a requalification package, used on 5-10 more lines. 3) Own a regional network of repurposed lines (water in the Southwest and Texas, CO2 in the Midwest, hydrogen blends near Gulf hubs). 4) Add owned compression and pumping, and storage (salt caverns, aquifer storage and recovery). 5) Become a midstream-scale owner of repurposed transport infrastructure: the 'resurrection fleet' applied to linear assets.
numbers: Asset base: about 3M+ miles of US gas pipelines (transmission plus distribution) and about 230k miles of hazardous liquid lines under PHMSA (est., https://www.phmsa.dot.gov/data-and-statistics/pipeline/annual-report-mileage-gas-distribution-systems). New-build cost (est.): about $3-10M per mile for large-diameter pipe, before years of permitting. Summit Carbon's roughly 2,500-mile CO2 project was estimated at about $8.9B and stalled on eminent-domain and state bans (est.), which shows the right-of-way is the scarce asset. Idle-line acquisition price (est.): often near salvage or a negative value net of abandonment liability, about 5-15% of replacement cost. Precedent: Tallgrass converted the roughly 390-mile Trailblazer natural gas line to CO2 service (est.). Tariff (est.): CO2 transport about $10-30/t; water conveyance about $0.5-2.0 per 1,000 gal. Capital: about $20-60M per first line, including requalification and repairs. Time to $100M revenue (est.): about 6-9 years with 4-8 lines. Ceiling comparables: Kinder Morgan (market cap about $60B, est.) and Tallgrass (Blackstone-owned). Note: the search budget was exhausted this run; numbers without URLs are est. from memory.
ai_role: (1) ML on decades of in-line-inspection (MFL, UT, EMAT) runs aligns and grows defects, predicts remaining life and flags crack and corrosion clusters, which narrows dig verification to the fewest excavations. (2) Material verification: ML on in-situ hardness, strength and chemistry tests plus records infers pipe grade and toughness where records are missing. That is the 'decompiler' for traceable, verifiable, complete records gaps. (3) Paperwork: drafting MAOP reconfirmation, engineering critical assessments, conversion-of-service filings and shipper due diligence. (4) Operations: leak detection and pressure-cycle fatigue management across a fleet of heterogeneous lines.
main_killer: Permission on two fronts. First, PHMSA requalification and conversion-of-service rules; for CO2, PHMSA's pending CO2 safety rule after the Satartia, MS rupture. Second, easement law: many old easements are limited to oil or gas, and landowners will litigate a change of commodity. Hydrogen also embrittles older steels.
ai_answer_to_killer: Use pathways that already accept engineering evidence. PHMSA's 2019 gas rule (49 CFR 192.624 MAOP reconfirmation and 192.607 material verification) explicitly allows engineering critical assessment and non-destructive material testing, so AI-cut evidence cost fits an existing accepted channel and needs no new regulator behaviour. Pick commodities and lines the easement language covers: water and CO2 in states with clear statutes, and conversion-of-service under 192.14. AI-driven title and easement review across thousands of parcel documents ranks lines by legal risk before purchase, so the company buys only clean ones. Hydrogen comes later, and only on low-hardness steels identified by the material models.
competitors: Tallgrass (CO2 conversion, Blackstone-backed); Kinder Morgan and Enterprise (CO2 and gas, could repurpose their own lines); Summit Carbon, Wolf Carbon Solutions (new-build CO2); water-transfer firms such as WaterBridge and Aris Water (produced-water pipe; Aris merged into Western Midstream in 2025, est.); integrity-tool vendors such as Baker Hughes, ROSEN and ONEbyONE (service).
principles_used: P5/P12 (installed base plus evidence held as a permission, not knowledge), P4 (AI drives acceptance cost below build cost through existing engineering-assessment rules), P9 (ILI history becomes the owner's evidence), P10 (take-or-pay tariffs on cheap assets).

score.name: Second Life Pipeline Co.: buying idle steel pipelines and requalifying them with AI for water, CO2 and hydrogen
score.rationale: Web search budget was exhausted, so these scores rest on prior knowledge. The Tallgrass Trailblazer conversion (about 390 miles, gas to CO2) and the Summit Carbon stall are real precedents. They show that rights-of-way are the scarce asset and that idle lines can be requalified. N: buying lines near salvage value is plausible. But water tariffs at $0.5-2 per 1,000 gal on a 50-300 mile line give thin revenue per mile, and CO2 volumes depend on 45Q and on capture projects that stall. T: first revenue needs purchase plus 12-24 months of requalification plus an anchor shipper, so roughly 2-3 years; $100M within 7 years needs 4-8 lines and is borderline. C: the midstream comparables are real. A: ML on in-line inspection and material verification fits PHMSA's existing 192.624/192.607 engineering-evidence pathways. But ROSEN, Baker Hughes and ONEbyONE already sell this, so AI is not what makes the pain solvable. The main killers are easement scope and landowner litigation, and AI title review only screens which lines to buy; it does not change the law. D: owned pipe plus right-of-way is a strong permission and installed-base moat, though Kinder Morgan, Enterprise and Tallgrass can repurpose their own lines first.
score.biggest_risk: Easements limited to oil or gas, plus state CO2 pipeline opposition, turn each conversion into multi-year litigation. Meanwhile the obvious buyers of idle lines (Tallgrass and other midstream owners) convert their own best lines before a startup can bid.

name: Kilovolt: an owned 800 VDC solid-state power train, sold per delivered MWh
sector: Data-centre power distribution: solid-state transformers and 800 VDC rack power
one_liner: Build a characterised, UL-listed modular solid-state power cell from commodity SiC parts. It takes medium-voltage AC straight to 800 VDC racks and replaces the GOES-steel transformer, switchgear, UPS and PDU chain. Kilovolt keeps ownership of every installed cell and charges per MWh delivered with an availability SLA.
what_it_owns: The frozen target, a 'PDK for power' (P1/P13): one published, characterised cell design (for example 250 kW-1 MW blocks) with design rules, UL listings and an accelerated-life evidence base. Also the installed fleet, kept on the balance sheet under power-train-as-a-service contracts, plus the fleet's operating history, which is what eventually lets it be financed.
wedge_first_revenue: Nvidia's 800 VDC architecture for Kyber/Rubin Ultra racks (from 2027) needs MV-to-DC conversion that does not yet exist at scale (NVIDIA technical blog, May 2025, https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-800-v-hvdc-architecture-will-power-the-next-generation-of-ai-factories/, prior knowledge). First revenue: a 2-5 MW pilot hall at a neocloud or AI colo, owned by Kilovolt and billed per MWh delivered plus a capacity fee. The customer avoids roughly 2 years of transformer and switchgear lead time and the floor space of the UPS and PDU rooms. Target 12-18 months to first pilot, using UL field evaluation for the pilot cells while the full listing proceeds.
ladder: 1) Rack-adjacent 800 VDC sidecar/PSU replacement fed from existing LV AC. 2) A full MV-to-800 VDC solid-state transformer, removing the GOES transformer and the UPS (DC-bus batteries and supercaps sit on the same bus). 3) A campus 'power block' that also connects on-site generation, solar and batteries on a common DC bus. This is where the value is, because it becomes the energy router between grid, generation and GPUs. 4) A fleet of tens of GW under per-MWh contracts, securitised. 5) The same cell sold, or kept on our books, for EV depots, electrolysers and grid substations, which have the same transformer bottleneck.
numbers: Market (est.): the data-centre power-distribution pool (UPS, switchgear, transformers, PDUs/busway) is est. $25-35B/yr in 2025 and growing 15-20%. Vertiv's 2025 revenue was est. about $10B, and Schneider's data-centre segment is est. about a quarter of its roughly EUR 38B revenue (prior knowledge, verify). Per MW (est.): a conventional MV transformer + switchgear + UPS + PDU chain is about $0.8-1.5M/MW. An SST cell target of $0.5-0.8M/MW at volume, with 2-4 points higher end-to-end efficiency (fewer conversion stages). On a 100 MW AI campus at $70/MWh, 3 points of efficiency is about $1.8M/yr. Delivered-MWh contracts at est. $8-15/MWh on top of the energy pass-through give a 6-9 year payback on a 20-year asset, with leverage at infrastructure spreads after 24-36 months of history. Capital: est. $40-80M to reach a listed product and pilot fleet, then asset-level debt. Time to $100M revenue: est. 5-6 years (about 1-1.5 GW under contract). Ceiling comps: Vertiv (market cap est. more than $50B, prior knowledge); Eaton bought Boyd Thermal for about $9.5B in 2025 (prior knowledge, verify); Schneider bought 75% of Motivair for about $850M in 2024 (prior knowledge).
ai_role: (a) A design compiler: AI-driven topology and magnetics optimisation of the high-frequency transformer and SiC stages, retargeted to whichever SiC/GaN module and magnetic material is in stock. This counters part scarcity, because the design is re-compiled to available components instead of waiting on one SKU (P1/P7). (b) Cheaper evidence: physics-informed reliability models plus active test selection choose the fewest highly accelerated life and power-cycling tests that support a 20-year MTBF claim. AI drafts the UL 1741/62368/IEEE 1547-style dossiers. (c) Software-defined capacity (P8): each cell's control law is updated over the air across the fleet we own, for example GPU load-swing smoothing, which Nvidia names as a 2027 problem, fast frequency response and dynamic derating. We hold update authority because we own the asset. (d) Fleet telemetry turns operating hours into the reliability case that lenders and insurers price (P9/P10).
main_killer: Reliability evidence. Hyperscalers and lenders want years of field history before they trust a new topology in the critical power path, and incumbents (Eaton, Vertiv, ABB, Delta, Schneider) are on Nvidia's 800 VDC partner list with installed-base trust. Well-funded startups are also already here: Heron Power (Drew Baglino), Amperesand, DG Matrix.
ai_answer_to_killer: Ownership turns evidence into a fleet asset. Because Kilovolt owns the cells and sells MWh with an SLA, the customer never has to trust the topology: it gets a contract, backed by a captive insurer and N+1 cell redundancy (P14). The cells are small and modular, so operating hours accumulate in parallel. 2,000 cells x 8,760 h is about 17.5M cell-hours a year, which gives an ETOPS-style statistical failure-rate case (P9) within 12-18 months, years ahead of a monolithic design. AI-picked accelerated tests and per-cell anomaly detection convert rare failures into frequent near-miss data. The SST startups sell boxes. Kilovolt competes by being the owner and operator, so its moat is the delivered-MWh book and its cost of capital, not the circuit.
competitors: Eaton, Vertiv, Schneider Electric, ABB, Delta Electronics, Infineon/Navitas reference designs (Nvidia 800 VDC ecosystem). Startups: Heron Power (Series A about $38M, 2025, prior knowledge), Amperesand (Singapore/US, SST, raised est. tens of $M), DG Matrix, Resilient Power (acquired by Eaton, 2023? verify). Integrators: Hitachi Energy (HVDC).
principles_used: P1/P13 (own the frozen, characterised target, 'PDK for power'), P6 (the 800 VDC interface is a new contract, so own the layer behind it), P8 (update authority over an owned fleet), P9 (evidence from parallel modular hours), P10 (power-train-as-a-service is a financing business), P14 (own the risk to own the gate).

score.name: Kilovolt: an owned 800 VDC solid-state power train, sold per delivered MWh
score.rationale: Search budget was exhausted, so this relies on prior knowledge. Nvidia's 800 VDC architecture announcement (May 2025) and Heron Power's roughly $38M Series A (2025) are real. N: keeping every cell on the balance sheet at $0.5-0.8M/MW means about $500-800M of capital per GW before $100M revenue. Margins of $8-15/MWh with 6-9 year paybacks are infrastructure returns, but they need cheap debt that a new topology cannot get until it has field history. That circularity caps N at 3. T: a UL-listed MV solid-state transformer in 12-18 months is optimistic, and 1-1.5 GW under per-MWh contracts by year 5-6 is a stretch. C: whoever owns the MV-to-800 VDC layer in AI factories, EV depots and electrolysers has a credible $10B+ ceiling (Vertiv). A: AI topology and magnetics compilation, plus test selection for accelerated-life evidence, is plausible. Pooling modular cell-hours to build a statistical failure-rate case is a real answer to the reliability killer. But the AI lift is a design-efficiency gain that Heron, Amperesand, Delta and Eaton can also use. D: ownership and the operating book compound slowly. The incumbents on Nvidia's partner list hold installed-base trust, and funded startups are ahead on hardware.
score.biggest_risk: Capital intensity combined with the trust gap. Owning the fleet needs hundreds of millions per GW of cheap debt that lenders will not give an unproven topology, while Eaton, Vertiv, Delta and Heron ship listed 800 VDC hardware first through the Nvidia ecosystem.

name: Foundry Zero: a qualified non-Chinese battery cell foundry with a published PDK
sector: Batteries (cell manufacturing for defence, drones, robotics)
one_liner: Buy a stranded Western cell line out of the 2024-2026 battery bust (Northvolt, Natron, Freyr/iM3NY-type estates) for cents on the dollar. Use AI to characterise it into a frozen, published 'battery PDK' (formats, electrode design rules, formation recipes, qualification evidence), and run it as the TSMC of FEOC-compliant cells for fabless battery designers in drones, defence and robotics.
what_it_owns: The physical cell line and its qualified process, which is the frozen target. It also owns the design rules and PDK, the UL 1642/2054/9540A and MIL qualification files, DoD and Blue-UAS supplier approvals, and per-cell manufacturing data. Over time it adds its own branded catalogue cells, as TSMC's role plus a fabless-product arm.
wedge_first_revenue: Multi-project pilot runs, the MOSIS analogue. Drone, robotics and defence primes that today buy Chinese 18650/21700 or pouch cells submit a cell spec inside Foundry Zero's design rules. They get 1,000-50,000 qualified cells in 8-12 weeks at a premium price. First revenue is about $2-5M from pilot runs in year 1. The hard deadline that creates demand: FY2024 NDAA Sec. 154 bars DoD from buying batteries from CATL, BYD, Envision, EVE, Gotion and Hithium starting October 2027 (https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/2670).
ladder: 1) Acquire a distressed line or pilot plant (about 0.1-1 GWh/yr) and its equipment. 2) Spend 6-12 months running designed experiments with in-line sensing to characterise it into a PDK, then publish the design rules. 3) Pilot runs for fabless designers (drone makers, robot firms, defence startups). 4) Volume contracts plus DoD and prime qualification, which makes Foundry Zero the approved source. 5) Add lines and formats, including sodium-ion and silicon-anode variants, as further 'process nodes'. 6) Launch a branded cell catalogue and take equity or royalties in designs that ramp. The value stays at the frozen target: line plus evidence plus capacity (P1, P13).
numbers: Supply side: Northvolt filed for bankruptcy in March 2025 after about $15B raised, and Lyten agreed to buy its Swedish plants in 2025 (est., from memory; searches were unavailable for this run). Natron Energy ceased operations in 2025 (est.). Several US cell projects (KORE, Freyr US, iM3NY) were cancelled or went into restructuring (est.). Used equipment changes hands at an est. 10-30% of new cost. Demand side: the US DoD drone push (2025 'drone dominance' directive; plans for hundreds of thousands to millions of small UAS, est.) and robotics need non-Chinese cells. Defence and drone cells sell at an est. $300-1,500/kWh, against Chinese LFP cells at about $50-60/kWh (est.). Market: a defence, drone and robotics non-FEOC cell market of an est. $3-8B/yr by 2030. Unit economics: 0.5 GWh/yr at $400/kWh is $200M revenue. The 45X production credit of $35/kWh for cells and $10/kWh for modules (est., retained in 2025 law with FEOC limits) adds $17.5M/yr at 0.5 GWh. Capital: about $40-120M to buy and recommission a distressed line, against $300M-1B greenfield (est.). Time to $100M revenue: est. 4-5 years. Ceiling comps: TSMC ($122.5B 2025 revenue, prompt data), Samsung SDI and LGES (each about $15-25B revenue, est.), EnerSys (about $3.6B, est.), Saft (TotalEnergies; about EUR 1B+, est.).
ai_role: AI does three jobs. (a) Process characterisation: Bayesian design of experiments and in-line vision and electrochemical sensing (coating thickness, calendering, electrolyte fill, formation curves) turn an undocumented line into a characterised one with predicted yield and quality windows. That is building the PDK, which until now took years of expert ramp; Northvolt died on yield ramp. (b) A design-rule checker and cell-design compiler: a customer's spec compiles into an electrode stack and a formation recipe the line can actually run (P1). (c) Early life prediction from formation data, so qualification cycling and the evidence package are shorter and cheaper. Published ML predicts cycle life from the first ~100 cycles, est. Severson et al. 2019. AI also drafts UL/MIL qualification paperwork.
main_killer: Yield and cost. Battery lines are notoriously hard to ramp (Northvolt, Britishvolt), and Chinese cells cost 3-10x less. Defence demand may be lumpy, and DoD qualification queues (12-18 months) delay the bankable revenue.
ai_answer_to_killer: Do not compete on commodity $/kWh. Sell only into the market Sec. 154 creates by law, and into segments where cell cost is a small share of system value (drones, munitions, robots, space). There, price tolerance is 5-20x LFP. The yield risk is attacked directly: AI-driven DOE and in-line defect detection on a small line (0.1-0.5 GWh) learn faster per dollar than a gigafactory. While DoD qualification runs, commercial drone and robotics customers (UL only, no DoD queue) give revenue in year 1-2. Starting the DoD queue in 2026-27 lines it up with the October 2027 cliff, so the queue becomes a moat once cleared.
competitors: Amprius, Enovix, Lyten (Northvolt assets), KULR, EnPower, Sila and Group14 (materials), Our Next Energy, American Battery Factory, Ultium/LGES and Panasonic US (automotive), EnerSys/Saft (defence). Most are product companies; none is positioned as an open-PDK foundry for fabless cell designers (est.).
principles_used: P1 (compiler useful only against a frozen target; own the target), P3 and P13 (pooled qualified capacity behind a PDK interface: the TSMC/MOSIS pattern), P11 (abundant fabless battery designers, value at the qualified cell), P4 (fast early-life evidence).

score.rationale: Search budget was used up, so I checked from memory: Northvolt filed for bankruptcy in March 2025, and Lyten agreed to buy its Skellefteå and Västerås assets in 2025. Natron shut down in September 2025. FY2024 NDAA Sec. 154 bars DoD from buying batteries from CATL, BYD and others from October 2027. The demand deadline and distressed supply are both real. AI answers the main killer, yield ramp, plausibly: Bayesian design of experiments, in-line defect detection and early life prediction (Severson et al.). That earns A=4. N is weak. $40-120M to buy and recommission a line before any revenue is heavy for a seed company. name: Grid Socket: retiring coal plants turned into owned thermal-storage power stations
sector: Industrial heat and long-duration storage
one_liner: Buy retiring coal plants mainly for their scarce grid connection and steam island. Replace the boiler with AI-dispatched thermal batteries (crushed rock, graphite or sand heated by cheap off-peak and curtailed power), and sell firm capacity, steam and 10-100-hour storage as owner-operator.
what_it_owns: Interconnection rights at existing points of interconnection (the permission that takes about 5 years to get from scratch), the land, water rights and steam turbine-generators, the thermal storage it builds, and capacity and steam contracts. It also owns an AI-built parts and controls library for orphaned 1960s-80s steam turbines.
wedge_first_revenue: Option and buy 1-2 coal units (200-600 MW) scheduled to retire. Many sell for near-zero or negative value once decommissioning liabilities are counted (est.). Keep the turbine and switchyard. The first revenue is immediate: run the existing unit to its retirement date under a DOE 202(c) order or capacity commitment, or sell capacity, while adding a 50-100 MWh-thermal pilot charged from grid power to prove the steam swap. Use FERC surplus interconnection service (Order 845) to add resources behind the existing connection without re-queuing (est. applicability per ISO).
ladder: 1) Buy the site and capture the capacity payments. 2) Pilot thermal storage feeding the existing steam cycle. 3) Fully convert: storage plus turbine sells firm capacity at PJM-cap levels and arbitrage across 10-100 hours. 4) Add steam and heat sales to neighbouring industry and co-locate data centres that want an existing connection and firm power. 5) Roll up 5-20 sites (5-10 GW) with standardised conversion skids; the reverse-compiled turbine-control and parts library becomes a cost edge across the fleet. 6) Finance it like a utility once there is operating history (P10).
numbers: Interconnection scarcity: about 2,300-2,600 GW was waiting in US queues in recent Berkeley Lab counts, with a median of about 5 years from request to operation (https://emp.lbl.gov/queues; figures est. from memory, searches unavailable this run). Supply of sites: US coal fleet about 170-180 GW, with tens of GW scheduled to retire by 2030 (est., EIA). Capacity value: PJM cleared at the $333.44/MW-day cap for 2027/28, about $122/kW-yr (prompt data), so a 500 MW converted unit earns about $60M/yr from capacity alone. Storage cost: thermal media plus containment is an est. $10-30/kWh-thermal. At about 35-40% heat-to-power efficiency through an existing turbine, that is an est. $30-80/kWh-electric of storage, against $200-300/kWh installed for Li-ion BESS (est.), and it suits 10-100-hour durations Li-ion cannot serve economically. Capital: about $150-400M per 500 MW conversion (est.); site purchase at an est. $0-50M. Time to $100M revenue: est. 3-4 years, because capacity revenue starts on day one at the first site. Ceiling comps: Vistra (about $17B+ revenue, est.), NRG, Talen and Constellation; data-centre-adjacent firm power trades at high multiples (est.). Peer funding: Antora about $150M Series B in 2024 (est.), Rondo backed by Breakthrough Energy (est.), Fourth Power about $19M Series A (est.).
ai_role: AI does four jobs. (a) It reverse-compiles 40-60-year-old turbine control logic (relay, analog, early DCS) into a modern owner-controlled stack, and builds a scan-to-TDP parts library for orphaned steam turbine components (P8, P12). (b) It forecasts and dispatches thermal charging against nodal prices, curtailment and capacity-performance windows. (c) It drafts the interconnection and surplus-interconnection studies, environmental and decommissioning permits, and state public-utility-commission paperwork, which is per-unit labour. (d) It builds a site-selection model that ranks every retiring unit by connection value, turbine condition, neighbouring heat demand and liabilities. AI does not shorten FERC or ISO queues; owning an existing connection avoids them.
main_killer: Round-trip efficiency (about 35-40% heat-to-power) makes pure arbitrage weak against Li-ion. Coal-site environmental liabilities (ash ponds, CCR rules) can exceed asset value. ISOs may not let a storage-turbine hybrid keep the full existing connection rating or the capacity accreditation.
ai_answer_to_killer: Do not sell round-trip efficiency; sell scarce attributes. Capacity accreditation (ELCC) for 10-100-hour firm resources is worth far more than its arbitrage spread, and the connection itself is the asset. Steam and heat sales to co-located industry or data centres use the heat without converting it back to power, which lifts system efficiency to an est. 70-90%. AI-driven due diligence on environmental records, groundwater data and CCR filings rejects sites with uncapped liabilities. Structures where the seller keeps or indemnifies ash-pond liabilities make sites buyable. On accreditation: keep the same turbine-generator and the same connection point, so the generator 'looks' the same to the ISO, and add resources through surplus-interconnection rules; the existing fleet interface is the moat (P6).
competitors: Rondo, Antora, Fourth Power, Electrified Thermal Solutions, Kraftblock, Brenmiller, Malta (est. status), utilities and IPPs (Vistra, NRG, AEP) repowering their own coal sites with gas or batteries, and data-centre developers buying coal sites for their connections (est.). Thermal-storage firms sell tech; Grid Socket owns the site, the connection and the output.
principles_used: P6 and P12 (the existing interconnection as the frozen interface; reuse it instead of queueing), P8 (update authority over orphaned turbine controls), P3 (owned, scarce, pooled firm capacity), P10 (output sale as financing), P1 (thermal storage modules compiled to the turbine's frozen steam conditions).

score.name: Grid Socket: retiring coal plants turned into owned thermal-storage power stations
score.rationale: Search budget was used up, so I checked from memory: PJM 2027/28 cleared at the $333.44/MW-day cap, and US queues hold over 2,000 GW with a median of about 5 years. The connection is a real, ownable asset (D=4), and day-one capacity revenue at one site gives a fast T. The buy-near-zero assumption breaks the 'sellers price in hope' law. Since 2024-25, retiring coal sites have been bid up by data-centre developers who want their connections (for example, Homer City-type redevelopments). DOE 202(c) orders are also keeping units online. So site prices, plus $150-400M per conversion and ash-pond and CCR liabilities, make N only 3. A fails the bar. The killers are round-trip efficiency, environmental liabilities and ISO accreditation of a storage-turbine hybrid, and those are answered by deal structure and choice of market. AI site diligence and turbine-control reverse engineering are marginal to all three. The thermal storage technology itself is non-AI (Rondo, Antora). Total 17, and A is below 3.
score.biggest_risk: Data-centre developers outbid it for coal-site connections, and the AI role is peripheral to accreditation and liability, the things that actually decide the idea.

name: Steam Commons: an owner-operated industrial heat utility that is its own boiler gate
sector: Industrial heat (steam and process heat, electrification, thermal storage, optional hydrogen)
one_liner: Buy the boiler houses of US factories in sale-leasebacks, run them as one fleet under its own National Board R-stamp repair authority and its own HSB-style inspection-and-insurance captive, and electrify them over time with electrode boilers, heat pumps and thermal storage. Sell steam per tonne on 10-20-year contracts.
what_it_owns: The heat plants themselves (boilers, steam networks, thermal storage, electric heaters), long-term steam purchase agreements, its own R-stamp and repair procedures, a captive insurance vehicle, and a pooled fleet operating and inspection record. That record is the evidence for risk-based inspection and for cheaper capital. It also owns an AI parts and burner-management library for orphaned boiler brands.
wedge_first_revenue: Mid-size food, beverage, chemical, paper and pharma plants with 20-60-year-old gas boilers. Their pains are capex for replacement, emissions-permit pressure and lost boiler-operator labour. Steam Commons pays about 0.5-1x book value for the boiler house, takes over operations, staff, insurance and compliance, and bills about 5-15% below the customer's current all-in steam cost. First revenue arrives at the first takeover, about 4-6 months from signing.
ladder: 1) Take over existing gas boiler houses and run them with remote AI monitoring and shared operators (one licensed operator watching several sites where state rules allow). 2) Get an ASME/National Board R-stamp and an in-house repair organisation, so repairs stop waiting on OEM service. 3) Form a captive insurer with telemetry-priced risk (the HSB 1866 model, revived by AI). 4) Electrify where power is cheap: electrode boilers plus thermal storage charged in low-price hours, with heat pumps for under 200C. 5) Use the fleet record to argue for risk-based inspection intervals with state jurisdictions and insurers. 6) At 500-2,000 sites, become the Veolia of US industrial steam, with a heat platform that can add hydrogen or biogas firing where it pencils out.
numbers: Market: about 40,000+ US industrial boilers above 10 MMBtu/h (est., DOE/ORNL boiler inventory). Industrial process heat is about 7-9 quads/yr of US final energy (est.). Typical industrial steam costs about $8-20 per 1,000 lb (est.), so a 50,000 lb/h plant at 70% load produces about 300M lb/yr, worth about $3-6M/yr of steam revenue. 300 sites gives about $1-1.8B revenue. Unit economics: the takeover price per site is an est. $1-5M; operating margin after fuel pass-through is an est. 15-25%; electrification projects add an est. $3-15M capex per site with fuel savings when off-peak power runs $20-40/MWh (est.). Capital: about $20-50M equity to reach 20-30 sites, then infrastructure debt. Time to $100M revenue: est. 4-5 years, at about 25-35 sites. Ceiling comps: Veolia (about EUR 44B revenue, est.), Engie Solutions, Ameresco (about $1.5-1.8B revenue, est.), Vicinity Energy (district steam, Antin-owned, est.), Redaptive (efficiency-as-a-service, about $1B+ raised, est.). Insurance precedent: HSB (Munich Re) reported about 506% ROI for its top 10 sensor clients (prompt data).
ai_role: AI does five jobs. (a) It audits sites in days from utility bills, DCS/historian data and photos, and prices a takeover offer, which used to cost weeks of engineering per site. (b) It runs remote condition monitoring and combustion optimisation (O2 trim, blowdown, trap failures), worth an est. 5-15% fuel savings. (c) It is the evidence engine for the captive insurer and for risk-based inspection arguments: AI-read ultrasonic and tube-thickness data with pooled failure models across non-identical boilers (P9). (d) It reverse-engineers parts and burner-management logic for orphaned boiler brands and drafts R-stamp repair packages (P12). (e) It co-optimises the electrified and thermal-storage dispatch against power prices.
main_killer: Each site is bespoke and sales cycles are long. Factory closure or bankruptcy strands the asset. State boiler jurisdictions and licensed-operator rules may block shared or remote operation, so the labour savings the model depends on do not materialise.
ai_answer_to_killer: AI site audit and standard takeover contracts compress the sales cycle. Targeting only investment-grade or long-lived plants (food staples, chemicals, pharma) and keeping equipment movable (skid-mounted electrode boilers and storage) limits stranding; a skid moves to the next site. For operator rules, start in states that already allow remote or unattended operation for some boiler classes (est., varies by state) and grow the insurer-grade record there. Then use the captive insurer plus the fleet record as the evidence for jurisdictions, the way NRC TSTF-425 moved test intervals to operator-controlled programmes on PRA evidence. Be your own gate where you hold the asset and the risk (P14).
competitors: Veolia, Engie and Ameresco (energy-as-a-service), Redaptive, Vicinity Energy, Rondo and Antora (heat-as-a-service from their own storage), Skyven Technologies (steam heat pumps, DOE-funded, est.), Cleaver-Brooks and Babcock & Wilcox (OEMs and service), independent boiler service firms. None runs a vertically integrated R-stamp, captive-insurance and owned-fleet model (est.).
principles_used: P14 (be your own gate: own the asset and risk, and the insurer-plus-inspection model), P10 (output sales as a financing engine with lower variance), P9 (pooled fleet evidence for inspection intervals), P8 and P12 (control and parts authority over orphaned boilers), P3 (pooled, owned heat capacity).

The fleet ownership model is real (Veolia, Vicinity and Ameresco are comps), so C=4, and first revenue at the first takeover makes T=4. N is thin. Most of the $3-6M per site is fuel passed through, so gross margin is about $0.5-1.5M per site on $1-5M takeover price plus $3-15M of electrification capex, which makes it an infrastructure-return business. name: Blue Foundry (the qualified, allied-made drone component foundry)
sector: Security / defence hardware: drone and counter-drone supply chain
one_liner: Build the TSMC of non-Chinese small-drone hardware: owned, automated, qualified lines for the 6-8 components every drone and interceptor needs (motors, ESCs, flight controllers, gimbal cameras, datalink radios, battery packs, thermal cores). It publishes a 'drone PDK' (design rules plus reference designs) so any drone builder compiles to it, and holds the compliance approvals that every integrator inherits.
what_it_owns: (1) Scarce qualified capacity: highly automated motor-winding, PCB-assembly and cell-to-pack lines in the US and allies. (2) The frozen, characterised process and its PDK: design rules, test data and reliability curves per component family (P1, P13). (3) The signed compliance status: NDAA Sec. 848/817 provenance, Blue UAS Framework component listings, FCC equipment authorisations and any exemptions from the Covered List restrictions on foreign drones and components, TAA compliance. Drones built from its parts inherit these approvals the way a fabless chip inherits a foundry's qualification (P7 'signed equivalence'). (4) Multi-year take-or-pay supply agreements with drone primes and with DoD consumable-drone programmes.
wedge_first_revenue: Start with the component that has the worst Chinese dependence and the simplest qualification: brushless motors plus ESCs for Group 1-2 drones and interceptors (est. 70-90% Chinese-sourced today). Sell qualified drop-in motor/ESC sets with full provenance and an FCC-ready data package to the 50+ US drone startups and interceptor makers that are blocked by the component rules. First revenue within about 9-12 months from a pilot line (est. $5-10M capex), priced at about 1.5-2.5x Chinese equivalents but well below current US boutique pricing (est.).
ladder: Rung 1: motors and ESCs. Rung 2: flight controllers and a compliant autopilot board (with a frozen open firmware target, the 'ISA' for drones). Rung 3: gimbal EO/IR and thermal cores (thermal is the hardest Chinese dependency). Rung 4: battery cells-to-packs with non-Chinese cells (partnering with US and Korean/Japanese cell makers). Rung 5: datalinks and anti-jam radios. Rung 6: full 'reference airframes' that any startup can brand. The company becomes the mandatory substrate: thousands of drone designers (abundant builders, P11), one qualified foundry. Later: allied replicas (Ukraine, Taiwan, Poland, Baltics) under licence, and counter-drone interceptor airframes built entirely on its own parts.
numbers: Web search was unavailable in this run, so figures are prior knowledge, marked est. Demand: in July 2025 the Pentagon directed services to treat small drones as consumables and scale purchasing ('Unleashing U.S. Military Drone Dominance' memo, est.); DoD plans to buy hundreds of thousands to about a million small drones over 2-3 years (est. $1B+ programme). Ukraine produced an estimated 2-4M drones in 2024-2025 (est.), largely on Chinese components. The FCC's Covered List (https://www.fcc.gov/supplychain/coveredlist) was extended in late 2025 to foreign-produced drones and critical components, subject to security exemptions (est., confirm details). DJI held about 70-90% of the US market (est.). Comparables: Skydio has raised about $740M+ (est.); Neros (FPV drones) raised a Series A/B in 2025 (est.); ModalAI (US flight controllers) is privately held; Unusual Machines (NYSE American: UMAC) is a public US drone component maker (est. small revenue). Unit economics (est.): a motor/ESC set at $60-150 in volume with 35-45% gross margin on automated lines; one line of about $8M capex makes about 500k sets/yr, about $50M of revenue. TAM (est.): about $3-5B/yr of US and allied military small-drone components by 2028, plus about $10B+ of commercial and public-safety drones forced off Chinese supply. Time to $100M revenue: about 4-5 years. Ceiling comparables: TSMC ($122.5B 2025) for the foundry pattern; at sector scale, TransDigm/HEICO-type component owners (est. $8B and $4B revenue) and Amphenol for an interconnect-like component franchise.
ai_role: (1) AI design compilers turn a customer's spec (thrust, kV, weight, duty cycle) into a component variant inside the frozen PDK in hours, so the foundry serves thousands of designs while running a small number of qualified process families (P1). (2) In-line ML inspection (winding resistance and back-EMF signatures, X-ray of solder, cell formation data) gives every unit a machine-generated evidence record, so 'qualified once, built many' holds (P13). (3) AI-run, lights-out lines close the labour-cost gap with China. (4) LLM-generated compliance and provenance dossiers (NDAA, FCC, Blue UAS, TAA, customs traceability) turn months of paperwork into days per SKU. (5) Reverse-engineering of best-in-class Chinese parts into clean-room US equivalents (the Phoenix BIOS move, P12).
main_killer: Chinese cost and scale, plus demand volatility. DJI and the Shenzhen supply chain produce components at a fraction of US cost and can cut prices or flood allied markets. US military demand is lumpy, budget-dependent and often routed through primes who may vertically integrate (Anduril, Skydio, AeroVironment build in-house), leaving a merchant foundry with idle capacity.
ai_answer_to_killer: (1) Policy sets a hard floor: the Covered List, NDAA provenance rules and tariffs mean the competitor for most US and allied buyers is not Shenzhen but expensive boutique US supply, so the target is 'cheaper than other compliant parts', not 'cheaper than DJI'. (2) AI-run automated lines plus a small set of frozen process families give Wright's-law volume on few SKUs (P5), which in-house prime lines building small volumes cannot match. That is the TSMC argument against IDMs. (3) Take-or-pay and capacity-reservation contracts, plus DoD capacity grants (DPA Title III and Office of Strategic Capital loans, est.), de-risk utilisation the way CHIPS did for fabs. (4) Inherited approvals are the lock-in: a prime that builds in-house must qualify and document every part itself, while Blue Foundry parts arrive pre-cleared, so even vertically integrated primes buy commodity layers. (5) Allied demand from Ukraine, Taiwan and NATO evens out US budget lumpiness.
competitors: Chinese incumbents (T-Motor, DJI internal, Hobbywing, iFlight, Shenzhen supply chain); US and allied: Unusual Machines (UMAC), ModalAI (flight controllers), Orqa (Croatia, FPV components), KDE Direct (motors), Teledyne FLIR (thermal cores), Amprius and Lyten (cells), Doodle Labs and Silvus (radios, Silvus est. acquired by Motorola 2025 for about $4.4B). Integrators that build in-house: Skydio, Anduril, AeroVironment, Neros, Shield AI. No one owns a multi-component qualified foundry with a published PDK.

score.rationale: Search was unavailable, so this is judged from prior knowledge. To my knowledge the FCC added foreign-produced UAS and critical components to the Covered List in Dec 2025, and the July 2025 'drone dominance' memo treats small drones as consumables. That gives a real policy floor and a fast motor/ESC wedge with revenue in 9-12 months. The economics (about $8M line, about $50M/yr revenue, 35-45% gross margin) are plausible but depend on take-or-pay contracts, and military demand is lumpy. N=3, T=4. The ceiling has good comparables (TransDigm/HEICO, Silvus at about $4.4B), but a $10B foundry outcome is a stretch. C=4. The killer is Chinese cost plus volatile demand.
