score.biggest_risk: Primes and funded drone startups bring motors and electronics in-house or get their own approvals, leaving a merchant foundry with weak lock-in, idle capacity and margins squeezed by a policy floor that could shift.

name: Hartford Shield (an insurer-operator for sabotage, drone and physical-attack risk)
sector: Critical-infrastructure protection: physical security, insurance and hardening hardware
one_liner: Do for sabotage what Hartford Steam Boiler did for boilers in 1866: underwrite infrastructure owners against physical attack, drone, vandalism and copper-theft losses, on the condition that the company installs and operates its own sensor, hardening and response fleet at each insured site. It owns the risk book, the fleet and the loss data, and uses AI to make the risk priceable.
what_it_owns: (1) The insurance book: an MGA first (underwriting authority from a fronting carrier and reinsurers), becoming a risk-bearing carrier or protected-cell captive as it builds a record. (2) The owned protective fleet at insured sites: perimeter sensors (fibre-optic fence sensing, radar, thermal, acoustic gunshot detection), ballistic barriers for transformer radiators, autonomous patrol units, and integration with the Overwatch-style drone layer where available. (3) The loss-and-telemetry record that insurers, regulators (NERC CIP-014) and lenders accept: the 'operating hours become admissible evidence' asset (P9). (4) Its own physical-security standards ('Hartford standards' for substations, cell towers, pipelines, water plants), which can become the industry code (P14).
wedge_first_revenue: Start with the most frequent, best-measured losses: copper and equipment theft, vandalism and gunfire at substations, cell towers and solar and BESS farms. Solar and battery sites are a good wedge, because owners face rising theft and insurers are already restricting cover (est.). Offer a bundled policy plus hardening-and-monitoring service at about $15-60k per site per year (est.), with lower deductibles and higher limits than the market because the company's own fleet cuts expected loss. Target independent power producers, tower companies and co-ops. First premium within about 9-12 months via an MGA plus a fronting carrier.
ladder: Rung 1: theft and vandalism cover with an owned sensor fleet at renewable, BESS and tower sites. Rung 2: substation physical-attack and business-interruption cover for utilities and co-ops, priced against CIP-014 and E-ISAC data. Rung 3: drone and UAS-attack cover for data centres, refineries and ports (pairing with the airspace-utility layer). Rung 4: become a full carrier or captive with its own capital, and parametric products (pay-on-trigger when an owned sensor confirms an attack and outage), securitised as cat bonds. Rung 5: the 'Hartford standard' becomes what utilities, regulators and lenders reference, and the company certifies third-party sites (the UL position) on top of insuring its own.
numbers: Web search was unavailable in this run, so figures are prior knowledge, marked est. Precedent: HSB, founded 1866, combined inspection with insurance; Munich Re's HSB reported about 506% ROI for its top sensor clients and 13B+ sensor readings (from the P9 brief). UL Solutions had about $3.1B revenue in 2025 with about a 17% operating margin (from the P4 brief). The TRIA federal terrorism backstop exists (https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-markets-financial-institutions-and-fiscal-service/federal-insurance-office/terrorism-risk-insurance-program). Threat: physical-security incidents reported to the E-ISAC in the thousands per year (est.); the Moore County attack (2022, about 45,000 customers out for days); widespread copper theft and solar-farm theft (est. tens of millions of dollars a year). Market (est.): US commercial property premium about $150B+; the sabotage, theft and terror slice for energy, telecom and water infrastructure about $5-10B of premium; physical-security spending on critical infrastructure about $20B+/yr. Unit economics (est.): $40k average premium-plus-service per site, about a 45% loss-and-LAE ratio after sensor-driven loss reduction, about $8-12k/site of fleet capex amortised over 5 years. Time to $100M revenue (premium plus service): about 5-6 years (about 2,500 sites). Ceiling comparables: HSB (acquired by Munich Re for about $742M in 2009, now a much larger specialty franchise, est.), Hiscox/Beazley specialty carriers ($5B+ revenue, est.), and Lemonade/Kin-type insurtechs where owning the risk book is the value.
ai_role: (1) Per-site, per-hour risk pricing from live telemetry, threat intelligence, geography and site layout: the underwriting paperwork AI collapses, letting a small team price thousands of heterogeneous sites (P9, P14). (2) Sensor fusion and vision models that cut false alarms enough for one operations centre to cover thousands of unmanned sites, and that dispatch response or derate equipment early (detect-and-derate in place of rollback). (3) Automated claims and forensic evidence: an attack's sensor record becomes the claim file and the police file at once, with parametric triggers paid within days. (4) Generative site-hardening design (barrier placement, camera and fibre layouts) priced against modelled expected-loss reduction, so each hardening dollar maps to a premium credit. (5) Portfolio correlation modelling to avoid concentrated common-mode exposure.
main_killer: Insurance capital and catastrophic correlation. A coordinated attack campaign or a terror event creates a fat-tailed, correlated loss that a young carrier cannot absorb. Fronting carriers and reinsurers demand years of loss history before giving underwriting authority or capacity, and state insurance regulation adds licensing queues, the 'lenders want 24-36 months of history' law in insurance form.
ai_answer_to_killer: (1) Start where loss frequency is high and severity is bounded (theft and vandalism, with sublimits), so loss history builds within 12-24 months instead of waiting for rare catastrophes. (2) The owned telemetry fleet is the evidence reinsurers lack elsewhere: AI-scored per-site risk with a measurable before/after loss reduction lets reinsurers price a new MGA's book on data rather than history, as Swiss Re priced Waymo's miles. (3) Push the catastrophic tail to the instruments built for it: the TRIA backstop for certified terrorism, parametric cat bonds, and reinsurance layers. Keep the attritional layer, where the AI-driven variance reduction becomes margin. (4) The MGA-then-carrier route (as Lemonade, Kin and Coalition did for cyber, est.) sidesteps the initial licensing queue. (5) Being the operator of the protection fleet as well as the insurer makes the company its own gate (P14): it controls the risk it underwrites rather than relying on the customer's compliance.
competitors: Specialty and terror insurers (Munich Re/HSB, Lloyd's syndicates, AIG, Chubb, Beazley, Pool Re in the UK); physical-security operators (Allied Universal, Securitas, ADT Commercial); infrastructure-security hardware (Prosegur, Senstar, Ameristar ballistic barriers, Knightscope, LiveView Technologies mobile towers, Asylon drone patrol, Cobalt Robotics, Flock Safety); and insurtech MGAs in adjacent risks (Coalition for cyber at a reported $5B valuation, est.; Kettle for wildfire). None bundles owned protection hardware with an owned risk book for infrastructure sabotage.

name: Upgrade Capital (owner of the uprate megawatts and the open safety-I&C platform)
sector: Nuclear: operating fleet capacity expansion (uprates, digital I&C, restarts)
one_liner: Fund and execute power uprates and analog-to-digital I&C modernisation for reactors outside the big fleets, in exchange for owning an undivided interest in the incremental megawatts. Use an NRC-approved, AI-built open safety platform and measurement-uncertainty methodology that the company owns as its update authority.
what_it_owns: (1) Contractual undivided ownership of uprate MW and their output (P8: the software uplift becomes an owned asset). (2) The NRC-approved topical reports (safety I&C platform plus feedwater-flow/thermal-power measurement methodology), which every plant can reference, so later licence amendments are 'by precedent' (P2/P6: owning the approved equivalent). (3) The control layer and update channel on each modernised unit under long-term agreement (P8). (4) Fleet performance data that lowers its cost of capital (P10).
wedge_first_revenue: Measurement-uncertainty-recapture (MUR) uprates, ~1.5-1.7% of output, at single-unit, municipal, co-op and merchant owners that lack Constellation's engineering bench. These are the lowest regulatory risk and cheapest $/kW of any uprate. Pair with analog I&C replacement that SLR plants must do anyway (Oconee ~$100M/unit; EPRI >$80M for two units first-of-a-kind). First revenue is the sale of the company's share of uprate MWh into PJM/MISO or to a data-centre offtaker under a PPA (hyperscalers are already paying for uprates).
ladder: 1) MUR uprates for an ownership share (~15-25 MW per unit). 2) Bundled digital I&C modernisation on the company's own platform, which creates update authority and recurring service revenue. 3) Stretch and extended power uprates (5-20%) using fleet-wide AI thermal-hydraulic and component-margin analysis. 4) Co-investment in restarts (the Palisades/Duane Arnold/Crane model) for owned slices. 5) Become an independent owner of 1-3 GW of 'found' nuclear capacity, a nuclear IPP built without new reactors.
numbers: Constellation's uprate programme costs ~$4.3B for ~890 MW, ~$4,800/kW, backed by Google (https://technologyreview.com/2026/10/15/1146577/nuclear-power-upgrade; https://www.powermag.com/google-deal-backs-890-mw-of-constellation-nuclear-uprates-at-11-pjm-reactors/). The NRC expects ~2.4 GW of uprate applications through 2032, and 3-8 GW is available in total (same MIT TR source). Browns Ferry: $475M for +14% (same). 171 uprates approved as of 2022 (https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/fact-sheets/power-uprates.html). Digital I&C: Oconee ~$100M/unit and EPRI >$80M for two units (https://nuclearplantmod.epri.com/MTA-EN-009; https://www.power-eng.com/operations-maintenance/the-battle-of-obsolescence/). Restart loans: Duane Arnold $1.9B (https://www.kcrg.com/2026/09/08/19-billion-federal-loan-moves-duane-arnold-nuclear-plant-closer-restart/). Unit economics (est.): an MUR uprate costs ~$1,500-3,000/kW, below the stretch/EPU cost. At ~$80/MWh firm clean power (hyperscaler PPA) and a 92% capacity factor, each kW earns ~$645/yr, so payback is ~3-5 years. 1 GW of owned uprate MW is ~$650M/yr of revenue (est.). Capital: ~$2-3B for 1 GW, project-financed after the first 2-3 projects (DOE LPO eligible) (est.). Time to $100M revenue: ~150 MW owned at about year 5-6 (est.). Ceiling comparables: Constellation (~$100B market cap, est.), Talen and Vistra nuclear fleets.
ai_role: AI makes the control layer and the engineering abundant. It translates and replaces legacy analog/relay logic, generates and verifies safety software against IEEE 7-4.3.2 and NRC BTP 7-19 (diversity and defence-in-depth) requirements, and auto-produces V&V documentation. ML-calibrated thermal-power measurement reduces uncertainty, which is the physical source of MUR megawatts. Fleet-learned component-margin models (turbine, generator, feedwater, heat exchangers) identify where stretch uprates fit. LLMs draft licence amendment requests referencing approved precedent, and the owner-operator keeps fleet before/after evidence.
main_killer: The gatekeeper queue and incumbency. Uprate LARs and digital I&C reviews go through NRC on human timelines, and a new safety platform topical report historically takes years. Large fleet owners (Constellation, Vistra) do uprates themselves and will not give up MW, and Westinghouse/Framatome hold the approved platforms.
ai_answer_to_killer: Use the queue once and reuse it many times. MUR uprates already follow a standard NRC review path, and with the 2025 executive order's 18-month review target and the NRC's increased use of AI in review, precedent-referencing LARs get faster. The company invests once in a platform/methodology topical report (or licenses an approved platform, such as TXS Compact which recently received an SER, as a bridge) and every later plant references it. That is the PDK move, owning the approved target. Target the ~30-40% of US units held by single-unit, municipal, co-op and smaller owners without engineering benches, whose alternative is no uprate at all. AI-driven engineering cuts the $/kW enough to give them free MW plus modernisation in exchange for a share. Hyperscaler PPAs (Google, Amazon already pay for uprates) supply the offtake that finances it.
competitors: Constellation, Vistra and NextEra (in-house uprates); Westinghouse (Common Q) and Framatome (TELEPERM XS / TXS Compact, https://www.neimagazine.com/?p=105475); GE Vernova (Hitachi BWR uprates); Curtiss-Wright, Rolls-Royce (Spinline), Lockheed MeTAS (FPGA platforms); Sargent & Lundy and Enercon (engineering services). No one found who takes ownership of uprate MW as a business model.
principles_used: P8 (update authority over an installed base), P6/P2 (an approved platform as the reusable equivalence), P10 (selling output, financed on fleet predictability), P9 (fleet evidence), P1 (own the approved target the AI compiler emits to).

score.name: Upgrade Capital (owner of the uprate megawatts and the open safety-I&C platform)
score.rationale: Note: no web search ran (turn budget used up); scored from prior knowledge and the cited sources. Owning uprate MW is a real ownership shape, and 1 GW owned at about $80/MWh is ~$650M/yr, so a $1B+ outcome is credible (C4). The weak part is the wedge. MUR is only ~1.5% of a unit, ~15-17 MW. Most US units already belong to large fleets (Constellation, Vistra, Duke, Southern, Dominion, TVA, NextEra, Entergy), and many have already done their MUR. The real pool of single-unit, municipal and co-op owners is roughly 10-15 units, so MUR alone gives ~200 MW. Utilities can raise capital cheaply and hyperscalers already pay them directly, so the reason to give away a share of the MW is weak. Ownership needs a co-licensee amendment plus a refuelling-outage cycle, which pushes first revenue to about 2.5-3.5 years (T3). AI shortens engineering and drafting of licence amendment requests (LARs), but a new safety-I&C topical report is still a multi-year NRC queue, and Westinghouse and Framatome hold the approved platforms. Licensing TXS as a bridge removes the moat. Defensibility comes from approvals reused as precedent plus owned MW, but large fleets can copy it in-house.
score.biggest_risk: Few reachable plants: the large fleets do their own uprates with cheap capital, and the remaining small owners give only a few hundred MW of MUR.

name: Jointworks: the actuator foundry (a TSMC for robot joints)
sector: Robotics: actuators, reducers, motors
one_liner: Freeze and characterise a small family of robot joints (motor, strain-wave or cycloidal reducer, encoder, drive) as a published 'robot PDK', make them on owned AI-run lines, and sell those joints with their evidence to every humanoid, cobot and defence-robot builder that today waits on Harmonic Drive and Nabtesco or buys from China.
what_it_owns: The frozen target. That means the qualified joint lines (gear grinding, heat treat, assembly, end-of-line dyno), the published design rules and simulation models (the PDK), and a growing life-test record. That record is millions of instrumented joint-hours from an owned accelerated-life farm plus field telemetry from customer robots, and it is what lets a buyer trust a stated L10 life. It also owns the brand and listing (UL/CE, later defence source approval) attached to each SKU. The record cannot be copied with a drawing.
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1: 3-4 SKUs of a strain-wave joint (about 20-150 Nm) that bolt in place of Harmonic Drive CSG/SHG sizes for US humanoid and cobot startups and research labs. The pitch is a 4-8 week lead time against months, about 40-50% below Japanese list, US/allied origin rather than Chinese (NDAA/tariff-safe), and a datasheet backed by published life-test curves. First revenue is est. $2-5M from 5-10 design wins, each a few hundred to a few thousand joints. The 'compiler' (an AI joint configurator: pick torque, speed, envelope, get a validated joint and URDF/sim model in minutes) is free and is the funnel. The line and the evidence are what Jointworks sells.
ladder: 1) Strain-wave joints for humanoid and cobot startups, US/allied-made. 2) A cycloidal/RV-class high-torque joint for industrial arms and legs (Nabtesco's territory) plus a replacement-reducer catalogue for the installed base of about 4M+ industrial robots (est.), where failed reducers are a large recurring aftermarket. 3) Defence-qualified joints (UGVs, EOD arms, loaders) using MOSA interfaces, where non-Chinese origin is mandatory. 4) Volume humanoid supply as the merchant joint fab every humanoid OEM without its own line uses, the way fabless chip firms use TSMC; Wright's-law cost decline on cumulative joints. 5) Integrate up into owned robot fleets (see the other ideas) as the captive buyer.
numbers: Market: strain-wave and RV precision reducers are est. $2-3B/yr today, and the joint module market (motor+reducer+drive) is est. 3-4x that. Actuators are est. 40-60% of a humanoid's BOM (est.; widely cited by sell-side teardown reports, not verified this run). If humanoids reach 1M units/yr at about 20-28 joints each, joint demand is 20-28M/yr; at $300-800 per joint that is est. $6-22B/yr. Incumbents: Nabtesco has an est. ~60% share of RV reducers and Harmonic Drive Systems is the leading strain-wave supplier (est., widely reported; not re-verified this run). Unit economics: est. joint ASP $400-1,500, 35-45% gross margin at scale (TSMC 59.9% GM is the ceiling comparable; https://marklapedus.substack.com/p/tsmc-gains-foundry-share-but-others-lose-ground). Capital: est. $15-25M to the first line (precision gear grinding and dyno farm), $150-300M for a 1M-joint/yr plant. Time to $100M revenue: est. 5-6 years (about 150-250k joints/yr at about $500). Ceiling comparables: Harmonic Drive Systems and Nabtesco are each multi-billion-dollar public companies (est.), and the fabless/foundry precedent is TSMC at $122.5B of 2025 revenue (https://ocacnews.net/article/422076). Web search was unavailable this run, so market figures marked est. need checking.
ai_role: (1) Design compiler: generative gear-tooth and flexspline design with surrogate stress and fatigue models, sweeping thousands of variants against the line's own measured behaviour. (2) Process compiler: AI CAM and closed-loop gear grinding with in-process metrology, so a novice-staffed line reaches master-gear-grinder quality (the 34% novice-lift mechanism, https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161). Precision gear-making know-how is the actual Japanese moat. (3) Evidence compiler: an accelerated-life farm whose current, vibration and thermal signatures train a remaining-life model per joint, so each shipped joint has its own birth certificate. That record is the hardware lockfile. (4) Active test selection to reach a credible L10 life with the fewest physical life tests.
main_killer: Chinese reducer makers (Leaderdrive and others) already sell strain-wave reducers far below Harmonic Drive. Big humanoid OEMs (Tesla, Figure, Chinese makers) are vertically integrating their own actuators. So a merchant joint fab may be squeezed between cheap Chinese supply and captive in-house lines, and precision gear-making know-how is famously slow to acquire.
ai_answer_to_killer: Compete on owning the evidence and on origin, not on lowest price. Western defence, industrial and medical buyers increasingly cannot use Chinese reducers (tariffs, NDAA-style sourcing rules), and they need a trusted life number, which Chinese suppliers do not publish. AI-run grinding and metrology collapse the decades-long know-how curve into data from the line itself, and the life farm produces trust faster than history alone. For captive OEMs, the TSMC lesson applies: most humanoid makers (dozens of startups) cannot fund a precision gear fab, so the merchant fab gets the long tail, and even integrators second-source. The PDK (sim models plus design rules) makes Jointworks the default target, so switching away means re-qualifying a robot.
competitors: Harmonic Drive Systems (JP), Nabtesco (JP), Leaderdrive and other Chinese reducer makers, Sumitomo Drive (cycloidal), Schaeffler and Timken (entering humanoid actuators, est.), in-house actuator programmes at Tesla, Figure and Unitree, and startups building actuators for their own robots. Funding of those startups was not re-verified this run.
principles_used: P1 (freeze and characterise the target: a robot PDK), P3/P11/P13 (own the scarce qualified capacity, TSMC-style), P7 (signed equivalence: drop-in for HD/Nabtesco sizes), P5 (Wright's law on standard modules)

score.name: Jointworks: the actuator foundry (a TSMC for robot joints)
score.rationale: Search budget was exhausted. From prior knowledge, Harmonic Drive Systems has roughly $400-500M of annual revenue (multi-billion market cap, not revenue) and Nabtesco's precision reducer segment is several hundred million. So today's reducer comparables are mid-sized, and the $1B+ case rests on humanoid volume. N3: a first line at $15-25M is raisable and joint ASPs of $400-1,500 at 35-45% GM are plausible, but Chinese strain-wave reducers sell far cheaper and a 1M-joint plant costs $150-300M. T3: first design-win revenue within 2 years is plausible, while $100M by year 5-6 depends on humanoid ramps. C4: if humanoids scale, merchant joint supply is a multi-billion market; reshoring and defence add a floor. A3: AI closed-loop grinding and metrology plausibly compress the precision know-how gap, and life-farm evidence plus non-Chinese origin answer the China killer for defence and industrial buyers. AI does not answer captive in-house actuator lines at Tesla, Figure and the Chinese OEMs. D3: qualified capacity, life-test records and design-in switching costs compound, though Schaeffler, Timken and Japanese incumbents can build US capacity. Passes the owns-the-asset rule. Short of 19 because the price squeeze from China and captive OEMs is only partly answered.
score.biggest_risk: Squeeze between cheap Chinese reducers and vertically integrated humanoid OEMs leaves a merchant Western joint fab with subscale volume, and Schaeffler/Timken/HDS can localise in the US.

name: Gatehouse Labour: a humanoid and mobile-robot labour utility with its own captive insurer
sector: Robotics: humanoids, AMRs, mobile manipulators
one_liner: Own and operate a mixed fleet of humanoids and mobile manipulators (buying from whichever OEM is cheapest), deploy them only behind customer fences (warehouses, plants, yards, military depots), and sell guaranteed labour-hours. A captive insurer prices the risk from the fleet's own safety telemetry, so the operator becomes its own gate while humanoid safety standards are still being written.
what_it_owns: The fleet. It also owns the safety-evidence record (incident and near-miss data per robot-hour, the hardware analogue of Waymo's Swiss Re dataset), the captive insurance entity and its loss history, the ISO safety-case documentation per site class, and the multi-OEM control and teleoperation layer that makes any brand of robot callable.
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1: 30-60 robots (est. $20-100k each, from Chinese and US OEMs) doing tote moving, trailer unloading and machine tending at 3-5 sites on a 3-shift model. Price is est. $15-25 per robot-hour, below fully loaded human cost of est. $30-40/hr for shift work. Teleoperators cover the gaps (one remote operator per 5-10 robots at first). First revenue is est. $2-5M.
ladder: 1) Fenced industrial sites in the US. 2) A captive insurer with fleet-priced premiums, which turns safety data into a margin and a sales argument (customers' insurers accept the captive's cover). 3) Depots, shipyards and military logistics (DoD pulls for labour-short depot work). 4) Securitise labour-hour contracts. 5) Become the de-facto source of evidence for humanoid safety standards and the largest buyer of robots in the West, so OEMs build to its specification and interface (the Facebook/OCP move: a dominant buyer imposes the standard).
numbers: Labour pool: about 1.9M US warehouse and storage workers (BLS, est.) and a $1T+ global manual-handling wage pool (est.). Humanoid hardware prices are falling: Unitree G1 listed at about $16k (est., widely reported), and Figure raised at a $39B valuation in 2025 (est., widely reported; not re-verified this run). Unit economics (est.): a $50k robot running 5,000 hr/yr at $18/hr is $90k/yr of revenue. At 50% gross margin after teleop, maintenance and insurance, payback is under 1.5 years. Capital: est. $15-20M equity for the first 200 robots, then asset debt. To $100M revenue: about 1,200-1,500 robots at about $70-80k each, est. 5-6 years. Ceiling comparables: staffing firms (Adecco, Randstad at tens of billions of revenue, est.), United Rentals as owned-fleet rental, and Waymo/Swiss Re as the evidence precedent (25.3M miles, 88%/92% fewer claims; from P9). Insurer comparable: HSB/Munich Re's IoT loss model (P9).
ai_role: (1) Foundation models for robot manipulation (VLA) make general-purpose tasks feasible; the operator uses whichever model is best across OEMs. (2) Fleet learning: every deployed hour produces training data that only the owner holds, so skills compound (the P9/P11 point that craft data compounds only for the owner of the cell). (3) Safety telemetry and anomaly detection turn rare incidents into frequent, cheap near-miss events, which give an actuarially useful loss table quickly. (4) AI drafts the per-site risk assessments and the ISO 10218/25785-style safety case, plus the insurance submissions.
main_killer: Humanoids may not be reliable or productive enough yet (low mean time between failures, slow cycle times, heavy teleop dependence), so cost per useful hour could exceed human cost for years. OEMs such as Figure, Agility and Tesla may also run their own RaaS and refuse to sell to an operator.
ai_answer_to_killer: Stay multi-form-factor: deploy wheeled mobile manipulators and AMRs where humanoids are not ready, and humanoids only where tasks justify them, so revenue starts now. Price on outcome, and use teleoperation (AI-assisted, with one operator covering many robots) as the bridge. Each teleop hour is training data that raises autonomy, so the cost curve falls with the fleet's own hours. On OEM refusal: Chinese and second-tier OEMs (est. dozens) will sell, and the operator's demand aggregation plus its safety evidence make it the buyer OEMs want. Owning the captive insurer means OEMs that refuse to sell also lack the risk record that customers' insurers ask for.
competitors: Agility Robotics (RaaS for Digit), Figure, Apptronik, Tesla Optimus, Boston Dynamics/Hyundai, Formic, Locus Robotics (AMR-as-a-service), GXO and staffing firms piloting humanoids, and Chinese makers (Unitree, UBTech) with their own leasing. Funding figures were not re-verified this run.
principles_used: P14 (the gate sits at the ownership boundary; be your own approver behind the fence), P9 (operating hours become evidence that an insurer prices), P10 (labour-hours as financeable recurring revenue), P3 (pooled fleet behind an API), P6 (the dominant buyer imposes the interface)

score.name: Gatehouse Labour: a humanoid and mobile-robot labour utility with its own captive insurer
score.rationale: Not searched this run (budget used up); figures recalled. The Figure $39B valuation (Sept 2025) and the Unitree G1 at about $16k base are as recalled. Agility has publicly priced Digit RaaS near $30/hr, which is about the same as human cost, not $15-25. The unit economics need 5,000 productive hours a year at 50% margin after teleop. Current humanoids fall well short of that on MTBF and cycle time, so near-term revenue would come mostly from AMRs and mobile manipulators, a crowded field (Locus and others). First revenue in 2 years is possible; $100M in 7 depends on humanoid maturity. The ceiling is large: a labour pool in the trillions, staffing-firm comparables, and a fleet-plus-insurer model. The captive insurer and the safety-evidence record are the novel moat, and fleet learning compounds for the owner. But OEMs (Agility, Figure, Tesla) are running their own RaaS with far more capital, and GXO and staffing firms can aggregate demand too. AI is the bridge (teleop data to autonomy), but whether humanoids become productive soon enough is outside the operator's control.
score.biggest_risk: Cost per useful robot-hour stays above human cost for years while capital-rich OEMs run their own RaaS and keep the best hardware and the fleet data.

name: Rotable Pool: power-by-the-hour for the world's orphaned industrial gearboxes and main bearings
sector: Industrial machinery: gearboxes, main bearings, large rotating drivetrains (wind, mining, cement, pulp, steel, marine)
one_liner: An airline-style rotable exchange pool for heavy drivetrains. The company owns thousands of remanufactured, AI-characterised gearboxes and main-bearing assemblies, swaps them into customers' assets ahead of failure, and charges per operating hour or per MWh. Uptime risk moves onto the company's balance sheet, and failure evidence piles up in its own data.
what_it_owns: (1) A fleet of rotable gearboxes and main-bearing units (owned inventory, financeable like aircraft engines). (2) Owned remanufacturing and dynamometer test-stand capacity, which is scarce: multi-MW back-to-back test rigs cost $5-20M each and are few in North America (est.). (3) A reverse-engineered parts library for orphaned designs (gear sets, planet carriers, bearing replacements, including upgraded designs). (4) The fleet telemetry and failure database that prices the hourly contract and lowers its cost of debt.
wedge_first_revenue: Out-of-warranty US wind turbines from 2005-2014. Many come from OEMs that have exited or orphaned platforms (Clipper, Gamesa G8x in the US, early GE 1.5 variants, Suzlon, Acciona/Nordex AW, Mitsubishi MWT). Gearbox failures there are a leading driver of downtime cost. A gearbox swap costs about $300-600k including crane, and lead times for some platforms are 6-12+ months (est.). Wedge: sell remanufactured gearboxes on exchange (core credit), shipped in weeks from pool stock, at about 30-40% below new OEM. Then convert customers to a per-MWh drivetrain availability contract.
ladder: 1) Exchange sales on orphaned wind gearboxes and main bearings. 2) Per-MWh or per-hour drivetrain uptime contracts (the TotalCare model) across a fleet of about 10-20 GW. 3) Upgraded 'generic' drivetrain designs: AI-designed replacement gear sets and bearing arrangements that fix known failure modes (white-etching cracks, planet-bearing failures) and are standardised across several orphaned platforms, cutting SKU count the way GE's nozzle went from 20 parts to 1. 4) Extend to mining mills, cement, pulp and paper, and marine thrusters: same physics, same orphaning, higher hourly value per failure. 5) Own the repowered assets themselves: buy distressed old wind farms whose drivetrains you control, keep them alive with the pool, and sell the power, a materially different angle from the turbine resurrection idea.
numbers: Global wind installed base is about 1,000+ GW (GWEC Global Wind Report, https://gwec.net/global-wind-report-2024/), of which the US is about 150 GW (est.). Turbines past warranty are about 60%+ of US capacity (est.). Wind O&M is about $15-20B/yr globally, with drivetrain major components about 20-30% of that (est.), so about $3-5B of addressable drivetrain spend in wind alone. Industrial gearbox and bearing aftermarket outside wind is about $10-15B (est.). Unit economics: a reman gearbox costs about $120-200k to rebuild and sells or exchanges at $250-400k (est.). An uptime contract earns about $4-8k/MW/yr (est.), so 10 GW gives about $40-80M/yr recurring at 30-40% contribution margin (est.). Capital: $15-30M to seed a pool of about 50-100 rotables plus one test stand, then debt-financed inventory, since rotables are collateral the way engines are for aircraft lessors. Time to $100M revenue: 5-7 years (est.). Ceiling comparables: AerCap/engine lessors (Willis Lease ~$500M+ revenue, est.), GE Vernova services, Rolls-Royce TotalCare, Timken/Kaydon industrial services. Note: the search budget ran out in this run, so figures are from prior knowledge, est.
ai_role: (1) Reverse-engineering orphaned gear sets and bearings from scans, metallurgy and failure analysis, and designing improved replacements with surrogate contact and fatigue models. (2) Fleet prognostics: time-series foundation models on SCADA, vibration, oil debris and acoustic data predict remaining useful life across heterogeneous units, so swaps can be scheduled before failure (avoiding crane remobilisation and secondary damage). This is the variance-reduction engine that makes an hourly price and cheap debt possible (P10). (3) Automated inspection of returned cores (CV on gear tooth flanks, borescope, NDT) to grade and route cores. (4) AI-drafted repair procedures and test reports, so one engineer supports many platforms.
main_killer: Capital intensity and correlated failure. A pool of $200-400k rotables needs a lot of inventory before contracts exist. A design flaw in an AI-redesigned gear set could hit the whole fleet at once. And funded independents and PE-backed players (for example ZF and Moventas reman, Gearbox Express, Broadwind) already hold the first rung.
ai_answer_to_killer: Inventory: start core-backed, since customers trade in their failed units and each core becomes the next rotable, so the pool grows from customer-supplied iron. Then use asset-backed facilities once 24-36 months of AI-measured MTBF exist, the same path as engine-lessor ABS. Correlated failure: canary releases. A new design goes first to a few instrumented units with tight anomaly thresholds, and keeps design diversity across the pool (P14 break 3). Funded incumbents: they sell repairs, not uptime, and they cover few platforms. AI's per-SKU reverse-engineering cost advantage plus owning the risk-priced contract is a different business, and incumbent repair shops can become the company's overflow capacity.
competitors: OEM service (Siemens Gamesa, Vestas, GE Vernova, Nordex). Gearbox OEM reman (ZF Wind Power, Flender/Winergy, Moventas). Independents: Gearbox Express (US), Broadwind (gearing), Stork/Fluor, Timken (Philadelphia Gear), Brüel & Kjær Vibro and ONYX Insight (monitoring only: tools, per P9 not value capture). Main bearing: SKF, Schaeffler. None sells drivetrain availability per MWh across orphaned multi-OEM fleets at scale (est.).
principles_used: P10 (output/uptime subscription as financing; telemetry lowers cost of debt), P9 (owner of asset, data and risk captures monitoring value), P3 (pooled owned capacity: the rotable pool plus test stands), P12 (breaking orphaned-OEM aftermarket locks), P5 (standardised generic replacement modules reduce SKU count), P14 (owning the risk moves the gate inside)

Prior knowledge: a wind gearbox replacement including crane typically runs ~$300-500k, and orphaned platforms (Clipper, Gamesa G8x, Suzlon, AW) are real. N: core-backed pools reduce upfront capital, but a pool of $200-400k units plus multi-MW test stands is inventory-heavy, and $4-8k/MW/yr uptime pricing is unproven. name: Tonne Utility: owned autonomous haulage fleet sold per tonne
sector: Heavy mobile equipment - quarries, operating mines, large earthworks (haulage only, no drilling or exploration)
one_liner: Buy mid-life 90-240 t haul trucks and wheel loaders that have been orphaned by fleet replacement, re-control them with an independent autonomy and electric-assist stack, and own and run them as a haulage utility that sells tonne-kilometres moved to quarries, aggregates producers and producing mines under long-term contracts.
what_it_owns: The truck fleet, the independent autonomy stack and update authority across the fleet (P8), a reverse-engineered component library for wheel motors, final drives, engines and frames, and a haul-cycle and incident record that insurers and mine safety teams price. Long-term take-or-pay haulage contracts form the cash-flow book that gets securitised (P10).
wedge_first_revenue: Aggregates quarries and cement plants, about 10,000 in the US (est.), run small fleets of 40-100 t trucks with chronic driver shortages and cannot justify Cat Command/FrontRunner, which are OEM-locked to new fleets. Wedge: run haulage at 2-3 quarries with 4-8 owned, autonomously retrofitted used trucks and charge per tonne. A haul road inside the quarry lies behind the ownership boundary: MSHA plus the operator's own risk assessment, no type approval, so the company is its own gate (P14).
ladder: 1) Quarry haulage per tonne. 2) Large earthworks and infrastructure: dams, data-centre site preparation and highways, where cut-and-fill is huge and short-term. 3) Producing mines (overburden and ore haulage), competing with contract miners on cost per tonne. 4) Electrification: trolley-assist and battery retrofit of owned trucks; the company owns the energy uplift too. 5) Become the contract miner of choice: an asset-heavy, AI-native Thiess or MACA with the lowest cost per tonne and the cheapest debt, from its fleet record.
numbers: Market: global contract mining services est. $60-100B/yr (est.); Australian contract mining alone is est. A$20B+. US crushed stone and sand-and-gravel production is about 2.5B t/yr (USGS, est.), with hauling est. $1-3/t. Unit economics (est.): new Cat 793 or Komatsu 930E-class trucks cost $5-7M with lead times of 12-24 months; 10-15-year-old used trucks sell for est. $0.8-2M. Haulage operating cost is est. $0.5-1.5/t-km, with labour about 30-50% of cost in developed markets. Autonomy cuts labour and adds 10-20% productivity (OEM claims for Cat/Komatsu AHS: est. 15-30% productivity lift). A fleet of 8 trucks hauling est. 4Mt/yr x $1.5/t gives about $6M/yr per site, so $100M is about 17 quarry-sized sites or 3-4 mine contracts. Time to $100M revenue: est. 5-7 years. Capital: est. $10-15M for the first 2-3 sites, then equipment finance. Ceiling comparables: Thiess (Elliott bought 50% in 2023 at an implied est. A$4B+ valuation), Macmahon (est. A$700M+ market cap), NRW Holdings (est. A$1.5B+), United Rentals ($16.1B revenue, 2025, per the P3 brief). Autonomy comparables: Pronto (est. tens of millions raised), SafeAI (est. $38M+), ASI. Note: live search was unavailable this run; figures are marked est. and need verification.
ai_role: (1) Independent autonomy retrofit for mixed, older OEM trucks: the Phoenix-BIOS move (P12) on drive-by-wire. (2) Per-site digital twin and dispatch optimisation, the compiler from tonnes needed to truck assignments (P1). (3) Fleet predictive maintenance plus an AI-built component library (P5) keeps 15-25-year-old trucks at high availability. (4) Haul-cycle telemetry becomes the safety and reliability record that lowers insurance and debt cost (P9, P10). (5) AI drafts MSHA risk assessments, training records and site safety documentation.
main_killer: OEM and incumbent lock plus customer risk aversion. Cat and Komatsu control autonomy on their new fleets, and Cat and Komatsu dealers own the service relationship. Big miners trust contract miners with decades of record, and a single autonomous incident at a pit ends a contract. Truck utilisation is also tied to mine plans and commodity cycles.
ai_answer_to_killer: Start where the OEMs will not go: small and mid quarries and earthworks, with mixed-make fleets too small and too old for OEM AHS. There, autonomy plus electrification on cheap used iron is the only way to cut cost per tonne. AI makes the retrofit and the long-tail parts cheap enough per truck, and the site twin and remote supervision keep incidents within a canary-site, staged-rollout envelope. The cyclicality killer is answered by aggregates and infrastructure first (counter-cyclical, government-funded IIJA demand) and by take-or-pay contracts securitised against fleet records.
competitors: Caterpillar MineStar Command and Komatsu FrontRunner (OEM AHS), Hitachi/ABB, Epiroc/ASI Mining, Pronto, SafeAI, Built Robotics (exited heavy autonomy, est.), contract miners (Thiess, Macmahon, NRW/MACA, Downer, Ledcor, North American Construction Group), and equipment rental (United Rentals, Sunbelt). None owns an independent autonomous, resurrected fleet sold per tonne.

score.name: Tonne Utility: owned autonomous haulage fleet sold per tonne
score.rationale: Haulage only, not drilling or prospecting, so no rule breach. It owns a fleet and sells tonnes, and the contract-mining comparables are solid (Thiess about A$4B+, NRW, Macmahon). But contract mining runs on thin EBIT margins (about 8-12%), and used-iron economics depend on availability. The $6M-per-site figure assumes a large 4 Mt/yr quarry hauling at $1.5/t. Typical US quarry haul cost per tonne is lower, so revenue per site is likely overstated. The independent retrofit autonomy that is the AI wedge already exists and is sold as a service (Pronto in quarries, SafeAI). AI makes the job doable, but it does not answer the real killers: big aggregates owners (Vulcan, Martin Marietta) could buy retrofits themselves, and one incident ends a contract. Defensibility is fleet record plus contracts, which is moderate and copyable by contract miners partnering with Pronto.
score.biggest_risk: The owned-fleet layer adds capital and cyclical utilisation risk without a moat. Quarry owners can buy the same retrofit autonomy from Pronto or SafeAI and keep the margin, which leaves the startup as a thin-margin, capital-heavy contract hauler.

name: Iron Exchange: the HEICO plus component pool for heavy iron
sector: Heavy mobile equipment and rail - aftermarket components (locomotive engines and traction motors, mining wheel motors, final drives, ag and construction powertrains)
one_liner: Build and own the largest evidence-backed, reverse-engineered library of form-fit-function replacement components and a rotating pool of remanufactured major components (engines, power assemblies, traction motors, wheel motors, transmissions) for out-of-patent or OEM-locked heavy machines, and sell them per hour or per exchange with warranties underwritten by its own captive insurer.
what_it_owns: (a) A reverse-engineered TDP library of tens of thousands of part numbers, each with its own equivalence evidence: scan, metallurgy, test data and field hours. (b) A physical rotating pool of owned cores and remanufactured major components, which is scarce capacity, since cores are what the OEMs control. (c) A captive insurer and a warranty record, which act as the 'mark' (P4, P14). (d) Rights to substitute: approved-supplier status with railroads, mines and AAR (AAR M-1003 quality certification for rail parts). (e) Its own remanufacturing cells.
wedge_first_revenue: Start with EMD 645/710 power assemblies and GE traction motors (thousands of out-of-production units still running), plus Cat 3500/Komatsu large-engine and wheel-motor components for mining. OEM exchange prices there are high and lead times long. Offer a pooled exchange, same-week, priced est. 30-40% below the OEM, with a warranty equal to or better than the OEM's. Off-highway mining equipment and rail parts mostly need no FAA-style permission, so the gate is the buyer's acceptance plus warranty, and AI-built evidence plus a captive warranty is that gate.
ladder: 1) Locomotive engine and traction parts exchange (short lines, then Class I mechanical departments). 2) Mining and construction major-component pools: wheel motors, final drives, engines, hydraulics, priced per operating hour (power by the hour, P10). 3) Ag: open-repair parts and controllers for Deere, CNH and AGCO fleets, aided by the right-to-repair tailwind (FTC suit against Deere, Jan 2025). 4) Become the qualified second source for DoD ground vehicles (MRAP, HEMTT, M113 families) once the commercial record exists; DLA queues are long but the record shortens the case. 5) Own a fleet: use the pool cost advantage to lower owner-operator cost in the Horsepower Utility or Tonne Utility, being both library and fleet, so the library is a cost edge nobody else can use (P2 conclusion).
numbers: Market: Caterpillar alone targets about $28B of services revenue by 2026 (from about $24B in 2024, est., Caterpillar investor day). Global mining equipment aftermarket est. $40-60B/yr; North American locomotive and freight-car parts and services est. $5-10B (est.); global heavy-equipment remanufacturing est. $20B+ (est.). Unit economics (est.): a remanufactured EMD power assembly or traction motor exchange at $15-60k with 35-45% gross margin; a mining wheel motor or large engine exchange at $250k-1M with 30-40% margin. Per-part reverse engineering cost cut by AI from about $50-200k to about $5-20k (P6 brief), so the break-even moves from the top 2-5% of part numbers to the top 30-50%. Pool capital: est. $20-50M of cores to reach $100M revenue; time to $100M: est. 5-6 years. Ceiling comparables: HEICO (11,500+ PMAs, about 70% of OEM price, market cap est. $35B+ in 2026), Cat Reman, Wabtec Global Services, TransDigm (aftermarket-driven, est. $80B+). Note: live search was unavailable this run; figures are marked est. and need verification.
ai_role: (1) Reverse compilation: CT scans, CMM, spectroscopy and metallography to a TDP, plus AI-inferred tolerances and critical characteristics (P1, P2, P12). (2) AI ranks which parts to clone first, by price gap times volume, from OEM manuals, bulletins and customer usage data. (3) Surrogate physics and active test selection cut the anchor tests per part (P4). (4) Remanufacturing cells run with AI-captured craft (Hadrian-style ramp for machinists and welders, P11) and per-part inspection records. (5) Fleet telemetry from exchange units feeds the warranty actuarial model, so the captive insurer prices risk better than OEM warranties (P9).
main_killer: No permission gate means no permission moat: anyone with the same AI can clone the same parts, and OEMs (Cat, Komatsu, Wabtec) respond by cutting prices on contested parts, tying warranties and service agreements (CSAs) to genuine parts, and controlling cores. Long tail economics may also fragment revenue across too many low-volume SKUs.
ai_answer_to_killer: Since knowledge is levelled, the moat moves to three things AI does not level: (1) the owned core pool (scarce physical capacity: cores are finite, and the company buys them aggressively, including from stored locomotives and retired trucks); (2) the warranty and field-hours record underwritten by its own captive, which a fast-follower clone cannot copy; (3) being the operator's own fleet supplier in ideas 1 and 3, which guarantees volume. Like HEICO, it caps share at about 30% per part to avoid triggering OEM price wars, and uses AI to cover 10-100x more SKUs per engineer than incumbents, so it is the cheapest broad-line second source.
competitors: Caterpillar (Cat Reman, dealers), Komatsu Reman, Wabtec Global Services, Progress Rail, Cummins Reman, independent rebuilders (Swanson Industries, Hydraquip, Motive Power), aftermarket parts sellers (ITR, Berco for undercarriage, TRP/Paccar, Hensley), and in rail, Koppers/Amsted for rail-car parts. Digital inventory and reverse-engineering entrants: Haddy, Divergent (aero/auto), Re:Build Manufacturing, Physna/Thangs (search). None owns a pooled, warrantied, AI-built library across locomotive, mining and ag platforms.

score.name: Iron Exchange: the HEICO plus component pool for heavy iron
score.rationale: This runs straight into the law that hardware monopolies are held by permission, not knowledge. HEICO's moat is the FAA PMA. Rail and mining parts have no comparable gate, as the idea itself admits, and AI levels reverse engineering for everyone. The EMD 645/710 power assembly and GE traction motor wedge is already a contested aftermarket: Progress Rail, Wabtec, MotivePower, National Railway Equipment and many independent rebuilders sell remanufactured assemblies, so a 30-40% discount is unlikely to be there. First revenue is fast and margins of 30-45% are plausible, so N and T are fine. The pool of owned cores is real but thin scarcity: incumbents and core brokers already compete for cores. AI cuts reverse-engineering cost but does not answer the no-permission killer. It falls back on captive warranties and on being its own fleet customer, which needs a fleet idea first. Defensibility below 3 fails the gate.
score.biggest_risk: There is no permission moat in an already crowded remanufacturing aftermarket. OEMs and existing independent rebuilders match price on contested SKUs, so the company becomes a low-moat parts distributor.

name: Tributary Water: an AI-run owner of small US water utilities, built on one pre-approved standard plant
sector: Water / wastewater utilities (regulated drinking water and sewer systems)
one_liner: Buy failing small water and sewer systems, replace their one-off plants with one frozen, pre-approved modular treatment design, run hundreds of them remotely with AI under a few licensed operators, and earn regulated returns on the rate base we build.
what_it_owns: The utilities themselves: certificates of public convenience, service territories, and a rate base that earns an authorised return. It also owns the 'ISA': one characterised standard plant (skids for treatment, PFAS/arsenic/nitrate removal and lift stations) with its state plan approvals, operating history and parts library. That design is reused across every system it buys, and its fleet telemetry becomes the evidence regulators and rate cases rely on.
wedge_first_revenue: Start with privately owned systems in states with fair-market-value or distressed-system acquisition laws (PA Act 12, MO, TX, NC, etc.). Target trailer parks, subdivisions and small towns with 50-1,000 connections, a standing violation or consent order, and an owner who wants out. Pay a few hundred thousand dollars per system. First revenue is customer bills from day one. Install the standard skid and file the first rate case at month 12-24. Of roughly 50,000 US community water systems, about 80% serve 3,300 people or fewer, and small systems have most of the health-based violations.
ladder: 1) Roll up 20-50 tiny private systems in 2-3 states. Remote SCADA plus an AI operator copilot lets one licensed operator cover many systems. 2) Get the standard skid approved by each state drinking-water program once, then cite it on every later plan submittal ('approve once, deploy many'), the equivalent of a PDK. 3) Move to municipal systems under fair-market-value laws, PFAS-driven sellers, and sewer systems (the Clean Watersheds need is about $630B). 4) Build a captive skid factory and parts library, the TSMC-like position: our own plant design, built by us, operated by us. 5) Become a multi-state regulated water holding company worth $5-20B of rate base, priced like AWK/Essential.
numbers: Market: EPA's 7th DWINSA puts drinking-water capital need at $625B over 20 years and estimates about 9.2M lead service lines (https://www.epa.gov/dwsrf/epas-7th-drinking-water-infrastructure-needs-survey-and-assessment). EPA's 2022 Clean Watersheds Needs Survey puts wastewater need at about $630B over 20 years (https://www.epa.gov/cwns). Systems: about 50,000 community water systems, about 80% of them serving 3,300 people or fewer (https://www.epa.gov/dwcapacity). Unit economics (est.): authorised ROE about 9.5-10.5% on equity in rate base. A 500-connection system needs $1-3M of capex, so 1,000 systems is $1-3B of rate base. Fair-market-value laws let the seller be paid at appraised value, which the acquirer then recovers in rates. Opex lever (est.): remote operations take labour cost per system from about $60-120k/yr to about $15-30k/yr. Capital: about $20-50M of equity plus utility debt (around 50/50 regulated capital structure) for the first 100 systems. Time to $100M revenue (est.): about 7-9 years. That is about 100k connections at roughly $1,000/yr combined water and sewer bills, or fewer if they are sewer-heavy. Ceiling comparables: American Water Works, market cap about $25-28B (est.). AWK and Essential Utilities announced an all-stock merger in Oct 2025 (est., unverified this run). Direct comparable: Central States Water Resources, a private-equity-backed small-system consolidator with 100+ systems (est.). Note: the web-search budget for this run was exhausted, so figures without URLs come from memory and are marked est.
ai_role: (1) Remote autonomous operation: anomaly detection on SCADA, chemical dosing control and alarm triage. One licensed operator can then supervise 20-50 systems where state rules allow remote or 'direct responsible charge' oversight. (2) Reverse-compiling each acquired system: AI turns as-builts, scans, sampling history and violations into a digital asset register in days instead of a consultant's months. (3) Paperwork at near-zero marginal cost: consumer confidence reports, monitoring schedules, lead service line inventories, state plan submittals referencing the pre-approved skid, and rate-case filings. (4) Capex targeting: models pick which pipe, pump or skid to replace, so the rate base built is the one that cuts violations and loss the most.
main_killer: Regulatory time, not technology. Rate cases take 9-18 months per state. Each state program reviews plans for each project. Licensing ties operators to specific systems, and some states require on-site visit frequencies. Meanwhile American Water, Essential, Nexus Water Group and CSWR already roll up systems, and sellers price in fair-market-value hope.
ai_answer_to_killer: Go below the incumbents' minimum deal size: systems under 1,000 connections are too small for AWK's deal teams but profitable under AI-run operations. Make the regulator's job easier, not slower. One frozen skid with growing operating history turns each plan review into a short delta review, and AI drafts complete, standardised rate-case and plan packages, which cuts review rework (per-unit paperwork, where AI does help). Use statutory pathways like PA Act 12 and Missouri's distressed-system rules, where the state wants a buyer for violating systems. The fleet's compliance record becomes the evidence for remote-operation waivers state by state.
competitors: Central States Water Resources (private-equity backed, small-system roll-up); Nexus Water Group (formerly Corix US); SouthWest Water Co.; American Water Works and Essential Utilities (merging, est.); California Water Service, SJW/H2O America; Aqua (Essential). Modular-plant vendors (Evoqua/Xylem, AdEdge) sell equipment but own no utilities.
principles_used: P1/P13 (frozen target: one characterised plant design reused everywhere), P10 (owner earns predictable cash flow, so cheap capital), P14 (the owner-operator becomes its own internal gate within its rate base), P9 (fleet telemetry becomes compliance evidence).

score.name: Tributary Water: an AI-run owner of small US water utilities, built on one pre-approved standard plant
score.rationale: It owns regulated monopolies with a rate base, so the asset ownership and defensibility are excellent per territory, and the AWK/Essential comparables support a $1B+ ceiling. AI fits squarely what it can do: per-unit labour (remote ops) and paperwork (CCRs, plan submittals, rate-case packages). The killer, though, is the gatekeeper queue: rate cases take 9-18 months per state, plan review is state by state, and operator licensing and visit rules apply. Under the learned law, AI does not shorten these. Also, opex savings from remote ops are largely passed through to customers at the next rate case, so returns are capped at the authorised ROE. Revenue arrives on day one, but $100M needs about 100k connections, which means 200+ tiny systems at about 500 connections each. CSWR, Nexus and the big IOUs already work this exact roll-up with PE capital, and the idea itself estimates 7-9 years to $100M, which fails the time leg. Sellers under fair-market-value laws price in hope.
score.biggest_risk: Time: getting to $100M through hundreds of tiny acquisitions, each with its own state-commission rate case and plan review, takes too long for a venture timeline. A PE-backed consolidator (CSWR) already holds the first rungs.

name: Terminus PFAS: a permitted network of PFAS destruction hubs that issues certificates of destruction
sector: Water / wastewater: PFAS treatment residuals, biosolids and contaminated water
one_liner: Own the scarce permitted capacity to destroy PFAS (supercritical water oxidation and electrochemical destruction hubs near clusters of water utilities and military sites), take spent filter media, concentrates and biosolids, and sell per-tonne destruction with an auditable certificate that ends the generator's liability.
what_it_owns: Permitted destruction capacity: air and water permits, waste-acceptance approvals and host-community agreements, which are hard to obtain because several states have incineration moratoria for PFAS. It also owns the per-batch evidence record (mass-balance destruction data, fluoride recovery, non-detects), which becomes the trusted mark that generators, insurers and regulators accept, the UL/HSB position for PFAS. Plus long-term take-or-pay offtake contracts with utilities and the DoD.
wedge_first_revenue: The first hub, co-located at a large wastewater plant or industrial site (host fee plus offtake of its biosolids or concentrate), destroys PFAS from utilities installing granular activated carbon, ion exchange or reverse osmosis to meet the 4 ppt PFOA/PFOS limits. First revenue is a gate fee per tonne of spent media or per gallon of concentrate from neighbouring utilities and DoD aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) cleanup sites, about 12-24 months after permit.
ladder: 1) One hub with a few anchor generators (utility consortium, military base AFFF stockpile). 2) Prove destruction efficiency per batch and publish the evidence record, so the certificate becomes the accepted end-of-liability document. 3) Build 10-30 regional hubs (atoms are regional, so many hubs, like rental depots). 4) Add thermal regeneration of spent carbon and resin, an owned loop: utilities rent media, we regenerate and destroy, and sell 'PFAS-free water treatment media as a service'. 5) Become the permitted national PFAS 'end of pipe', a Clean Harbors-scale owner of a new waste class.
numbers: Rule: EPA's 2024 PFAS drinking-water rule set PFOA/PFOS at 4 ppt. In May 2025 EPA said it would keep those limits and extend compliance to 2031 while reconsidering other PFAS (https://www.epa.gov/sdwa/and-polyfluoroalkyl-substances-pfas). EPA estimated compliance at about $1.5B/yr; AWWA's estimates were several times higher, about $3.8B+/yr (est.). Funding: 3M's water-utility settlement of $10.3-12.5B (2023) and DuPont/Chemours/Corteva's $1.185B settlement fund utility treatment, and therefore residuals disposal (est.). DoD AFFF cleanup: tens of billions of dollars across about 700+ installations assessed (est.). Unit economics (est.): spent GAC/IX disposal by incineration or landfill is about $1-5/lb; destruction gate fees about $0.5-3/gal for concentrates. A 10-20 tpd hub could earn about $15-40M/yr revenue at about 30-45% EBITDA. Capex about $20-60M per hub. Time to $100M revenue (est.): about 6-8 years, at 4-6 hubs. Ceiling comparables: Clean Harbors, revenue about $5.9B, market cap about $11-13B (est.); Waste Management's Stericycle and other permitted-capacity owners. Competitor scale: 374Water (NASDAQ: SCWO) is small and pre-scale; Revive Environmental (Battelle Annihilator) and Aquagga are early (est.). Note: the search budget was exhausted this run; figures are from memory unless a URL is given (est.).
ai_role: (1) Process control: SCWO's killers are salt plugging and corrosion. ML on reactor temperature, pressure, conductivity and spectroscopic signals predicts and prevents them, raising uptime from pilot-level to industrial-level, the P3 'programmable heterogeneous capacity' move for mixed waste streams. (2) Feed characterisation: fast ML-assisted analytics map each incoming batch's PFAS profile and set recipes, so one hub accepts many waste types like a multi-tenant fleet. (3) Evidence compiler: per-batch destruction and mass-balance certificates generated automatically, with chain of custody, in a form insurers and regulators can audit. (4) Paperwork: permits, waste-acceptance plans and environmental-justice community filings drafted fast.
main_killer: Policy and permitting risk. EPA's 2025 rollback and the 2031 delay shrink near-term demand urgency, CERCLA liability rules for PFAS may change, and new destruction facilities face local opposition and long air-permit timelines. Incumbents (Clean Harbors, landfills) can keep taking media cheaply as long as landfilling is allowed.
ai_answer_to_killer: Sell liability termination, not compliance. Even with federal delays, state limits (NJ, MI, NY, PA and others), the retained PFOA/PFOS limits and tort exposure make generators want a documented end-of-life for PFAS, and AI-generated per-batch destruction certificates make that auditable at low cost. Site hubs inside existing permitted fences (wastewater plants, industrial sites, military bases) so they modify an existing permit instead of seeking a greenfield one. Behind the fence, the owner-operator is closer to its own gate (P14). The AI uptime advantage converts a pilot technology into contracted capacity faster than competitors can, and landfill bans on PFAS waste, already advancing in several states, raise the price of the incumbent option.
competitors: Clean Harbors (incineration, the incumbent end-point); 374Water (SCWO, public); Revive Environmental (Battelle's Annihilator); Aquagga (hydrothermal alkaline treatment); Claros Technologies; Onvector (plasma); Gradiant and Veolia (treatment trains and disposal services); Calgon Carbon/Kuraray (GAC reactivation, which does not fully destroy PFAS).
principles_used: P3 (owned, pooled, scarce, permitted capacity behind an AI 'compiler' interface; many regional winners), P4 (the owner of accepted destruction evidence captures the value), P14 (insurer and liability gate; the certificate as the mark), P11 (codified operator craft in a scarce physical cell).

score.name: Terminus PFAS: a permitted network of PFAS destruction hubs that issues certificates of destruction
score.rationale: Search budget was exhausted, so this relies on prior knowledge. EPA did keep the 4 ppt PFOA/PFOS limits and move compliance to 2031 in May 2025, and the 3M and DuPont settlements are real money flowing to utilities. N: about $20-60M capex per hub for $15-40M of revenue is plausible if gate fees hold. But Clean Harbors' incineration (allowed under EPA's 2024 destruction guidance) and landfills set a low price ceiling, and 374Water's slow commercial progress suggests SCWO economics are not yet proven. T: getting permits for hubs, even inside existing fences, plus 12-24 months to first gate fee puts first revenue at about 2-3 years. $100M by year 7 needs 4-6 hubs and is tight. C: a Clean Harbors-scale comparable is credible but needs landfill bans to spread. A: ML process control against salt plugging and corrosion is a plausible uptime lever, and auto-generated destruction certificates cut paperwork. But AI does not create demand or beat cheap landfilling, which is the killer. D: permitted capacity and the evidence record are moderate moats. Many funded destruction startups (Revive, Aquagga, Claros, Onvector) are chasing the same certificate position, and Clean Harbors already holds permits.
score.biggest_risk: Demand urgency collapses under the federal rollback and 2031 delay while landfilling and incineration stay legal and cheap, so hubs run under-utilised against Clean Harbors pricing.

name: Overwatch Utility (protected-airspace fleet for critical infrastructure)
sector: Security tech / counter-UAS / critical-infrastructure protection
one_liner: Own and operate a shared, multi-tenant low-altitude sensor and interceptor network over clusters of critical sites (data-centre campuses, substations, ports, refineries, prisons) and sell 'protected airspace' per site-month with a detection/response SLA. This is the AWS of airspace security: one owned fleet serves many tenants instead of each site buying its own counter-UAS kit.
what_it_owns: (1) The physical network: radar, RF, EO/IR and acoustic nodes plus a drone-in-a-box interceptor fleet (net-capture first, kinetic only where authorised) sited on leased towers and rooftops. (2) The national low-altitude track archive: every detection, classification and outcome, which becomes the evidence base insurers, regulators and courts price and accept. (3) Long-term site contracts and the authority relationships (MOUs with federal and state agencies) that let the network act. Tenants never own the kit, so the fleet's utilisation, data and evidence compound with the owner.
wedge_first_revenue: Detection-and-attribution only, which is legal for private operators today. Start with 1 to 3 dense clusters where many tenants share one sensor footprint (Northern Virginia data-centre alley; Gulf Coast refinery and LNG corridor; one port). Charge each tenant about $8-25k per site-month (est.) for 24/7 detection, AI-classified alerts and court-grade evidence packages handed to FBI, DHS or local police. One cluster node set (about $1.5-3M capex, est.) covers 10-40 tenant sites, which is the statistical-multiplexing win a single-site buyer cannot get (P3). First revenue is plausible within 6-9 months.
ladder: Rung 1: detection and evidence as a utility (legal now). Rung 2: response under partner authority. Federal and state agencies with mitigation authority (DHS/DOJ under 6 U.S.C. 124n, DoD 10 U.S.C. 130i, DOE 50 U.S.C. 2661, and any state/local pilots that expanded authority creates) use the company's owned interceptors and sensors under contract, 'government-operated, company-owned', like the GOCO model. Rung 3: delegated mitigation for the company's own certified operators, an ODA-style delegation (P14) earned on the operating record. Rung 4: insurance and SLA products priced on the track archive, plus selling airspace-awareness data to the FAA's low-altitude traffic management and BVLOS operators. Rung 5: a national multi-region network and allied-country replicas (EU airports and energy sites after the 2025 drone closures).
numbers: Web search was unavailable in this run (the shared per-turn search budget was used up), so figures come from prior knowledge and are marked est. where unverified. Counter-UAS market about $3-6B in 2025, growing about 20-30%/yr (est.). Comparables: Axon bought Dedrone in 2024 (https://investor.axon.com, est. ~$500M+ valuation); Epirus raised a $250M Series D in 2025 (est.); DroneShield FY2025 revenue about A$200M+ (est., https://www.droneshield.com/investor-centre); Anduril valued about $30B in 2025 (est.). Demand signals: the June 2025 executive order 'Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty' (https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/06/restoring-american-airspace-sovereignty/); the New Jersey sightings in late 2024; drones closing Copenhagen, Oslo and Munich airports in Sept-Oct 2025 (est.). Unit economics (est.): about $2M of capex per cluster serving 25 tenant sites at $15k/month is $4.5M/yr of revenue, roughly a 2-year payback with 60%+ gross margin once the network is in place. TAM (est.): about 16,000 critical US sites (substations above 100 kV, data centres, refineries, ports, prisons, stadiums) x $150k/yr is about $2.4B/yr for the US detection layer alone; mitigation-as-a-service and insurance products could double that. Time to $100M revenue: about 5-6 years (about 550 tenant sites, est.). Ceiling comparables: ADT ($4.9B revenue, est.) and Allied Universal (about $20B+, est.) show physical security as a recurring service is a very large pool.
ai_role: AI makes heterogeneous, cheap sensors behave as one fused, callable fleet: multi-sensor fusion and classification that tells birds, hobbyists and hostile drones apart at a low false-alarm rate, which is the thing that makes unattended multi-tenant operation possible. It also does automated RF-protocol fingerprinting and pilot geolocation, LLM-generated evidence and chain-of-custody packages for prosecutors and agencies (per-unit paperwork, which AI does fix), autonomous interceptor guidance for net capture, and swarm-aware scheduling of the interceptor fleet across tenants. A shared operations centre of a few operators can watch hundreds of sites because AI triages the alerts.
main_killer: Legal authority to mitigate. Private parties cannot jam, spoof, take over or down a drone in the US: the Wiretap Act, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, 18 U.S.C. 32 (aircraft sabotage) and the FCC's jamming ban all apply. Federal counter-UAS authority sits with a few agencies and has run on short-term extensions. Without mitigation, 'detection only' risks looking like a sensor-alarm service with thin pricing power.
ai_answer_to_killer: Be the owner of the fleet that authorised actors use, and earn delegated authority on evidence instead of waiting for a statute. (1) Detection and evidence are legal today, and AI-built court-grade packages turn them into enforcement: drone-pilot geolocation plus automated FAA/FBI referrals deters repeat incursions, which tenants pay for. (2) Mitigation agencies are short of equipment and staff, so a company-owned, AI-run interceptor fleet operated under their authority (GOCO) is cheaper for them than buying kit per site. The company still owns the asset and the archive. (3) The archive of classified incursions and outcomes, at low false-alarm rates, is exactly the evidence a legislature or regulator needs to grant certified private operators narrow mitigation rights, the way FAA ODA was earned. (4) Net-capture interceptors avoid RF jamming entirely, which removes the FCC problem and leaves a narrower legal question. Optimism case: expanded authority for state/local and critical-infrastructure owners has been proposed repeatedly (est.), and the company is the turnkey network ready on the day it passes.
competitors: Dedrone (Axon), DroneShield, D-Fend Solutions, Fortem Technologies, Epirus (high-power microwave), Anduril (Lattice and Anvil, mainly military), Hidden Level (passive RF airspace network, raised est. $100M+), Sentrycs, Ondas/American Robotics (Iron Drone), AeroDefense, Echodyne (radar). Nearly all sell kit or software per site; Hidden Level is the closest network-owner analogue, but it is detection only and focused on government.

score.name: Overwatch Utility (protected-airspace fleet for critical infrastructure)
score.rationale: Web search was unavailable (the shared per-turn search budget was used up), so key numbers could not be checked and are judged from prior knowledge. Demand is real: the June 2025 airspace executive order, the 2025 European airport closures, and the FY2026 NDAA C-UAS changes, which as I recall widen mitigation for trained state and local law enforcement but not for private operators. Rung 1 detection is legal and can earn revenue in under a year. But the $15k/site-month x 25 tenants per $2M cluster figure assumes tenants are dense and willing to pay a mitigation-level price for alerts only. N=3. The killer is statutory authority, a gatekeeper queue that by the project's own law AI does not fix. AI improves the evidence, but the legislature or regulator still decides on its own timeline, and the GOCO route depends on agency procurement. A=2. The owned network and track archive compound somewhat. But Hidden Level (passive RF network), Dedrone/Axon and Anduril are well funded and can copy a multi-tenant model, so D=3. Fails because the A leg is below 3.
score.biggest_risk: Without private mitigation authority the product is a detection and alerting service with weak pricing power, and authority depends on Congress, not on AI or the operating record.

name: Grid Reserve (an owned strategic-spares fleet for physical-attack and disaster restoration)
sector: Critical-infrastructure protection / grid security hardware
one_liner: Own the national reserve of 'universal' spare high-voltage transformers, mobile substations and pre-built substation modules, stationed in hardened regional depots, and sell restoration capacity by subscription: utilities pay an annual fee for a guaranteed replacement within days instead of a 2-4 year wait after an attack, fire, storm or failure.
what_it_owns: (1) The scarcest physical asset in grid security: built and in-stock spare transformers and mobile substations (P3 'scarce capacity'; in a shortage, 'whoever owns it sets the price'). (2) An AI-generated universal interface library (P6): designs for multi-ratio, multi-impedance spare units plus bolt-on adapter kits (bushings, tap ranges, cooling, protection settings) that let one spare stand in for dozens of utility-specific nameplates, with each substitution signed as an engineering equivalence. (3) Hardened, geographically distributed depots and the logistics fleet (heavy haul, rail cars). (4) Multi-year subscription contracts that become an infrastructure-grade cash flow (P10).
wedge_first_revenue: Start with the band of the market where spares are most standardisable and lead times hurt most: 115-230 kV, 30-100 MVA substation transformers and mobile substations for distribution co-ops and municipals (about 2,800 US co-ops and munis, most with no spare pool). Buy units already in the secondary market or from overseas factories with open slots, plus mobile substations. Sell 5-10 year 'restoration-guarantee' subscriptions at about 6-10% of unit value per year (est.), plus a deployment fee when a unit is used. First revenue in 6-12 months, using existing transformers bought at today's prices as the starting fleet.
ladder: Rung 1: mobile substations and standard 115-230 kV spares for co-ops and munis. Rung 2: AI-designed 'universal' spare families procured in batches, which bulk orders make cheaper than custom units. Rung 3: 345-765 kV large power transformers (LPTs), the hardest category, with Grid Assurance-type utility consortia and DOE as anchor buyers. Rung 4: own refurbishment and rewinding shops (scarce capacity, turning failed units back into fleet), then a transformer factory line making the company's own universal design (vertical integration). Rung 5: lease spares to data centres and large-load interconnections that cannot wait for new units, and sell to allied grids (Ukraine, Baltics, Taiwan).
numbers: Web search was unavailable in this run, so figures are prior knowledge, marked est. Lead times: power transformers about 120-130 weeks and GSUs about 140+ weeks in 2025 (Wood Mackenzie, est.; https://www.woodmac.com); LPTs 2-4 years and prices up about 60-80% since 2020 (NREL 2024 transformer report, est.). The US imports about 80% of LPTs (DOE, est.). Physical-security incidents reported to the NERC E-ISAC ran in the thousands per year in 2022-2023 (est.). The Moore County, NC attack (Dec 2022) cut power to about 45,000 Duke Energy customers for up to 5 days; the Metcalf attack (2013) caused about $15M of damage (est.). Comparables: Grid Assurance (utility-owned spare-sharing company founded 2016, https://www.gridassurance.com); the industry's STEP programme. Unit economics (est.): a 100 MVA spare costs about $3-6M; a 7%/yr subscription from each of 4-8 utilities sharing that unit (a pooling multiple, P3) earns about $1-1.7M/yr, or 20-35% unlevered yield on asset cost, before deployment fees. A larger LPT at about $8-15M with 4-6 subscribers is similar. TAM (est.): US transmission and distribution spare demand of about $5-10B of asset value. A $1.5B fleet subscribed at 4-6x pooling gives about $400-500M/yr of revenue. Time to $100M revenue: about 5-6 years (about $400M of fleet). Ceiling comparables: United Rentals ($16.1B 2025 revenue, $22.5B fleet at cost) and Aggreko-style rental power for the 'own the scarce iron' model.
ai_role: (1) AI mines utility nameplates, FERC 715/EIA-860 filings, one-line diagrams and protection settings across the US fleet to find the smallest set of universal spare designs that covers the most units (a set-cover problem over thousands of heterogeneous transformers). (2) Generative electrical and thermal design of multi-ratio, multi-impedance units plus AI-written equivalence packages per substitution (impedance matching, short-circuit duty, relay setting changes) that utility engineers can sign quickly. (3) Fleet condition monitoring (dissolved-gas analysis, thermal, partial discharge) on stored and deployed units to keep the reserve 'warm' and to predict failures across subscribers' installed bases, which turns into an early-warning product and better depot placement. (4) Attack and hazard modelling (wildfire, hurricanes, physical threat intelligence) to price subscriptions and position depots.
main_killer: Transformers are custom: voltage, impedance, footprint, cooling, bushings and protection settings differ by utility, so a 'universal spare' may not fit, and utilities may prefer their own spares or consortium sharing (Grid Assurance). It is also capital-heavy ($3-15M per unit) with lumpy, rare deployment events, which makes revenue look like insurance and needs patient capital.
ai_answer_to_killer: (1) AI-driven set-cover across the national fleet's nameplate data plus adapter kits turns 'custom' into 'a dozen families cover most units'. The universal design trades about 10-20% extra copper and steel for 5-10x more substitution coverage, which is the P6 move of writing the de-facto interface specification no OEM published. (2) AI-generated equivalence packages cut the engineering-review time to accept a substitution from months to days, and utilities sign them themselves (the asset owner is its own approver), so no regulator queue applies. (3) Capital: subscription contracts with investment-grade utilities, plus fleet telemetry that makes the asset base low-variance, can be securitised or project-financed (P10). DOE grid-resilience grants and loan programmes (est.) and possible regulator recognition of subscriptions as recoverable costs widen the funding path. (4) Grid Assurance proves willingness to pay but is utility-owned and focused on its members; an independent, nationally pooled fleet with universal designs reaches the thousands of co-ops and munis it does not serve.
competitors: Grid Assurance (utility consortium), EEI STEP spare-sharing, utility in-house spares, OEMs with mobile substation fleets and rental (Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova Prolec, Virginia Transformer, WEG), rental-power fleets (Aggreko, Sunbelt Rentals power), mobile substation makers (Delta Star, IEM). None owns a pooled, universal-design reserve offered as a subscription.

score.name: Grid Reserve (an owned strategic-spares fleet for physical-attack and disaster restoration)
score.rationale: Search was unavailable, so this uses prior knowledge: transformer lead times of 2-4 years, roughly 80% of LPTs imported, Grid Assurance in operation, and DOE's RecX recovery-transformer precedent. Owning scarce iron in a shortage is a valid moat, and a starter fleet of secondary-market units and mobile substations gives revenue in 6-12 months. T=4. But the 20-35% yield needs 4-8 co-ops or munis each paying about 7% of unit value a year for a rarely used guarantee.
