Budget-constrained co-ops tend to treat that as insurance, and $400M of fleet for $100M of revenue is heavy, rate-recovery-dependent capital. N=3. AI set-cover over nameplate data plus equivalence packages plausibly answers the 'transformers are custom' killer, and utilities sign substitutions themselves. A=3: willingness to pay and capital remain unanswered. The ceiling looks more like a $1-3B specialised lessor than United Rentals, because the shortage premium fades as factories expand. C=3. Grid Assurance, OEM rental fleets and infrastructure funds can copy the model with cheaper capital. D=3.
score.biggest_risk: Low utilisation and insurance-like revenue on a capital-heavy fleet, with utilities reluctant to pay standing subscriptions, plus the shortage premium fading as new transformer capacity comes online by around 2028-2030.

name: Steamworks: an owner-operator steam and CHP utility that is its own boiler inspector and insurer
sector: Gas and steam power generation: industrial boilers, steam and combined heat and power
one_liner: Buy or build and operate the boiler houses and CHP plants inside US factories (food, chemicals, pulp, pharma, district campuses) and sell steam per tonne and power per MWh on 10-15 year contracts. Become a National Board owner-user inspection organisation with a captive insurer, so that fleet telemetry rather than an outside inspector's calendar sets inspection and risk.
what_it_owns: The boilers, CHP units and steam plants (thousands of assets over time). National Board NB-371 owner-user inspection accreditation, so it legally employs its own commissioned inspectors for in-service and repair inspections of equipment it owns or operates (https://www.nationalboard.org/SiteDocuments/AIAs/NB-371.pdf). A captive insurer holding the boiler-and-machinery risk. Standardised modular boiler and CHP skids, its own 'frozen target'. And the operating and loss dataset that sets insurance and debt pricing. It is the HSB model (inspection plus insurance, founded 1866) rebuilt around an owned fleet.
wedge_first_revenue: Steam-as-a-service on aging (30+ year) boiler houses at mid-size plants that want capital off their balance sheet. The company buys the existing boilers for a nominal sum or replaces them with its modular skids, runs them remotely, and bills per 1,000 lb of steam. The first 5-10 sites generate about $5-15M a year of contracted revenue (est.). Every site added grows the fleet's inspection and loss record.
ladder: 1) Steam supply contracts on existing boilers. 2) Add gas-engine or turbine CHP to sell power back to the host or the grid; firm power at factories is scarce. 3) Accreditation as an owner-user inspection organisation plus a captive insurer, internalising the gate and the risk premium. 4) Hybrid heat with electric boilers and thermal storage when power is cheap, arbitraged by AI. 5) Securitise the steam contract book (the SolarCity ABS move) and roll up district energy systems. 6) Hundreds of sites form a distributed CHP fleet bidding into capacity and demand-response markets.
numbers: Installed base: about 43,000 US industrial boilers, about 19,500 of them above 10 MMBtu/hr, totalling about 1.56M MMBtu/hr, a dated early-2000s estimate (https://corpora.tika.apache.org/base/docs/govdocs1/098/098946.pdf); much of that fleet is now 30-50+ years old (est.). US industrial boiler equipment market is about $1.5B a year (https://gminsights.com/industry-analysis/US-industrial-boiler-market). Steam value: 1.56M MMBtu/hr at about 50% average utilisation is about 6.8 quads a year; at $8-15/MMBtu delivered steam that is a US industrial steam spend of roughly $50-100B a year (est.). Gate: NB-371 lets an owner-user organisation employ its own commissioned inspectors for in-service, repair and alteration inspections accepted by jurisdictions (https://www.nationalboard.org/PrintPage.aspx?pageID=67). Unit economics (est.): a 50,000 lb/hr steam plant about $3-6M installed; steam contract about $2-4M a year; 20-30% gross margin rising with remote operations and in-house inspection and insurance. Insurance and inspection run about 1-3% of revenue for incumbents and become margin. Capital: $10-30M per first cluster, then project debt and ABS after 24-36 months of history (P10). Time to $100M revenue: about 5 years at 40-60 sites (est.). Ceiling comparables: Veolia, ENGIE energy services, Vicinity Energy (district steam, PE-owned), HSB (bought by Munich Re for about $742M in 2009, est.), Ameresco.
ai_role: AI does four jobs. (1) Per-site engineering, audits and contract sizing in days, from utility bills, steam-trap surveys and existing plant records (paperwork and per-unit labour, P1). (2) Remote multi-site operation: ML anomaly detection on drum level, combustion, water chemistry and tube metal temperatures, so one control room runs many boiler houses and uses each state's rules for remote monitoring (P8, P9). (3) An evidence compiler: AI-read ultrasonic and phased-array NDE, IR and water-chemistry history become the risk-based inspection record that the company's own inspection organisation and captive insurer act on (P4, P14). (4) Fleet loss data lowers the captive's loss ratio and the debt spread (P10), and AI builds parts and repair procedures for orphan boiler and burner makes (P12).
main_killer: Small tickets and host credit risk. Each site is a $3-6M project tied to one factory that can close, and enterprise sales cycles are 12-24 months. Jurisdictional acceptance of owner-user inspection and of remote or unattended operation varies by state. Veolia, ENGIE, Ameresco and thermal-battery startups (Rondo, Antora) all chase the same heat-as-a-service customers.
ai_answer_to_killer: Make each site close to zero marginal engineering and sales cost with AI audits and standard skids, and the long tail of mid-size plants becomes economic where incumbents need $20M+ projects. Diversify host credit across hundreds of sites so the contract book is securitisable like residential solar. Modular skids are relocatable assets that keep residual value if a host closes. Start in states that already reference owner-user inspection organisations and remote monitoring (e.g. the Iowa owner-user provisions, https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/publications/LGI/77/HF502.pdf) and use the accumulated loss record to expand. Treat thermal-battery startups as partners for electrified steam rather than as rivals.
competitors: Energy-as-a-service: Veolia, ENGIE, Ameresco, Johnson Controls, Redaptive, Bernhard, Vicinity Energy (district steam). Boiler OEMs with service: Cleaver-Brooks, Babcock & Wilcox, Miura (on-demand modular boilers). Insurer-inspectors: HSB (Munich Re), FM Global, Zurich. Thermal storage: Rondo, Antora, Electrified Thermal Solutions. CHP developers: Caterpillar and Solar Turbines dealers, 2G Energy.
principles_used: P14 (be your own gate: owner-user inspection organisation plus captive insurer), P10 (output-as-a-service as financing), P9 (operating hours become priced evidence), P4 (risk-based inspection as cheap verification), P5 (standard modules), P8 (remote software-defined operation of orphaned assets)

score.name: Steamworks: an owner-operator steam and CHP utility that is its own boiler inspector and insurer
score.rationale: Web search budget was used up, so I could not run fresh checks. The NB-371 owner-user program exists, and the boiler population figure is a dated early-2000s DOE estimate. N: $3-6M per site at 20-30% gross margin is a thin, small-ticket infrastructure business. ABS is possible only after years of history, and the claimed $50-100B steam spend is mostly fuel pass-through, not margin. T: enterprise sales cycles of 12-24 months and 40-60 sites for $100M means about 5+ years, which is borderline. C: comparables are energy-as-a-service books inside Veolia, ENGIE and Ameresco, and HSB sold for about $742M. $1B is credible only through a large rollup, so 3. A: AI audits and remote multi-site monitoring cut per-site labour as the laws predict. But many states still require attended boiler operation, and AI cannot change those statutes; it only helps with the evidence. D: NB-371 status plus a captive insurer and a loss dataset is a real but modest moat, and incumbents (Veolia, ENGIE, Ameresco, Vicinity) can replicate it.
score.biggest_risk: Small, slow and crowded. Host-plant credit and closure risk, state attendance rules that block the remote-operation margin, and decarbonisation pressure moving steam to electric boilers and thermal batteries. Large ESCOs and utilities with cheaper capital may undercut it.

name: Rotable Grid: an owned exchange pool and equivalence library for orphaned substation components
sector: Electric grid hardware: HV/MV circuit breakers, bushings, on-load tap changers, instrument transformers, protection relays, switchgear
one_liner: An aviation-style rotables pool for the grid. Own a pooled inventory of remanufactured and AI-reverse-engineered substation components for the millions of discontinued and out-of-support breakers, tap changers, bushings and relays in service. Swap failed units in days under 'power-by-the-hour' availability contracts, and convert the SF6 breaker installed base to SF6-free vacuum retrofits as the EU phase-out and US state rules bite.
what_it_owns: (1) The rotable pool, an owned inventory of exchange units, which is the AWS-style scarce fleet. (2) The equivalence library: AI-generated technical data packages and form-fit-function (FFF) equivalence dossiers for thousands of orphaned part numbers. Unlike aviation PMA, there is no regulator; acceptance is by utility engineering and IEEE/IEC type test, so the company is its own approver. (3) A characterised retrofit-kit line, for example vacuum interrupter or clean-air retrofits into existing breaker tanks and mechanisms, with type-test evidence. (4) Fleet failure-mode data across utilities.
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1: buy decommissioned and surplus breakers, bushings and OLTCs from utilities and retiring plants at salvage prices. Reverse-engineer the top 50 orphaned failure items with AI (OLTC contacts, bushings for discontinued models, breaker mechanism parts for obsolete GE/Westinghouse/ITE/ABB lines). Sell exchange units and emergency swaps to municipal utilities, co-ops and IPPs, which lack spare inventory and face 12-36 month OEM lead times. Revenue is an exchange fee plus a core charge, est. 40-60% of the new-unit price delivered in days.
ladder: Rung 1: emergency exchange and remanufactured units for orphaned models. Rung 2: availability subscriptions ('substation power-by-the-hour'), covering a utility's fleet of a given breaker or OLTC family for a fixed fee per bay-year with guaranteed swap times. Rung 3: SF6-free retrofit programme, converting installed SF6 breakers in place, which captures the regulatory replacement wave without full replacement. Rung 4: an approved-equivalent library large enough to be the 'HEICO of the grid', with 10,000+ part numbers. Rung 5: owned operation and maintenance of whole bays (fold into Substrate).
numbers: Ceiling comparables: HEICO owns 11,500+ PMAs and adds 300-500 a year, priced about 30-50% below OEM (https://www.ramapo.edu/rfg/wp-content/uploads/sites/370/2022/06/Heico-Pitch.pdf; https://scuttleblurb.substack.com/p/heia-heico-corp-niches-get-riches); its market cap is $16B+. Regulatory driver: EU F-gas Regulation 2024/573 bans new SF6 MV switchgear up to 24 kV from 1 January 2026, with higher voltage classes from about 2028-2032 (https://blog.sintef.com/energy/what-is-the-status-of-phasing-out-sf6-gas-in-switchgear-and-circuit-breakers/). SF6-free 420 kV is only being piloted in 2026 (Statnett, Siemens Energy), so retrofit demand is ahead of supply. Grid component prices are up 40% (CRS, inflation-adjusted 2020-24) to 70-75% (WoodMac) (https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R48933.html). Unit economics (est.): a remanufactured 138 kV breaker costs about $40-80k to restore against a new price of $150-300k and a lead time of 12-24+ months. Exchange gross margin is about 40-50%. Capital (est.): $20-40M for the initial pool, a reman facility and a type-test partnership. Time to $100M revenue (est.): 5-6 years, from about 1,500-2,500 exchanges a year plus subscriptions across 100+ utilities. Market (est.): US T&D substation equipment aftermarket of $8-15B a year.
ai_role: Reverse compilation (P1, P12): CT and 3D scan, metallurgy and ML material ID turn obsolete parts into TDPs. LLMs mine OEM manuals, service bulletins and utility failure records to rank which part numbers to clone (price gap times failure rate). AI drafts FFF equivalence and type-test dossiers per application (P7 'hardware lockfile'), which takes the cost per part number from about $50-200k toward $5-20k so the long tail pays. Fleet-wide failure prediction sizes the pool (P3 statistical multiplexing: pooled spares across uncorrelated utilities). AI generates retrofit designs that fit a vacuum interrupter into an existing mechanism and tank.
main_killer: Liability and acceptance. A failed non-OEM breaker part can cause a fault that damages a substation or kills a lineman, and utilities fear voiding OEM warranties. OEMs also control some data rights and firmware for newer relays and controllers.
ai_answer_to_killer: Target only orphaned equipment the OEM no longer supports, so there is no warranty to void and the alternative is a 2-year outage of the bay. Carry the liability on the company's own balance sheet with insurer-priced performance warranties (P14), backed by the per-unit evidence record (type test, timing test, contact resistance, and in-service monitoring, P9). Because the grid has no FAA-style pre-market approver, each equivalence is accepted by the buyer's engineering staff. AI-written dossiers make that review take days, and accepted dossiers become reusable across every utility that runs the same model, a network effect at the equivalence layer. For firmware-locked newer relays, avoid them at first and provide Phoenix-BIOS-style compatible controllers for analog and electromechanical relays, where there is no lock.
competitors: OEM service arms (ABB, Siemens Energy, Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova, Eaton, Schneider). Independent reconditioners (ESCO-style shops, Circuit Breaker Sales, Group CBS, RESA Power, Southern States, Pemco). Surplus brokers. SF6-free entrants (Siemens Blue, Hitachi EconiQ, Nuventura, startups) that sell new equipment, not retrofits. None owns a pooled, subscription rotable fleet plus an equivalence library at scale (est.).
principles_used: P2 (own the approved equivalent, not the open drawing), P3 (pooled, owned spare capacity), P7 (a signed equivalence certificate per application, i.e. a lockfile), P12 (break the OEM aftermarket lock part by part, HEICO-style), P14 (the company is its own gate where no regulator sits).

score.name: Rotable Grid: an owned exchange pool and equivalence library for orphaned substation components
score.rationale: Fast to first revenue: buy surplus and decommissioned units at salvage and sell emergency exchanges to co-ops and municipal utilities facing long OEM lead times. AI reverse engineering and dossier drafting is the kind of per-unit labour AI does fix. But the HEICO analogy breaks on the moat. HEICO's value is its FAA PMA approvals, a permission moat. Here, with no regulator, there is no approval to own, so anyone with a reman shop can make the same equivalent. Utility engineering acceptance is per buyer, not a transferable credential. The first rungs are already held by PE roll-ups (RESA Power, Group CBS and other reconditioners), which matches the 'first rungs held by PE' law. The SF6-retrofit rung is real in the EU but weaker in the US. The ceiling is plausibly $1B but not obviously more, since the orphaned-equipment niche is a slice of the $8-15B aftermarket. Liability is answered only partly, by balance-sheet warranties. I could not check the lead-time and pricing figures because the search budget was used up.
score.biggest_risk: No permission moat. Without a regulator, the equivalence library and rotable pool are easy for PE-backed reconditioners and OEM service arms to copy, which leaves the business as a competitive reman and exchange shop.

name: Ghost Wing: an owned fleet of retired military jets selling flight hours
one_liner: Buy retired fighters, trainers and tankers at scrap-plus prices, keep them alive with an AI-decompiled parts library, and sell what the services can no longer generate themselves: adversary-air, tanker, ISR-test and training flight hours.
sector: Defence and aerospace sustainment (contracted air services, the aircraft version of the resurrection fleet)
what_it_owns: The airframes and engines; the operator's own airworthiness approvals (FAA restricted or experimental-exhibition plus DoD public-aircraft status under contract, and foreign military airworthiness authority acceptances); a growing library of reverse-engineered technical data packages and parts it makes for its own fleet; and its operating-hour and reliability record, which sets its insurance and debt cost. This is new against the gas-turbine idea: the output is a scarce military flight hour, not a MWh, and the buyer is already short of supply.
wedge_first_revenue: Start with a small type that already has a civil path and many retired airframes, such as ex-allied F-16A/B, L-39/L-159 or ex-Navy trainers. Buy 6-10 airframes plus a spares pile from a boneyard, an allied disposal sale or a broker. First revenue is a subcontract slot under an existing CAF ADAIR or Navy/Marine adversary-air IDIQ, or a NATO/Gulf air force training contract priced per flight hour. Within 18 months the AI parts library cuts cost per hour on its own fleet. That is internal use, so there is no DLA or FAA PMA queue.
ladder: 1) An adversary-air fleet of 10 jets selling hours. 2) Fleet-wide parts library and a captive depot. The company is its own approver for its own aircraft and later sells parts to other civil operators of the same types. 3) Add tanker and ISR test-bed hours from retired KC-135/KC-10-class and business-jet ISR conversions; the USAF tanker fleet averages about 60+ years old (est.). 4) Availability-based contracts with allied air forces whose US-type fleets are short of parts: they buy hours, not aircraft. 5) Become the largest non-OEM military aircraft operator. That position makes the fleet record, the approvals and the library the moat.
numbers: Market: USAF CAF ADAIR multi-award IDIQ ceiling about $6.4B (2019, est.). Navy, Marine and NATO adversary-air plus contracted tanker and test support take the global contracted-air-services pool to an est. $3-5B/yr. Asset cost: retired airframes from boneyards and allied disposals cost a small fraction of new. Top Aces bought 29 ex-Israeli F-16s (est.), against about $60-70M+ for a new F-16 Block 70 (est.). AMARG stores about 3,000+ aircraft (est.). Unit economics (est.): contracted fighter hours bill at about $15-40k/hr. A jet flying 300 hr/yr earns $4.5-12M/yr against an acquisition cost of $1-5M per airframe. The parts library is what keeps cost per hour below the bill rate. Capital: $40-80M for a first 10-jet squadron (est.). Time to $100M revenue: 25-30 jets in years 4-6 (est.). Ceiling comparables: Top Aces and Draken (Draken was taken private by PE); Rolls-Royce and GE capture lifetime value through service; GAO says lifetime F-35 sustainment alone is $1.6T and DOD launched a $13.7B readiness strategy in 2025, so the services cannot spare frontline hours for red-air (https://www.gao.gov/products/GAO-26-108113 ; https://legis1.com/news/f-35-readiness-crisis-collapses-as-pentagon).
ai_role: AI is the internal compiler for keeping orphaned airframes alive. CT and scan-to-CAD plus ML material ID turn worn parts from cannibalised airframes into TDPs and replacement parts. LLMs digitise decades of maintenance manuals and logbooks. Fleet telemetry and physics-informed models predict failures and justify inspection intervals for the operator's own approval. AI also drafts the airworthiness substantiation paperwork and insurer packages. Laws used: P8 and P14 (be your own approver and owner-operator), P9 (fleet hours become evidence), P10 (predictable hours lower the cost of capital), P12 (break the OEM spares lock by operating the fleet).
main_killer: Funded incumbents already hold the first rung (Top Aces, Draken, Tactical Air Support, ATAC/Textron), and airframes with a civil path are getting scarce and pricey. Military customers buy on long, lumpy IDIQ task orders, and there are safety and backlash risks if a contractor jet crashes.
ai_answer_to_killer: Compete on cost per hour and readiness, not on access to airframes. Incumbents run legacy MRO staffing. An AI-built parts library plus predictive maintenance on cannibalised spares should lower cost per hour about 20-30% and lift sortie generation (est.), which wins price-weighted task orders. Widen the airframe pool to types incumbents avoid because parts are orphaned (L-159, Mirage/Kfir variants, ex-Navy trainers). AI reverse engineering makes those types economic, so 'too hard to support' becomes the acquisition discount. Answer the safety risk with telemetry-based condition monitoring and a published reliability record (the Waymo/Swiss Re pattern), which also lowers insurance cost.
competitors: Top Aces (F-16, Alpha Jet), Draken International (PE-owned), Tactical Air Support, ATAC (Textron Airborne Solutions), Blue Air Training, Air USA, Metrea and Omega (contracted tanking), and Cobham/Babcock in Europe. The OEMs (Lockheed, Boeing) support only current types.
principles_used: P8, P9, P10, P12, P14 (also P5 digital inventory)

score.name: Ghost Wing: an owned fleet of retired military jets selling flight hours
score.rationale: Not search-verified this run (search budget exhausted); from prior knowledge, CAF ADAIR's roughly $6.4B multi-award ceiling and Top Aces' 29 ex-Israeli F-16s are broadly right. The idea owns an asset and sells its output, like the resurrection fleet, so it passes the ownership rule. The airframe arbitrage ($1-5M jet against $4.5-12M/yr billing) looks good on paper. In practice, military-type operating costs, the scarcity of airframes with a civil path, and long, lumpy IDIQ task orders compress it (N3). First revenue needs airframes plus restricted or experimental airworthiness approval plus a subcontract slot, so 2-3 years and incumbent-gated (T3). Realistic contracted-air-services spend is low single-digit $B a year. Draken went to PE, which signals a $1B-class ceiling, not $10B (C3). AI lowering cost per hour through scan-to-CAD parts and predictive maintenance is plausible. It answers price competitiveness, not the incumbent hold on task orders or the crash and backlash risk (A3). The moat is fleet record and approvals, which Top Aces and Draken already have (D3).
score.biggest_risk: Incumbents (Top Aces, Draken, ATAC, TacAir) already own fleets, records and contract vehicles, so a newcomer is squeezed on airframe supply and task-order access while carrying single-crash existential risk.

name: Heritage (a flight-heritage authority for space electronics)
sector: Space hardware: avionics and electronics
one_liner: Fly COTS and automotive-grade chips on its own test satellites, irradiate them in contracted beam time, and build the largest reference library of radiation and flight evidence. It then sells space-qualified parts and modules under its own pedigree, the HEICO of space electronics.
what_it_owns: The evidence library: radiation test data (TID, SEE) per part, lot and date code, plus on-orbit performance data. The Heritage-qualified parts list (the 'approved equivalent'). A small fleet of test satellites. Long-term beam-time contracts. Upscreened, lot-controlled inventory sold under its own part numbers.
wedge_first_revenue: New-space constellation builders (thousands of satellites a year) need cheap, characterised parts. Sell lot-controlled, upscreened COTS parts with a radiation report attached, at est. 10-30% of the price of rad-hard equivalents. Start with FPGAs, MCUs, DC-DC converters and memory. First revenue: inventory sales to 20-50 satellite builders (est. $3-8M year 1).
ladder: 1) Upscreened COTS parts with test reports. 2) A proprietary Heritage-qualified module family (on-board computer, power and radio boards) built from those parts. 3) Its own LEO test-bed satellites that add flight heritage every quarter. 4) Get the list accepted by NASA, SDA and ESA as an approved source; those agencies are already moving to class-D and risk-tolerant acquisition. 5) Expand to aircraft avionics obsolescence (DMSMS), where the same equivalence evidence lets it supply drop-in replacements for discontinued military and commercial avionics chips.
numbers: No 2025-26 market figures were checked: the web search budget ran out. Rad-hard electronics market est. $1.5-2B/yr, growing about 4-6% (est.). Space-grade avionics and subsystems est. $5-8B (est.). Comparable exits, unverified this pass: Honeywell's acquisition of CAES (Frontgrade parent) was est. about $1.9B in 2024, and Microchip, BAE and Infineon have rad-hard lines (est.). Rad-hard parts typically cost 10-100x their COTS equivalents (est.). Beam time est. $1-3k/hour at US cyclotrons, with long waits (est.). Capital: est. $15-30M to a first test satellite and a 2,000-part library. Time to $100M revenue: est. 5-7 years, which needs the module and DMSMS rungs. The ceiling is the main risk.
ai_role: Predict single-event-effect susceptibility from die images, process node and architecture (ML trained on public NASA/ESA radiation databases plus Heritage's own data). Then use active test selection to choose the fewest beam-hours needed to bound risk, cutting cost per part characterised by est. 5-10x. AI drafts the test plans, reports and equivalence (FFF) packages. On-orbit telemetry from its own satellites and from customer fleets becomes heritage evidence (P9). Matching across millions of SKUs finds drop-in substitutes for obsolete parts (P7).
main_killer: The ceiling: space electronics alone may cap below $500M revenue. Rad-hard incumbents (Microchip, BAE, Frontgrade/Honeywell, Infineon) have heritage and agency approvals. Beam time is a scarce, queued physical resource.
ai_answer_to_killer: Escape the small ceiling through the DMSMS rung. Defence and commercial avionics obsolescence is a multi-billion-dollar problem, est. tens of billions in redesign avoidance (est.), and it rests on the same equivalence evidence. Heritage then sells drop-in replacement modules, not reports. For beam-time scarcity, ML prediction cuts the hours needed, and a long-term contract or co-investment in a dedicated beamline (a scarce-capacity owner, P3) turns the bottleneck into Heritage's moat. On incumbents: they sell parts that cost 10-100x more, while the constellation builders want Heritage's 'characterised COTS'.
competitors: Microchip (rad-tolerant FPGAs and MCUs), Frontgrade/CAES (Honeywell), BAE Systems, Infineon/IR HiRel, Teledyne e2v, AMD/Xilinx space-grade, Vorago, Apogee Semiconductor, Zero-Error Systems, and test labs (Radiation Test Solutions, VPT).
principles_used: P2 (approved equivalent, not open design), P4 (cheap delta qualification), P7 (signed equivalence certificates), P9 (flight hours as evidence)

score.name: Heritage (a flight-heritage authority for space electronics)
score.rationale: Search budget was exhausted. Honeywell's CAES acquisition (about $1.9B, 2024) matches prior knowledge and sets an exit comparable. The rad-hard market of about $1.5-2B is consistent with industry estimates. N3: upscreened COTS is capital-light ($15-30M) with high margins, but lot-controlled inventory and beam time add working capital. T3: year-1 parts revenue is plausible, but $100M needs the module and DMSMS rungs in about 5-7 years. C3: space electronics alone caps near a few hundred million. DMSMS is large but contested (Rochester Electronics, Smart Microchip/legacy fabs, and defence primes' own redesign shops), so $1B+ is credible only through a CAES-like path. A3: ML SEE prediction plus active test selection to cut beam-hours is plausible and directly targets the scarce-beam killer, and AI FFF matching fits DMSMS. It does not move agency approval lists, which remain gatekeeper queues. D3: the evidence library and the flight-data flywheel compound, though it overlaps with public NASA/ESA databases and existing test labs. There is risk that it reads as a testing service, but it sells parts under its own pedigree, so it is not a violation.
score.biggest_risk: Ceiling: characterised-COTS for new-space is a few-hundred-million market, and the DMSMS escape route requires defence source approvals that are slow human queues.

name: Reborn Jets (an update-authority fleet of orphaned business jets)
sector: Commercial aerospace: business aviation and avionics
one_liner: Buy 15-25-year-old business jets whose resale values collapsed because of orphaned avionics, mandates and OEM support costs (Challenger 604/605, Gulfstream IV-SP, Falcon 2000, Citation X). Re-avionic them under its own STCs, built partly with AI. Keep them alive with a PMA and DER parts library, and sell flight hours through a fractional, jet-card and charter fleet it owns.
what_it_owns: The aircraft fleet. A library of STCs for an open avionics retrofit on each type (update authority, P8). A Part 145 repair station with DER repairs and PMA parts for those types. A Part 135 operating certificate. Per-tail operating and reliability data that sets its insurance and financing costs.
wedge_first_revenue: Buy 3-5 Challenger 604s or G-IVSPs at depressed prices (est. $2-5M each vs $25-45M for new mid- and large-cabin jets, est.). Put them on existing Part 135 certificates through managed charter while the first STC is underway. First revenue is charter hours (est. $4-8k/hour for large-cabin jets, est.) and est. $10-20M in year-1 revenue on 5 aircraft.
ladder: 1) Charter on bought-cheap jets. 2) Get the first STC: an open avionics retrofit (modern displays and FMS, ADS-B, data link) that ends the dependency on the orphaned OEM avionics and recovers resale value. 3) Sell the STC retrofit kit to other owners of the type, so the kit pays back the certification. 4) Add DER repairs and PMA for the type's long-tail parts, cutting maintenance cost per hour by est. 20-35%. 5) Fractional and jet-card programmes at below-NetJets pricing. 6) Extend the model to regional turboprops and to government special-mission aircraft (ISR conversions).
numbers: No 2025-26 market figures were checked: the web search budget ran out. Business aviation flight services (fractional, jet card, charter) est. $35-45B/yr globally (est.). Comparables: NetJets (Berkshire) est. $8-10B revenue (est.); Flexjet is privately held and has raised est. $1B+ (est.); Wheels Up failed because it owned neither its aircraft economics nor its maintenance (est.), which is a cautionary comparable. Avionics retrofits cost est. $0.5-2M per aircraft. One STC est. $3-10M and 12-30 months (est.). Capital: est. $25-50M equity plus asset-backed debt for the first 15-20 aircraft. Time to $100M revenue: est. 4-5 years at about 30-40 aircraft x 500-700 hours x $5k/hour (est.). Ceiling: fractional fleets reach multiple billions in revenue (NetJets).
ai_role: Reverse-engineering legacy avionics interfaces and ARINC data buses, plus auto-generating the STC data package (DO-178C/DO-254 artifacts, system safety assessments, EMI and integration analysis). That cuts per-STC engineering by est. 3-5x (P1, P8, P12). The PMA/DER library for each type is built from scans and AI material ID (P5, P7). Fleet health monitoring and predictive maintenance raise dispatch reliability and lower variance in maintenance cost, so insurance and debt cost less (P9, P10). AI dynamic pricing and repositioning to maximise utilisation of the owned fleet (P3).
main_killer: FAA STC queues (6-18+ months) and the cost of DO-178C software certification. NetJets, Flexjet and VistaJet hold scale and brand. Older jets have high fuel burn and maintenance cost, which caps the appeal to customers.
ai_answer_to_killer: AI shrinks the cost and time of building the STC data package, though the FAA queue stays human. Reborn Jets files early, operates the jets on legacy avionics through Part 135 while the STC is pending, and buys an existing STC holder or retrofit shop with an ODA where possible. On cost: the jets are bought at 5-15% of new price, and AI-built PMA parts cut maintenance, so the total cost per hour can sit 25-40% below new-jet fractional pricing (est.). That is a real wedge in mid-cabin, where demand outruns supply. On fuel burn: offer SAF blending and carbon accounting, and pick types with modern-enough engines.
competitors: NetJets, Flexjet, VistaJet/Vista, Wheels Up, Jet Linx, PlaneSense, avionics retrofitters (Garmin, Collins Pro Line Fusion retrofits, Duncan Aviation, Elliott Aviation), and OEM service networks (Bombardier, Gulfstream, Dassault).
principles_used: P8 (update authority over an orphaned fleet), P10 (sell output, finance on history), P12 (break the OEM aftermarket lock), P14 (owner-operator as its own gate)

score.name: Reborn Jets (an update-authority fleet of orphaned business jets)
score.rationale: Search budget was exhausted. From prior knowledge, used Challenger 604s and GIV-SPs trade around $2-5M, so the acquisition premise holds. N3: cheap airframes help, but engine programmes, inspections and high fuel burn make cost per hour on old large-cabin jets high, and charter margins are thin (Wheels Up). T4: charter revenue on existing Part 135 certificates comes fast, and 30-40 aircraft could reach $100M in 4-5 years. C4: the NetJets and Flexjet scale shows $1B+ is credible. A2: the core premise of orphaned avionics is weak, because Collins, Garmin and others already sell certified retrofits for many of these types (e.g. Pro Line 21/Fusion upgrades). AI does not fix the FAA STC queue, brand, or the fuel and maintenance burden of 20-year-old jets, which is the real killer. D2: STCs and PMA on a handful of aging types are a modest moat; incumbents with scale buy cheap old jets just as easily, and the fleet depreciates rather than compounds.
score.biggest_risk: Old-jet operating costs (engines, inspections, fuel) and established retrofit suppliers erase the cheap-airframe advantage, leaving a thin-margin charter operator like Wheels Up.

name: Second Shift: the resurrection fleet for industrial robots
sector: Robotics: industrial arms and automation cells
one_liner: Buy orphaned and off-lease industrial robots (out-of-support FANUC, KUKA, ABB, Motoman arms) at scrap-like prices. Keep them alive with an AI-built parts and reducer library and an owner-installed open controller. Deploy them as owned, financed work cells that sell finished output (welds, palletised cases, machined parts) per unit or per hour to factories that cannot afford or staff automation.
what_it_owns: The fleet of arms and cells, so it has update authority over them, and the controller layer it installs on them. It also owns the reverse-engineered parts library (reducers, servo motors, cables, teach-pendant and controller boards) and the fleet's operating-history dataset, which sets its cost of debt. Customers buy output, never the robot.
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1: buy 50-150 used six-axis arms at est. $5-25k each, against est. $50-150k for a new robot plus integration. Retrofit a standard AI-programmed cell (palletising, machine tending, MIG welding) and place each in a small or mid-sized manufacturer on a 3-5 year output contract. Example terms: est. $12-20/hr of robot runtime, or per part, with no capex and no programming staff for the customer. First revenue is est. $2-4M on 100 cells at about 4,000 hours each.
ladder: 1) Owned palletising and machine-tending cells in US small and mid-sized factories (the long tail that never automated). 2) Welding cells, competing with Path-style AI welding but owning the arms. 3) A parts and repair library sold internally first, later as approved replacement reducers and motors for the global installed base. 4) Securitise cell cash flows once there are 24-36 months of history (the SolarCity ABS move: https://www.ramapo.edu/rfg/wp-content/uploads/sites/370/2022/06/Heico-Pitch.pdf is the PMA-pricing precedent; the ABS precedent is in P10). 5) Merge into owned 'lights-out' contract factories that sell finished parts, which is the full vertical.
numbers: Installed base: about 4M+ industrial robots in operation worldwide, with est. 500k+ installed per year (IFR World Robotics 2024/2025 range, est.; https://ifr.org). The large share of arms installed 10-20 years ago is the cheap feedstock. US labour gap: about 400,000 welders projected short (https://seedtable.com/companies/path-robotics/funding-rounds/series-d-2024-10). Unit economics (est.): $40k all-in per cell (used arm $15k, retrofit and tooling $25k) earning $50-70k/yr is a 1-1.5 year payback before financing; a new-robot cell at $150k+ cannot match that. Capital: est. $10M equity plus asset-backed debt for the first 300 cells. To $100M revenue: about 1,500-2,000 cells, est. 5 years. Ceiling comparables: United Rentals at $16.1B revenue on a $22.5B fleet (the 'EC2 for iron' figure in P3), and AWS's fleet model at about $45.6B operating income (https://www.nasdaq.com/press-release/amazoncom-announces-fourth-quarter-results-2026-02-05). Automation-as-a-service comparables Formic and others are venture-funded (amounts not re-verified this run).
ai_role: (1) Vision-language-action and AI path planning remove the integrator's weeks of teach-pendant programming per cell, which is the per-unit labour that kept small factories un-automated. (2) Reverse compilation: scan and identify reducers and servo parts, infer specs, and build an equivalent or rebuilt-parts library for discontinued models. (3) An open controller retrofit that replaces orphaned OEM controllers (the P8 update-authority move), with AI translating legacy programs. (4) Fleet telemetry: motor current and vibration give remaining-life models per reducer. That turns fat-tailed downtime into a predictable fleet number, which lowers the cost of capital.
main_killer: Thin, labour-heavy deployment per site (the 'RaaS is just integration with a lease' problem). Customers' high-mix work changes constantly, and Formic-style operators have struggled to scale margins. New Chinese robots are also falling in price (est. under $20k for some arms), which erodes the used-arm cost advantage.
ai_answer_to_killer: AI programming collapses per-cell integration and changeover labour from weeks to hours, which is the core cost of RaaS and exactly the per-unit labour AI fixes. Standardised cell kits (one frozen target per application) make deployment repeatable. If new Chinese arms get cheap, Second Shift buys them too: the moat is not the cheap arm. It is the controller layer, the uptime data, the parts library and the financing spread, which compound together. Pricing per output ties revenue to throughput, and the fleet data shows which sites to redeploy cells away from.
competitors: Formic (automation-as-a-service), Rapid Robotics, Path Robotics ($100M Series D, https://seedtable.com/companies/path-robotics/funding-rounds/series-d-2024-10), Bright Machines, used-robot resellers (Eurobots, RobotWorx and similar), OEM refurbishment programmes (FANUC, ABB), and traditional system integrators.
principles_used: P8 (update authority over orphaned assets), P10 (sell output; recurring revenue as financing), P3 (pooled owned capacity), P12 (break the OEM aftermarket lock part by part), P9 (operating data the owner prices)

score.name: Second Shift: the resurrection fleet for industrial robots
score.rationale: No live search was possible: the shared web search budget for this turn was used up before this agent ran, so every figure here comes from prior knowledge and is unverified. Used six-axis arms (FANUC R-2000/M-710 class) do resell for roughly $10-30k, so the feedstock is cheap. But in a cell the arm is the small cost. Integration, tooling, guarding and changeover make up most of the $40k, and a $50-70k/yr take assumes about 4,000 billed hours at small factories that rarely run three shifts. First revenue from 100 cells is plausible inside 2 years. Getting to $100M means about 1,700 site deployments, each a field install, which is the scaling wall Formic and Rapid Robotics hit (Rapid Robotics largely stalled). The ceiling is a RaaS integrator, not United Rentals: the cells are customised and not fungible. AI programming does address per-cell labour, which is the right lever, but high-mix changeover and the site-by-site sales cycle remain. The defensibility leg fails. Used arms are a commodity, cheap Chinese arms remove the cost edge, and the open controller and parts library can be copied by Formic, integrators or the OEMs' own refurbishment programmes. The uptime data compounds slowly. One leg below 3, so it fails.
score.biggest_risk: Per-site deployment and changeover cost plus low utilisation at small factories keep gross margin thin, with no moat beyond what a funded RaaS competitor can copy.

name: Flow Utility: owning the pumps of public water and selling metered, guaranteed flow
sector: Fluid systems: pumps, motors, drives and valves in water, wastewater and district energy
one_liner: A fluid-system 'AWS'. The company buys or takes over the pumping assets of municipal water, wastewater and industrial sites under long concessions. It replaces thousands of bespoke pumps with a few frozen, characterised standard pump-drive modules, tunes each one with AI, and sells guaranteed delivered flow and pressure per cubic metre. The energy savings and the asset base stay with the company.
what_it_owns: (1) The installed pumping fleet under 15-25 year concession or ownership contracts. (2) A frozen standard module family (pump hydraulics plus PMSM motor plus VFD plus sensors) with published 'design rules', so one characterised target covers about 80% of duty points. (3) The fleet energy and reliability dataset that sets the price of flow and the cost of capital. (4) The parts library for the legacy pumps it keeps alive.
wedge_first_revenue: Energy-savings performance contracts (ESPC/ESCO structure, legal for US municipalities) on wastewater lift stations and water booster stations. Pumping is roughly 20-40% of a municipal water utility's energy bill and the biggest single cost after labour (est.; EPA/DOE commonly cite water and wastewater at 30-40% of municipal energy use). AI audits SCADA data remotely in days, finds oversized, throttled pumps running at 40-60% efficiency, and the company funds the swap to a standard module. The first contract keeps 50-80% of measured savings for 10-15 years. A lift station saves about $20-100k/yr (est.).
ladder: 1) Savings-share contracts on lift and booster stations. 2) Full 'flow-as-a-service' concessions: the company owns and operates all rotating equipment at a utility and guarantees uptime and pressure (DBOO/asset recycling). 3) Volume on the standard module drives Wright's-law cost declines and an in-house module factory, giving owned scarce capacity. 4) Extend to district heating and cooling, irrigation districts, industrial cooling water and data-centre cooling loops (pumps there are a fast-growing load). 5) International water concessions (Europe, India, Middle East) where pumping energy cost is high.
numbers: Market: about 16,000 US publicly owned wastewater treatment plants and about 50,000 community water systems (EPA, est. from memory, https://www.epa.gov/sustainable-water-infrastructure). Pumps use roughly 10-20% of world electricity (commonly cited Europump/Grundfos figure, est.). Global pump market is about $70-80B/yr (est.), and US water capex needs are $600B+ over 20 years (EPA DWINSA, est.). Unit economics: a standard module replacing a 100 hp pump costs about $40-80k installed. Savings of 20-40% on about $50k/yr of energy is about $10-20k/yr, a 3-5 year payback. Inside a 15-year contract that is an infrastructure-like 12-18% unlevered IRR (est.). 10,000 stations at about $15k/yr gives about $150M/yr recurring (est.). Capital: $5-10M seed for the module design, pilots and software. Then project finance and green bonds, which ESCO structures already access. Time to $100M revenue: 6-8 years (est.). Ceiling comparables: Veolia (~€44B revenue), American Water Works (~$4.7B revenue, ~$27B market cap), Ameresco ESCO (~$1.7B revenue). Note: the search budget ran out in this run, so all figures are est.
ai_role: (1) Remote, near-zero-cost audit: a model reads messy SCADA/historian data and pump curves and finds the savings, collapsing the per-site engineering labour that makes small ESCO deals uneconomic. (2) Per-site configuration: the generative design 'compiler' picks module size, impeller trim and control law for each duty point against the frozen module family (P1). (3) Per-unit control tuning and OTA control updates across the owned fleet, in pump scheduling, pressure management and leak reduction (P8). (4) Prognostics and measurement-and-verification evidence produced automatically, which proves savings to the municipality and to lenders (P10). (5) AI-drafted municipal procurement, M&V reports and bond documents.
main_killer: Municipal procurement is slow and political, and utilities resist ceding ownership of critical assets. Sales cycles of 12-24 months and public bidding favour incumbent ESCOs and OEMs (Xylem, Grundfos), which already sell 'smart pumping' plus financing.
ai_answer_to_killer: Pick channels that skip open bidding. ESPC statutes in most US states allow sole-source performance contracts with guaranteed savings, and the company can present a near-complete AI audit before the first meeting, which shortens the qualification step. Start with private and investor-owned water (American Water, Essential Utilities), industrial parks and data-centre cooling, where one decision-maker buys. The value-capture difference against Xylem and Grundfos: they sell boxes and want the next box sale. The company owns the asset and is paid on delivered flow, so it can standardise across OEMs and keep the savings, the AWS move over Dell. The AI audit makes small sites worth doing where incumbents walk away.
competitors: Xylem (~$8.5B revenue, est.) and Grundfos (~€4.5B, est.) with smart-pump and service offerings; Sulzer, KSB, Flowserve; ESCOs (Ameresco, Johnson Controls, Honeywell, Siemens); water operators (Veolia, Suez, Jacobs/Inframark); software tools (Pani, Fracta, Xylem Vue), which per P9 capture little. No one is an AI-native owner of a standardised, multi-OEM pumping fleet selling flow (est.).
principles_used: P1 (frozen, characterised module family as the target), P3 (owned pooled capacity sold as a metered utility), P5 (standard modules plus Wright's law), P8 (update authority over an owned fleet), P10 (output subscription as financing), P9 (asset plus data plus risk)

Prior knowledge: water/wastewater are commonly cited as ~30-40% of municipal energy use, and pumping dominates that, so the savings pool is real. N: per-site economics are small ($10-20k/yr per station), with 3-5 year paybacks; that is fine infrastructure IRR, but reaching $100M needs ~10,000 stations, which is a lot of field work. name: Liftwell: an elevator owner-operator built on an open controller
sector: Construction and buildings hardware: vertical transport (elevators and escalators)
one_liner: Own the elevators and charge buildings a monthly uptime fee. Modernise old and orphaned units with one AI-reverse-engineered, code-certified universal controller and an AI-built parts library, which breaks the Big-4 BIOS-style lock on service.
what_it_owns: (1) Title to the modernised elevator equipment in each building, held under 15-20 year 'vertical-transport-as-a-service' contracts like an ESCO or solar PPA. (2) One frozen controller platform certified once to ASME A17.1/CSA B44, with an A17.1 8.3 certification of the safety functions, plus a published 'design rules' interface spec for each legacy machine family. This is the PDK/ISA. (3) A library of form-fit-function replacement parts for proprietary boards, door operators and drives. (4) A fleet telemetry record of callbacks, entrapments and availability that sets its insurance and debt cost.
wedge_first_revenue: Orphaned and stranded elevators in mid-rise residential, hospital and municipal buildings (NYC, Chicago, Toronto). These are units where the OEM has discontinued the controller, or where the owner is captive to one OEM's proprietary diagnostic tool and pays rising maintenance fees. Revenue starts with an AI-diagnosed modernisation financed by Liftwell and repaid as a fixed monthly fee covering maintenance, parts and an availability guarantee (e.g. 99.5%). The first 50-100 units come through property managers who already buy elevator maintenance in portfolios. Later the same 'retrofit kit for an orphaned controller family' ships across thousands of identical cars.
ladder: 1) Orphaned-controller modernisation plus service contracts in one metro, using its own IUEC/union-signatory or licensed mechanics. 2) Become the certified controller and parts approver for 20-50 legacy machine families, so every independent service company buys kits from Liftwell (the HEICO/Red Hat position), while Liftwell keeps owning the units it finances. 3) Securitise the contract book once there are 24-36 months of availability history (the SolarCity ABS move). 4) Buy whole maintenance portfolios from PE-backed independents and roll them onto the platform. 5) Expand to escalators, parking systems and hospital pneumatic and lift systems, and to new-build installs on its own controller. End state: a TK Elevator-scale (EUR 17.2B LBO, 2020) service owner whose cost to serve is structurally below the Big-4's because parts and diagnostics are no longer proprietary.
numbers: Web search budget was exhausted, so these figures come from prior knowledge of filings and need verifying. Otis 2024 net sales about $14.3B. Service is about 64% of sales, at roughly 24-25% adjusted operating margin, on a maintenance portfolio of about 2.4M units. New equipment margin is about 7% (Otis 2024 10-K, https://www.otis.com/en/us/investors). Thyssenkrupp Elevator was sold to Advent/Cinven for EUR 17.2B in 2020 (https://www.thyssenkrupp.com/en/newsroom/press-releases). The EU fined the Otis/KONE/Schindler/ThyssenKrupp cartel EUR 992M in 2007, evidence of oligopoly pricing (https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_07_209). The US installed base is about 900k-1M elevators (est., NEII), of which about 50%+ are 20+ years old (est.). NYC has about 70-85k (est., NYC DOB). Unit economics (est.): modernisation $150-350k per car (mid-rise traction), maintenance contract $4-8k per car per year, as-a-service fee $2.5-4.5k per car per month over 15 years, implying 12-16% unlevered IRR at 98% availability. A Big-4 maintenance price premium of 20-40% over independents is est. Capital: $8-15M seed/A for controller certification, the first 100 cars and a mechanics crew, then asset-backed debt. Time to $100M revenue (est.): about 6-8 years, roughly 3,000-4,000 cars under contract plus kit sales. Ceiling comparables: Otis market cap about $38-40B, KONE about EUR 25-30B, TK Elevator EUR 17.2B.
ai_role: (a) Reverse compilation: AI reads relay and ladder logic, PCB photos and X-rays, legacy wiring diagrams and fault logs, and produces an interface spec and drop-in controller mapping for each orphaned machine family. Clean-room in the Phoenix-BIOS sense (P12, P6). (b) It generates TDPs for proprietary boards, door operators and sheaves from scans, which builds the parts library (P5, P7). (c) Per-car ML on motor current, door-cycle and vibration data predicts callbacks, roughly halving truck rolls, which is the biggest cost line. (d) It drafts the A17.1/B44 compliance and safety-function certification paperwork and the state acceptance-test packages (per-unit paperwork, P4). (e) Fleet availability data becomes the underwriting evidence for insurers and lenders (P9, P10). (f) AR and AI coaching takes apprentice mechanics to median-expert level faster (P11).
main_killer: The labour and permission gate. Elevator work in most US states needs licensed, typically IUEC-union, mechanics. Every modernisation needs a state or city permit, an acceptance inspection and certified safety components. The Big-4 also hold the installed base through long service contracts and proprietary tools, and a single entrapment death would end a startup.
ai_answer_to_killer: Liftwell does not try to beat the union or the inspector. It signs as a union employer and hires licensed mechanics, but AI remote diagnostics and parts certainty raise cars served per mechanic from about 80-100 to an est. 150-200, so the binding constraint (licensed hours) goes further. The safety gate is cleared once per controller platform, not per job: one A17.1/B44-certified frozen target is reused across thousands of cars, like a PDK, and the per-job paperwork is AI-drafted. The installed-base lock is broken at contract expiry by targeting units the OEM has orphaned (discontinued controllers, where OEMs push $200k+ modernisations anyway). Liftwell then finances the modernisation, so it owns the asset and becomes its own approver of parts, in the manner of nuclear dedication, under the A17.1 owner/contractor responsibility. Correlated-failure risk is handled by staged canary rollouts of controller firmware (P8, P14).
competitors: Otis, KONE, Schindler and TK Elevator (about 60-70% of global new installs, est.). Independent controller makers: Motion Control Engineering (Nidec), Smartrise, GAL (door equipment), Elevator Controls Corp. PE-backed independent service roll-ups (several regional platforms, est.). Elevator-IoT tools (e.g. Otis ONE, KONE 24/7 Connected Services; startups such as Uptime/Elevator-monitoring SaaS, est.). None owns the asset and also sells uptime on an open, certified controller.
principles_used: P12 (break the BIOS-style aftermarket lock), P6 (FFF interface spec), P1 (frozen, certified controller target), P8 (update authority over an owned installed base), P9/P10 (fleet evidence sets cost of capital), P14 (owner-operator becomes its own gate).

score.name: Liftwell: an elevator owner-operator built on an open controller
score.rationale: Not search-verified because the search budget ran out. From prior knowledge: Otis service is about 60%+ of sales at about 24% margin on about 2.4M+ units, so the profit pool is real. But the 'open controller' wedge already exists. Independent modernisations routinely use non-proprietary controllers from MCE/Nidec, Smartrise and GAL, so AI reverse-engineering does not unlock something new. The real killers are not answered by AI. IUEC labour supply, city permits and acceptance inspections are gatekeeper queues. Selling to property managers takes a long time. And an elevator is a building fixture whose title conflicts with the building's mortgage lender, which complicates both owning it and securitising the contracts. Getting to $100M needs about 3,000-4,000 financed cars at $150-350k each, about $0.6-1B of capex, inside 7 years. That is a stretch. Fleet telemetry and contract books do compound somewhat.
score.biggest_risk: Open controllers are already a commodity, so there is no proprietary unlock. Growth is capped by union mechanic hours, city inspection queues and the problem of owning a fixture, while the Big-4 and PE-backed independents already offer modernisation-plus-maintenance bundles.

name: Codehome: a HUD-code housing owner-operator
sector: Construction and buildings hardware: factory-built housing and structural systems
one_liner: Treat the federal HUD code, which preempts about 20,000 local building codes, as housing's frozen 'ISA'. Compile site-specific multi-section, attached and small-multifamily homes onto it with AI, build them in owned factories, and keep them as rental communities, so Codehome owns the homes, the land leases and the approved design library.
what_it_owns: (1) A library of DAPIA-approved HUD-code designs (attached, two-storey and stacked forms as federal rules allow) generated as a parametric family. Each approval is reused across every state, as a PDK is. (2) An owned, AI-run factory line, the scarce qualified capacity. (3) The rental communities and land leases, the asset that compounds like ELS and Sun Communities. (4) A per-home build and inspection data record that lowers insurance and financing cost (Fannie/Freddie chattel and MH Advantage-style lending).
wedge_first_revenue: Infill and by-right parcels in states that have recently forced manufactured homes to be allowed wherever single-family homes are (several 2023-2025 state laws, est.). Also existing older MH communities bought cheaply where 1970s pre-HUD units need replacement. First revenue: rent on the first 100-300 replaced or infill homes, from homes Codehome builds at est. $90-110/sq ft against site-built $180-250/sq ft. Sales of homes on the same approved designs to other community owners fund the factory.
ladder: 1) Buy 3-5 distressed older communities and replace homes with its own product (rent uplift plus density). 2) Get the approved HUD-code design library widened to attached and small-multifamily forms, and reuse it nationally. 3) Own 2-3 factories with ML-run quality control, which are the qualified capacity. 4) Securitise the community book (the MHC REIT model) and sell homes to third parties. 5) Expand from housing into other preempted or state-approved factory-built building classes (classrooms under state modular programmes, clinics, worker housing).
numbers: Web search budget was exhausted, so these figures are recalled or estimated. US manufactured-home shipments were about 100-105k in 2024 (MHI, https://www.manufacturedhousing.org/news/). The average new manufactured home sold for about $120-125k excluding land versus about $400k+ for a new site-built home (US Census MHS, https://www.census.gov/data/program-surveys/mhs.html; per-sq-ft gap about 50%, est.). Clayton (Berkshire) holds about 45-50% of HUD-code production (est.); Champion Homes FY2025 revenue about $2.5B (https://ir.championhomes.com); Cavco about $2B. Equity LifeStyle market cap about $12-13B and Sun Communities about $15-17B, both on high-NOI-margin land-lease models (est.). The HUD code preempts local building codes under 42 USC 5403(d) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/5403). Federal legislation (ROAD to Housing Act, 2025) moved to drop the permanent-chassis requirement; its final status needs checking (est.). US housing shortage about 4-5M units (est., Freddie Mac/Zillow). Unit economics (est.): 1,200 sq ft home at $120k factory cost plus $40-60k site and pad, renting at $1,600-2,200/month, about 8-10% yield on cost in Sun Belt markets. Capital: $25-60M for the first factory (or buying an existing small MH plant for est. $10-30M) plus community acquisitions on debt. Time to $100M revenue (est.): 5-7 years (about 3,000 owned homes plus about 1,500 sold per year). Ceiling comparables: ELS plus Sun, about $30B combined, and Clayton.
ai_role: (a) Compiler: AI turns a parcel, a target unit count and climate/wind/thermal zone into a HUD-code-compliant design. Structural, thermal and egress checks run against the code as a type checker, and the output includes production drawings and line instructions for the owned factory (P1, P4). (b) AI drafts the DAPIA submission and keeps the approved-design family coherent, so one approval covers a parametric family (P13, P7). (c) Vision and sensor QC on the line produces a per-home digital traveler for IPIA in-plant inspection (P13, P9). (d) AI parcel and zoning screening finds by-right sites and drafts the site permits (per-unit paperwork, P4). (e) Community operations: predictive maintenance on owned homes, which drives the financing spread (P10).
main_killer: Land and stigma. Local zoning still controls where HUD-code homes can go, and it often bans them. Site-built-equivalent appraisal and financing lag. Clayton's vertical integration (factories, retail, Vanderbilt and 21st Mortgage) holds the first rungs, and Katerra and Veev show that factory-built housing burns capital.
ai_answer_to_killer: Codehome never competes for zoned greenfield land. It starts on land already zoned for manufactured homes, meaning existing communities where it buys and replaces aged stock and adds density, and in states with new by-right MH laws, which AI screens parcel by parcel at near-zero cost. It avoids Katerra's failure mode (owning a national new-build general contractor) by owning the code-preempted target and the rental asset, so factory utilisation is anchored by its own replacement pipeline, as TSMC anchors to its biggest customer. Stigma is addressed with product: AI-compiled attached and two-storey forms that look like site-built housing. Financing improves as the per-home inspection and maintenance record builds a performance history lenders can price (P10).
competitors: Clayton Homes (Berkshire), Champion Homes, Cavco, and community REITs ELS and Sun Communities (own land, mostly buy homes). New-build factory and modular startups: Cover, Reframe Systems, Veev (failed), Katerra (failed, about $2B raised), Boxabl, Volumetric Building Companies. Most build to local IRC/IBC modular rules, not the preempting federal code, and do not own the rental asset.
principles_used: P1 (frozen national target, the HUD code, as the ISA), P13 (certify the design family, not the site), P11 (abundant designers through an owned qualified line), P14 (owner-operator carries the risk), P10 (owned rental cash flows set the cost of capital).

score.name: Codehome: a HUD-code housing owner-operator
score.rationale: Not search-verified because the search budget ran out. From prior knowledge: about 100k HUD-code shipments a year, an average home price of about $120-125k versus $400k+ for new site-built, preemption under 42 USC 5403, and ELS plus Sun worth about $30B. The ceiling comparables are real. But this is mostly a real-estate and factory play, and it sits outside the target sectors except as 'adjacent hardware'. Design is not the binding constraint. HUD-code design is prescriptive and cheap, so an AI 'compiler' does not make the pain solvable. Land, zoning and community acquisition are the binding constraints. MH communities are heavily bid by REITs and PE at low cap rates, which is the 'sellers price in hope, first rungs held by PE' law. DAPIA approvals are routine for incumbents, and Clayton/Berkshire controls production, retail and chattel finance. The plan needs a lot of capital for the factory plus communities, and the 8-10% yields are modest. The owned rental asset compounds, but copying it is easy for Clayton, ELS and Sun.
score.biggest_risk: There is no AI-specific edge. Land and community acquisition costs are set by REIT and PE bidders, and incumbents with cheaper capital and existing plants can match any approved design.

name: Heatwell: a thermal utility that owns building heat-pump plants
sector: Construction and buildings hardware: HVAC central plants (chillers, boilers, large heat pumps)
one_liner: Own the heating and cooling plants inside large buildings that face carbon fines (NYC Local Law 97 and similar building performance standards). Replace boilers and chillers with one AI-compiled, UL-listed modular heat-pump skid deployed as a frozen target, and sell tonne-hours of heat and cooling under 20-year contracts.
what_it_owns: (1) The plant equipment in each building: heat-pump skids, controls and thermal storage, held as an owned fleet. (2) One standard, UL-listed, factory-tested modular plant platform with published 'design rules' for fitting into legacy mechanical rooms. This is the PDK; per-site work becomes configuration, not engineering. (3) Update authority and control software across the fleet. (4) Metered performance and maintenance history, which lets the contract book be securitised.
wedge_first_revenue: NYC buildings over 25,000 sq ft facing LL97 penalties of $268 per tonne CO2e over their limits from 2030 onward (and in the 2024-29 period for the worst emitters). Also similar standards in Boston (BERDO), Denver, Washington State and Maryland. Many of these buildings have steam or oil boilers and 30-year-old chillers. First revenue: Heatwell installs and owns a modular heat-pump plant, the building pays a monthly thermal fee below its fuel plus fines plus maintenance baseline, and Heatwell keeps the IRA/48E-type tax credits and any utility incentives (where still available).
ladder: 1) A standard plant for one segment, NYC pre-war and 1960s multifamily and office, with 20-50 plants. 2) Get the skid listed once and characterised (performance maps, cold-climate COP), and build design rules for retrofit into existing risers and steam loops. 3) Securitise the contract book after 24-36 months of history. 4) Link plants into campus or block thermal networks (the Enwave/Vicinity model), turning building plants into a district utility with demand-response revenue. 5) Own the skid factory, the scarce capacity, and sell the frozen platform to other owners while keeping the fleet.
numbers: Web search budget was exhausted, so these figures are recalled or estimated. NYC LL97 covers about 50,000 buildings with a $268/tCO2e penalty (NYC Buildings, https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/ll97-greenhouse-gas-emissions-reductions.page). Buildings account for about two-thirds of NYC emissions (est., same source). Urban Green Council estimated about 3,000+ buildings over 2024 limits and a large majority over 2030 limits without retrofits (est., https://www.urbangreencouncil.org). Comparables: Vicinity Energy (Antin-owned district steam in Boston, Philadelphia and other cities); Enwave (Brookfield, then sold to others, est.); Redaptive and Budderfly (efficiency-as-a-service, each with hundreds of millions to $1B+ of capital facilities, est.); BlocPower (heat-pump-as-a-service). Carrier 2024 revenue about $22.5B after selling non-HVAC units (https://ir.carrier.com). Unit economics (est.): a 200-unit building plant of about 1-2 MW thermal at $1.5-3M installed, a thermal fee of $350-600k/yr against a fuel-plus-fines-plus-maintenance baseline of $450-750k/yr, giving 10-14% unlevered returns before credits. Capital: $10-20M for the platform and first plants, then project debt and tax equity. Time to $100M revenue (est.): 6-8 years, about 200-250 plants. Ceiling: a district-energy and thermal utility with regulated-like multiples (district-energy platforms trade at mid-teens EBITDA multiples, est.).
ai_role: (a) Compiler: AI turns building data (utility bills, BMS trends, a laser scan of the mechanical room, old drawings) into a sized plant configuration, piping and electrical tie-ins and a permit set, drawn from the standard skid library. That cuts per-site engineering from est. $150-300k to $20-50k (P1). (b) Per-plant ML control models (staging, storage, thermostat-reset optimisation, demand response) are deployed across the fleet under Heatwell's own update authority, with canary rollouts (P8). (c) Telemetry turns fat-tailed maintenance cost into a predictable fleet number, which sets the debt spread (P9, P10). (d) AI drafts LL97 compliance filings, incentive applications and investor reporting (per-unit paperwork). (e) Fault prediction keeps the availability guarantee at 99%+.
main_killer: Electrical capacity and capital. Many old buildings lack the electrical service for all-electric heat, and utility service upgrades (Con Edison) take 1-3 years. It is project-finance-heavy and returns are thin against well-funded efficiency-as-a-service players. Cold-climate peak heating performance also creates resistive-backup risk, and penalties have been softened before (LL97 alternative compliance and mitigation paths).
ai_answer_to_killer: Heatwell designs to the electrical service the building already has rather than queuing for a new one. AI-optimised hybrid plants with thermal storage and load-shifting, keeping the existing boiler as peak backup, size the heat pump to the spare service capacity, which is often 30-60% of design heating load and est. 70-90% of annual heating energy. That avoids the utility queue, the gate AI cannot shorten. On capital, the standard frozen skid plus fleet telemetry gives lenders a homogeneous, measured asset class within 24-36 months, which is SolarCity's ABS move, and AI-cut per-site engineering lowers the minimum economic building size, opening the long tail of mid-size buildings that efficiency-as-a-service players skip. If policy softens, the contract still beats the fuel-plus-maintenance baseline on owned-plant economics and does not depend on fines.
competitors: OEMs with as-a-service offers: Trane, Carrier, Johnson Controls (OpenBlue as-a-service), Daikin. District energy: Vicinity Energy, Enwave, Con Edison Steam. Efficiency and electrification-as-a-service: Redaptive, Budderfly, BlocPower, Bloom-type fuel-cell PPAs, Sealed. Modular heat-pump makers: Daikin/AAF, Mitsubishi, startups such as Harvest Thermal and Gradient (residential). None combines one listed frozen plant platform with an owned fleet and per-plant AI control in LL97-type buildings.
principles_used: P1 (frozen, characterised target: one listed skid platform), P3 (owned pooled thermal capacity sold per tonne-hour), P8 (update authority over an owned fleet), P9/P10 (fleet evidence sets financing cost), P14 (owner-operator behind the building's fence).

score.name: Heatwell: a thermal utility that owns building heat-pump plants
score.rationale: Not search-verified because the search budget ran out. From prior knowledge: LL97 covers about 50k buildings at $268/tCO2e, but the city has repeatedly softened enforcement through mitigation and good-faith paths. Tax credits for air-source commercial heat pumps are weak: 48E covers generation, and only ground-source heat pumps keep a clear ITC after the 2025 changes. The stated 10-14% returns before credits are therefore thin for capital-heavy, per-building project finance. Sizing hybrid plants to the building's existing electrical service, with storage and the boiler kept as backup, is a sound, AI-assisted answer to the Con Ed service-upgrade queue. AI-cut per-site engineering lowers the minimum building size. Defensibility is weak. Every building is a separate contract, and Trane, Carrier, JCI, Redaptive, Budderfly and infrastructure funds all offer as-a-service plants at lower capital cost. BlocPower's struggles show how hard it is to execute heat-pump-as-a-service in NYC. A district-energy end state supports a $1B+ ceiling, but getting there takes a long time.
score.biggest_risk: Policy softening and lost credits erode the savings against the baseline. Well-capitalised OEM and infrastructure-fund as-a-service players then win on cost of capital, so returns compress below what venture equity needs.

name: Garrison Water: 50-year owner of military and campus water networks, run on in-pipe robotics and AI
sector: Water and wastewater distribution networks: defence installations and private campuses
one_liner: Take ownership of the water, wastewater and steam pipe networks of military bases, ports, universities and industrial parks under 50-year utility privatization contracts, map them with in-pipe robots and AI, replace only the pipe that is actually failing, and sell guaranteed water service by the month.
what_it_owns: The networks themselves, as conveyed asset ownership under DoD Utilities Privatization (10 USC 2688) or long concessions, plus the condition dataset (robot inspection, acoustic leak data, break history) for every metre of pipe. That dataset sets its fixed-price bids and its cost of capital. It also owns an approved family of trenchless rehab processes (liners, robotic lateral reinstatement) used only on its own assets.
wedge_first_revenue: Bid on DLA Energy / service-branch utilities privatization solicitations for water and wastewater at mid-sized installations, many of which have been out for years with few bidders. In parallel, sign private campuses (universities, pharma or industrial parks, ports) that own aging networks and want them off their balance sheet. First revenue is a monthly utility service charge from contract start. Initial capital upgrades are recovered through the rate, like a regulated utility, under the contracting officer's economic price adjustment.
ladder: 1) Win 2-3 UP water contracts and 5 campus concessions, and robot-map every network in year 1. 2) Use the condition data to bid tighter than incumbents on the next solicitations (lower contingency) and to raise infrastructure-fund debt at narrower spreads. 3) Bring trenchless rehab and robotic inspection in-house as the scarce qualified capacity, used only on owned networks. 4) Extend to adjacent installation utilities (electric, gas, steam) and allied-nation bases. 5) Become the defence-and-campus utility platform, the American Water Military Services position at 5-10x its scale.
numbers: Market: US water systems lose about 6 billion gallons a day of treated water, and a main breaks every 2 minutes (ASCE, https://infrastructurereportcard.org/cat-item/drinking-water-infrastructure/). DoD UP: hundreds of installation utility systems are already privatized on 50-year terms, with American Water Military Services, Aqua/Essential Military, Corix/Nexus and Sundt/others holding about 20-60 contracts each (est.). A single water/wastewater UP award is typically $100M-$1B+ over 50 years (est.). Unit economics (est.): a 10,000-person installation network takes $2-6M/yr in service charges plus capital recovery. AI-targeted replacement cuts the replacement capex needed for the same reliability by about 30-50% (est., analogous to utility asset-management studies). Capital: about $30-80M equity for the first 5-8 contracts, levered with infrastructure debt. Time to $100M revenue (est.): about 6-8 years, at about 25-35 contracts. Ceiling comparables: American Water's Military Services Group is a profitable niche inside a roughly $25B company. Gecko Robotics reached a $1.25B valuation (2025, est.) selling inspection; Xylem bought Pure Technologies (pipe inspection) for about C$509M in 2018 (est.). Both are tool or service plays; the owner position is larger. Note: the search budget was exhausted this run, so figures without URLs are from memory (est.).
ai_role: (1) In-pipe robot plus acoustic/fibre data, read by vision and time-series models, gives a probability-of-failure model for every metre. (2) Reverse-compile undocumented base networks (decades of missing as-builts) into a GIS plus hydraulic model in weeks. (3) Fixed-price risk: the same models price 50-year obligations that incumbents pad with contingency. (4) Paperwork: UP proposals, sanitary surveys, cross-connection programs and capital-upgrade justifications drafted automatically. (5) Operations: remote pump and treatment control across scattered installations with few licensed staff.
main_killer: Government procurement time and concentration. UP solicitations take 2-5 years to award, incumbents with past-performance records win most of them, and contracting officers weight past performance heavily, which a startup lacks. Campus owners are slow to hand over assets.
ai_answer_to_killer: Build the evidence first on private campuses. Those 5-20 year concessions close in 6-12 months and create the past-performance and condition-data record UP evaluators score. Partner as a junior or teaming member on early UP bids, carrying the robotic inspection and rehab risk, then prime the next ones. AI makes the per-bid labour (survey, inventory, proposal) cheap enough to bid every solicitation instead of a few, and the condition data lets it bid lower contingency than incumbents still pricing from 1970s drawings. The procurement queue does not shrink, but the startup's win rate per queue slot rises.
competitors: American Water Military Services Group; Aqua Military / Essential; Nexus Water Group (Corix) and other UP holders (est.); Veolia and Jacobs as O&M contractors (service, not owners); inspection/tool firms Gecko Robotics, RedZone Robotics, Xylem/Pure Technologies, FIDO Tech, Utilis (sell data, own nothing).
principles_used: P8 (update authority over an owned installed base), P9 (operating hours become priced evidence because the company owns asset, data and risk), P10 (availability-based cash flows; variance reduction is a financing advantage), P14 (an owner behind a fence is its own gate: bases and campuses are private property).

score.name: Garrison Water: 50-year owner of military and campus water networks, run on in-pipe robotics and AI
score.rationale: Fifty-year conveyed-ownership contracts are a real owned asset, and pipe-condition data is a sensible pricing edge, so defensibility is strong once won. But the wedge is a gatekeeper queue: UP solicitations take 2-5 years to award, past performance is weighted heavily, and incumbents (American Water Military Services, Aqua/Essential Military, Nexus) already hold most awards. AI raises bid throughput but does not shrink the queue, which the idea concedes. The campus concession bridge is held by funded infrastructure funds and strategics (Engie/Axium at Ohio State and similar university P3s), so the first rungs are already taken. The ceiling is limited: even American Water's military group is a niche of a few hundred million in revenue inside AWK, so a credible $1B+ standalone company is a stretch without expanding into electric and gas. First revenue within 2 years is unlikely without a teaming slot.
score.biggest_risk: Procurement time and past-performance weighting. The startup may not win a prime UP award within 3-5 years, and campus concessions are dominated by infrastructure funds with cheaper capital and existing records.

name: Substrate: the owner-operator of private high-voltage interconnection (substations-as-capacity)
sector: Electric grid hardware: substations, switchgear, protection, transformers for large loads and generators
one_liner: Own and operate the customer-side and generator-side high-voltage substations, from 69-345 kV switchyards down to medium voltage, that data centres, factories, electrolysers and power plants need. Build them from one frozen, standard library of modular substation designs compiled by AI. Sell 'energised MVA-years' under 15-25 year contracts, so the customer never buys the steel.
what_it_owns: (1) An installed base of substations: transformers, breakers, GIS/AIS bays, protection and control. (2) The frozen, characterised 'substation ISA': a small set of standard modular bays and skids with pre-approved protection schemes and type tests, so the AI compiler emits a correct design from a load spec. (3) Pooled spares and a hot-swap inventory across the fleet. (4) Operating and protection telemetry, which supports insurance and debt pricing. (5) The update authority (P8) over protection settings and controls on every owned site.
wedge_first_revenue: Start with large loads that are already paying for their own substations, then keep ownership instead of donating the asset. Examples: Microsoft paying about $39M for a Cheyenne substation; Applied Digital funding a $110M powerline and substation that the cooperative will own (https://newprojectmedia.com/td-microsoft-to-pay-for-new-transmission-infrastructure-to-serve-data-center-expansion-in-wyomings-capital/; https://northdakotamonitor.com/?p=18215).
