First contract: the customer-owned high-side substation for a 100-300 MW data centre campus or a behind-the-meter generation island, delivered faster because the standard design and pooled long-lead inventory (transformers from Rewound, pre-bought breakers) remove the 2-4 year wait. Revenue is a capacity charge per MVA per month, est. $8-15k per MVA-year.
ladder: Rung 1: owned customer-side substations for data centres and industrial sites, on fixed-fee capacity contracts. Rung 2: generator interconnection substations and collector systems for IPPs, solar and storage. Rung 3: a portfolio securitised as infrastructure (utility-like returns without utility regulation, since customer-owned facilities sit outside the franchise). Rung 4: private-wire microgrids that combine owned generation and load behind one owned substation, selling firm power. Rung 5: merchant transmission or independent transmission developer status where FERC Order 1920 competitive windows allow it.
numbers: Large-load interconnection costs commonly run $40-110M per campus (Cheyenne about $39M; Fargo rose from $75M to $110M, links above). There is no standard federal large-load interconnection framework, and the customer funds studies and upgrades (Vermont VELCO testimony, https://legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2026/Workgroups/House%20Energy%20and%20Digital/Bills/H.727/Witness%20Documents/H.727~Shana%20Louiselle~VELCO%20Testimony~2-12-2026.pdf). Transformer lead times are 128-160+ weeks (https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/05/11/u-s-transformer-market/). Ceiling comparables: regulated wires utilities earn about 9.5-10.5% allowed ROE on rate base (est.). ITC Holdings was bought by Fortis for about $11.3B in 2016 (est., widely reported). Unit economics (est.): a 300 MVA site costs about $40-60M in capex and earns about $6-9M a year, a 13-16% unlevered yield before leverage. Capital: project debt or ABS after the first 3-5 sites. Time to $100M revenue (est.): about 12-15 sites, 5-7 years. Market (est.): US data-centre power demand of tens of GW to be added by 2030 implies $20-50B of high-side substation capex.
ai_role: Design compiler (P1, P6): from a load spec, single-line diagram and site survey, AI generates the substation layout, equipment schedule, grounding, protection settings and coordination studies against the frozen, type-tested bay library. Weeks of engineer labour become days, and every design stays inside pre-characterised rules. AI drafts utility interconnection applications, NERC registration and compliance paperwork (per-unit paperwork, which AI fixes). Fleet operation: AI protection-setting management, condition monitoring and remote operations let one control room run hundreds of sites (P3, P10). Ownership of update authority lets the company push validated protection and control improvements across the fleet (P8).
main_killer: The utility franchise and interconnection gatekeeper. Utilities control the point of interconnection, often insist on owning the high side, and run interconnection studies on human timescales. Customers may also prefer to own the asset outright and finance it cheaply themselves (hyperscalers have the cheapest capital in the world).
ai_answer_to_killer: Stay on the customer side of the meter or the change-of-ownership point, where customer-owned substations are legal and common (industrial customers have owned 138 kV substations for decades), and on the generator side, where IPP ownership is standard. The utility study queue is not compressed by AI, but the company removes the other gating items: equipment lead time (pooled, pre-bought long-lead inventory) and design and protection-study labour (AI compiler). Interconnection packages also arrive complete and consistent the first time, which reduces study rework. Against the hyperscaler capital argument, the product is time and operations, not money: guaranteed energisation dates plus a fleet O&M team, the way hyperscalers lease powered shells rather than build them. Later sell the contracted portfolio to infrastructure funds to recycle capital.
competitors: EPCs and contractors selling a service: Quanta Services, MasTec, Burns & McDonnell, Black & Veatch, POWER Engineers. OEM turnkey substation divisions: Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, Schneider. Modular substation makers: Delta Star (MacLean/Blackstone), ELSCO, Southwest Electric. Utilities themselves (regulated rate-base owners). Powered-land and data-centre developers (Crusoe, Fermi America, Lancium) who build their own substations. Note: no clear example was found of a developer keeping ownership of a transmission-level interconnection asset, which is the white space.
principles_used: P1 (freeze the target: a standard bay library), P3 (pooled owned capacity sold metered), P6 (a frozen interface between grid and load), P8 (update authority over protection and controls), P10 (sell MVA-years as a financing product), P14 (owner-operator behind its own fence).

score.name: Substrate: the owner-operator of private high-voltage interconnection (substations-as-capacity)
score.rationale: It owns an asset and taps a real, large pain: $40-110M per campus and multi-year transformer and breaker lead times. But the business is essentially infrastructure financing plus inventory. A 13-16% unlevered yield on substations is exactly what infrastructure funds and hyperscalers (capital at about 5%) can replicate or undercut. The real advantage is pre-bought long-lead inventory, which is a balance-sheet bet anyone with capital can make, not a moat. The AI design compiler fixes engineering labour, but the killers are the utility's control of the point of interconnection and study timelines (a gatekeeper queue AI does not move) and customers' cheaper capital, so A is weak. Defensibility is low: there is no approval, no scarce capacity, and a standard bay library is knowledge, which AI levels for incumbents (Quanta, OEM turnkey divisions, developers like Crusoe) too. The ceiling (ITC-style comparables) is credible only if it rolls up to merchant transmission, which is far up the ladder. I could not search to confirm the white-space claim (no developer retaining transmission-level interconnection assets) because the search budget was used up.
score.biggest_risk: Commoditised capital. Hyperscalers and infrastructure funds can own substations more cheaply, and nothing proprietary stops EPCs or OEMs from offering the same lease-style structure.

name: CoreBank: the second domestic source of transformer electrical steel, reclaimed and re-characterised from retired transformers
sector: Electric grid hardware: core materials (grain-oriented electrical steel and amorphous cores) for transformers
one_liner: Own the scarce physical input. Mine the steel in retired transformers' cores: AI magnetically images each recovered lamination, then re-anneal, recoat, sort and certify it, and cut and stack it into finished cores on an owned, characterised core line. Add amorphous-metal cores for distribution units. This becomes the only US alternative to Cleveland-Cliffs' grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) monopoly, sold as finished cores and core-and-coil assemblies under long-term offtake to transformer builders.
what_it_owns: (1) Scarce physical capacity: the reclamation, anneal and core-cutting line, sold as finished cores, which is the TSMC position for transformer magnetics. (2) A grade database: per-sheet magnetic characterisation (loss in W/kg, permeability) and a published 'core PDK' that transformer designers compile to. (3) Feedstock contracts: a scrap-transformer supply network from utilities, recyclers and its own Rewound teardown flow. (4) Long-term offtake agreements.
wedge_first_revenue: Year 1: buy cores from scrapped distribution and power transformers at near-scrap steel prices. Sort laminations with AI magnetic and optical imaging. Use the best grades in rewinds and rebuilds, where reusing original cores is already standard practice, and the rest, re-annealed and recut, to make cores for small and medium distribution and dry-type transformers. Sell to independent distribution-transformer makers and rewinders who cannot get GOES allocation from Cliffs or affordable imports. First revenue: finished cores at a discount to new GOES-based cores with a shorter lead time.
ladder: Rung 1: sorted reclaimed laminations and cores for rebuild shops and small distribution OEMs. Rung 2: an owned core-cutting and stacking line producing finished cores for a range of designs (the 'foundry' that core-less transformer assemblers compile to). Rung 3: an amorphous ribbon and core line for high-efficiency distribution transformers (DOE efficiency rules favour amorphous). Rung 4: virgin thin-gauge GOES or amorphous production capacity financed by offtake contracts and DoD/DOE support (the DLA already buys GOES sole-source). Rung 5: vertical integration into owned transformer fleets (with Rewound), so material, cores and units are all owned.
numbers: Monopoly: Cleveland-Cliffs is the only US GOES producer (Butler, PA). DLA awarded it a sole-source IDIQ of up to $400M for up to 53,000 net tons through September 2030 (https://www.steelorbis.com/steel-news/latest-news/cleveland-cliffswins-us-defense-contractworth400-million-1462295.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764065/000076406526000025/clf-20251231.htm), which implies about $7,500/t for defence-grade GOES. Historical imports come from Japan and Korea. The installed distribution base is 60-80M units, plus about 12k-30k LPTs averaging 38-40 years old, a large future scrap stream (https://reliamag.com/topics/guides/aging-transformer-fleet-statistics). NREL attributed shortages partly to simultaneous pressure across GOES, copper and aluminium (https://berlin.cwiemeevents.com/articles/new-normal-component-suppliers). Distribution padmount lead times are about 75 weeks (WoodMac, https://woodmac.com/news/opinion/4-years-into-a-difficult-transformers-market-in-the-us-is-there-a-potential-end-in-sight). Unit economics (est.): scrap core steel bought at $300-600/t; after reclamation and processing it sells as finished cores at an equivalent $3,000-6,000/t, a gross margin of about 35-50% at scale. Capital (est.): $40-80M for the first reclaim, anneal and core line (about 20-40 kt/yr); far more ($300M+) for virgin amorphous or GOES capacity, financed with offtake and government support. Time to $100M revenue (est.): about 25-30 kt/yr of finished cores, 4-6 years. Market (est.): US GOES and core demand of about 400-600 kt/yr, $2-4B.
ai_role: Characterisation at scale (P1, P13): computer vision plus magnetic Barkhausen and single-sheet loss imaging grade every recovered lamination, a per-sheet 'container checksum' that makes heterogeneous scrap into a characterised, frozen input. ML process control of the anneal and recoating cycle per batch. An AI core-design compiler optimises the core layout (step-lap, mixed grades placed where flux density is lowest) to use mixed-grade reclaimed steel without losing efficiency. AI drafts DOE efficiency compliance test documentation per design. Learned teardown planning makes disassembly of thousands of different transformer designs per-unit cheap.
main_killer: Physics and economics of reclaimed GOES. The grain orientation and insulation coating can be damaged by service ageing, cutting and handling; losses may exceed DOE efficiency limits; and reclaimed widths and lengths are irregular. The feedstock stream is fragmented and the core may be contaminated with oil or PCBs.
ai_answer_to_killer: Optimism rule plus AI: per-sheet grading means only sheets that measure good go into loss-critical positions, while lower grades go to yokes and low-flux regions in a mixed-grade design the AI compiler optimises to still meet DOE efficiency. That is the same move as binning chips by speed grade. Re-annealing and recoating restore much of the stress-relief and insulation (est., plausible). Irregular geometry is solved by designing cores to the inventory (generative stacking) rather than cutting inventory to a fixed design. On feedstock, sign take-back contracts with utilities and recyclers (utilities already pay to dispose of transformers, and PCB-free oil certification is routine), and feed it from the company's own Rewound teardowns. If reclaimed-steel physics caps out, the same customers, characterisation stack and offtake book finance the amorphous or GOES line (rung 3/4), so the ladder survives.
competitors: Cleveland-Cliffs (sole US GOES), importers (Nippon Steel, JFE, POSCO, Baosteel, thyssenkrupp Electrical Steel). Amorphous: Proterial (formerly Hitachi Metals) Metglas, plus Chinese producers. Core makers: Central Electric Manufacturing, Tempel (Worthington), and in-house OEM core shops. Transformer recyclers that sell scrap by the ton. Solid-state transformer startups that partly bypass core steel: Heron Power ($140M Series B, 2026), Amperesand ($80M), DG Matrix ($60M Series A) (https://www.powerelectronicsnews.com/solid-state-transformers-in-the-spotlight). Their success would cap long-run demand, but data-centre-first SSTs do not displace the bulk grid fleet this decade (est.).
principles_used: P1 (a frozen, characterised material target, the core PDK), P3 (owned scarce capacity beats the marketplace), P11 (own the qualified cell, not the craft tool), P13 (per-unit signatures make a heterogeneous input portable), P12 (break a sole-source supplier monopoly on the scarce next layer).

score.name: CoreBank: the second domestic source of transformer electrical steel, reclaimed and re-characterised from retired transformers
score.rationale: The target is a genuine scarce input (Cleveland-Cliffs is the sole US GOES producer; DLA's sole-source $400M IDIQ is cited in the idea) and fits the 'own scarce physical capacity' law. Under the optimistic frame, AI per-sheet grading and mixed-grade core design is a plausible chip-binning analogue. But reclaimed feedstock is mostly older, thicker, conventional grades whose losses are well above modern domain-refined HiB steel, and the binning answer only helps up to the best sheets in a fragmented scrap stream. Volumes and the share of the US $2-4B core market that reclaimed steel can serve are therefore capped. The real moat (virgin GOES or amorphous capacity) arrives only at rung 4 with $300M+ of capital. Until then, any recycler or core shop can copy the characterisation line, so D is weak. Solid-state transformers also cap long-run demand. Two to three points below a pass. Reclaim-physics claims could not be checked because the search budget was used up.
score.biggest_risk: Material quality and volume. Reclaimed old-grade laminations may not meet current DOE efficiency levels at useful volume, which pushes the real business to a capital-heavy virgin GOES or amorphous line where incumbents and importers dominate.

name: Free Rotor: sovereign sustainment for orphaned Soviet-origin fleets
one_liner: Own the parts library, the approvals and an availability-contract fleet for the thousands of Mi-8/17, Mi-24 and other Soviet-origin aircraft and vehicles still flown by Western-aligned militaries, now cut off from a sanctioned OEM.
sector: Defence and aerospace sustainment (orphaned-OEM fleets, allied and partner nations)
what_it_owns: A NATO-standard, AI-built library of TDPs for Soviet-origin airframes, engines (TV3-117/VK-2500 family), gearboxes and avionics. Approvals from each national military airworthiness authority, which is the user's own approver. Its own overhaul depot in a NATO country. A pool of airframes and engines it owns and leases out, sold as available flight hours or power-by-the-hour.
wedge_first_revenue: Russia's sanctioned OEMs cannot legally supply NATO and partner users, so their data-rights and spares monopoly is legally unenforceable for these customers. The usual path is a sanctions-compliant, often grey, legacy broker chain. The wedge is overhaul of life-limited dynamic components and engines for one or two Eastern European or partner air forces, paid per overhaul, using parts the company reverse-engineered and the customer's MAA approved. US and European security-assistance funds already pay for such sustainment.
ladder: 1) Component overhaul and parts for 2-3 national users. 2) Power-by-the-hour availability contracts on whole fleets. 3) Own and lease a pool of overhauled Mi-17s and spare engines to partners, plus humanitarian, firefighting and UN users. 4) Extend the same orphan-fleet playbook to other cut-off fleets (Soviet-origin armour, radars, air-defence spares) with the same approver structure. 5) Bridge financing and replacement as partners move to Western types, holding both legacy sustainment and transition fleets.
numbers: Fleet (est.): more than 12,000 Mi-8/17 built, with est. 2,500-3,000+ still in service across 50+ countries. Many users are Western-aligned or US security-assistance recipients (Eastern Europe, Central and South Asia, Latin America, Africa). Market (est.): sustainment for Soviet-origin aircraft outside Russia at about $3-6B/yr, rising as Western sanctions bar Russian supply. Unit economics (est.): a Mi-17 engine or main gearbox overhaul costs about $0.3-1M; a fleet availability contract runs about $1-3M per airframe per year; reverse-engineered dynamic parts at 50-60% gross margin. Capital: $30-60M for a NATO-country depot, reverse-engineering lab and initial rotable pool (est.). Time to $100M revenue: about 4-6 years with 3-5 national fleet contracts (est.). Ceiling comparables: HEICO-style approval library; GE/Rolls power-by-the-hour; independent turbine service firms took OEM share as the OEM share fell from 65-80% to about 62% (the colleagues' P12 figure). Note: web search budget ran out in this run, so fleet figures are est. from prior knowledge.
ai_role: Reverse compilation on a large scale for a fleet whose OEM data will never be available. Scan-to-CAD, ML metallurgy and coating ID, LLM translation and structuring of Russian-language manuals and service bulletins, and fatigue and life models fitted to the customers' own usage logs to justify NATO-standard component lives. AI drafts the airworthiness substantiation each national MAA reviews and builds an open FFF interface spec for the whole fleet that no OEM published. Laws used: P12 (break the monopoly where the OEM is legally dead), P6 (open FFF spec), P14 (customer MAA as approver), P9 and P10 (fleet evidence and availability contracts).
main_killer: Shrinking demand, since partners are being pushed to replace Soviet types with Western ones. Also political and sanctions-compliance risk, and the risk that national MAAs, lacking OEM data, will not accept substantiation of life-limited parts.
ai_answer_to_killer: Replacement takes 10-20 years and costs far more than many users can pay (a UH-60M runs about $20M+ against an overhauled Mi-17 at about $3-6M, est.), so the legacy fleet lasts long enough to earn returns. The company also owns the bridge and transition fleet. For MAA acceptance, AI fits physics-informed life models to fleet operating data, and the company runs anchor tests on its own rigs, so the evidence becomes a measurable reliability case that a sovereign authority can accept faster than the FAA would; customers are their own approvers. On compliance, the company sits in a NATO country, buys no Russian content and makes everything from its own clean-room data, so it is the compliant answer to the current grey market.
competitors: Aviation broker chains (often grey-market), Eastern European state depots (WZL-1 in Poland, LOM Praha in Czechia, Ukrainian Motor Sich-adjacent shops), and Elbit/IAI upgrade packages. No AI-native owner of a TDP library exists for these types (est.).

score.name: Free Rotor: sovereign sustainment for orphaned Soviet-origin fleets
score.rationale: Search budget exhausted, and the idea itself flags its fleet figures as estimates. From prior knowledge, more than 12,000 Mi-8/17 were built and roughly 2,000-3,000 remain in service, but a large share sits with Russia, China, India and non-aligned users who will not buy from a NATO-sited firm. Many Eastern European users have already transferred their Mi-series to Ukraine or are retiring them. The addressable allied pool is therefore shrinking and is far below the claimed $3-6B/yr, which caps the ceiling near or below $1B (C2). Unit economics on overhauls and availability contracts are fine (N3). Revenue depends on security-assistance funding cycles and national tenders, so T3. AI reverse engineering and Russian-manual translation are real enablers, and customer MAAs as approvers do escape the FAA-queue law (A3). But reverse engineering a whole life-limited rotor drivetrain without OEM data is a heavy evidence load. State depots (WZL-1, LOM Praha, Ukrainian plants) already hold the approvals and relationships (D3).
score.biggest_risk: Demand decays as allies divest Soviet types, and the remaining large operators are outside the reachable market, so the ceiling shrinks faster than the library compounds.

name: OrbitFab (TSMC-style payload foundry and owned hosting fleet in orbit)
sector: Space hardware: satellites
one_liner: Freeze and characterise one satellite bus line plus a published 'payload PDK' (mechanical, power, thermal, data and radiation envelope). Customers compile their payload against it, OrbitFab integrates it, then owns and operates the satellites and sells payload-months in orbit.
what_it_owns: The fleet in orbit (the satellites stay OrbitFab's). The characterised bus line and its design rules, which play the role of a PDK. Flight-heritage evidence that accumulates with every mission. Spectrum and ITU filings plus FCC licences. A ground segment.
wedge_first_revenue: Start with hosted payloads for defence and government: SDA, AFRL, NASA tech demos, and allied ministries that need flight heritage quickly. Fly 2-3 rideshare buses carrying 4-8 payload slots each and charge per slot-month (est. $1-3M per slot-year). Customers pay an NRE deposit 12 months ahead, so first revenue arrives before launch.
ladder: 1) Hosted payload slots on owned buses, with defence and government buyers paying NRE upfront. 2) A payload PDK with automated design-rule checking: customers submit payload designs, an AI 'payload compiler' checks them against the envelope and generates the ICD, thermal and EMI evidence. 3) A shared constellation that runs many tenants (EO, RF sensing, comms tests) at once, as AWS does with servers. 4) Own the spectrum filings and sell virtual missions. 5) A sovereign-constellation-as-a-service for mid-size countries, where OrbitFab owns and operates and the country leases capacity.
numbers: Comparable: Loft Orbital raised a $170M Series C in Jan 2025 ($300M total, reported unicorn) for this 'satellite infrastructure as a service' model (https://www.satellitetoday.com/finance/2025/01/14/loft-orbital-raises-170m-plans-to-scale-with-inter-satellite-links-and-ai ; https://seedtable.com/companies/loft-orbital/funding-rounds/series-c-2025-01). Bus-makers Apex and K2 have also raised large rounds (est., unverified in this pass). Global satellite manufacturing est. $15-20B/yr, and the government smallsat market est. $5-8B/yr (est.). Rideshare launch is about $6-7k/kg, so a 200 kg bus launches for about $1.4M (est.). Bus build cost: est. $3-8M per unit at volume. Capital: est. $40-80M to the first 6 satellites in orbit. Time to $100M revenue: est. 5-6 years at about 40 satellites with 6 slots each at $1M+ per slot-year, est. Ceiling comparable: TSMC-style capacity owners and AWS (P3); in space, Planet and Maxar-type operators that own their fleets.
ai_role: A payload compiler (P1, P13): AI checks a customer payload against the frozen bus envelope and auto-generates the evidence package (ICD, thermal/EMI analysis, vibe/test plans). That cuts integration from 9-18 months to est. 2-4 months. Surrogate thermal and structural models plus active test selection reduce environmental test runs. On-orbit, ML scheduling multiplexes tenants (power, pointing, downlink) and fleet telemetry builds flight heritage per bus, which becomes evidence buyers will pay for (P9).
main_killer: Crowded and capital-heavy: Loft, York, Apex, K2 and Terran Orbital already exist. Launch cadence depends on SpaceX rideshare manifests. Defence buyers often want to own their satellites outright.
ai_answer_to_killer: Competitors sell buses or virtual missions. OrbitFab differs by freezing the target and publishing design rules, as TSMC did. The AI compiler then makes onboarding a new tenant nearly free, so OrbitFab can serve the long tail of payloads (universities, startups, allied governments) that Loft prices out. Heritage accumulates on the bus line, so every payload flown makes the next one cheaper to qualify. Where a defence buyer insists on ownership, offer a sale-leaseback while OrbitFab keeps operating the satellite and retains the heritage data. Rideshare depends on SpaceX, but the PDK is designed to fit multiple launchers (Rocket Lab, Firefly, ISRO), which hedges cadence risk.
competitors: Loft Orbital ($300M raised), York Space Systems, Apex Space, K2 Space, Terran Orbital (Lockheed), Muon Space, NanoAvionics, Spire (space services), Rocket Lab (Photon).
principles_used: P1 (frozen target and PDK), P3 (multi-tenant owned capacity), P9 (operating evidence), P13 (certify the recipe, not the site)

score.name: OrbitFab (TSMC-style payload foundry and owned hosting fleet in orbit)
score.rationale: Search budget was exhausted; Loft Orbital's $170M Series C (Jan 2025) matches prior knowledge. N2: each bus (est. $3-8M build plus about $1.4M launch plus ops and insurance) earns at 4-8 slots x $1-3M per slot-year only if fully filled, with satellite lifetimes of 3-5 years and launch-failure risk. Capital to 40 satellites is several hundred million, and Loft's own unit economics are not public. T3: NRE deposits help, but $100M takes about 5-6 years and many flights. C4: space infrastructure-as-a-service can plausibly exceed $1B (Loft unicorn, Planet). A2: the AI payload compiler speeds integration paperwork, but the killers are a crowded, funded field (Loft, Apex, K2, York, Rocket Lab), launch dependence and defence ownership preferences, and AI does not answer any of these. The 'long tail' it targets (universities, startups) is low-willingness-to-pay. D3: the bus line's flight heritage and the spectrum filings compound, but Loft has the same playbook years ahead.
score.biggest_risk: Loft Orbital and funded bus-makers already run this exact multi-tenant model with years of heritage, so OrbitFab is a capital-heavy late entrant whose AI layer is copyable.

name: Custody (owner of the stranded spent-fuel ISFSIs and the fuel as a future asset)
sector: Nuclear: back-end fuel cycle hardware and storage
one_liner: Acquire, by NRC licence transfer, the standalone dry-cask storage installations (ISFSIs) left at decommissioned reactor sites, together with their DOE breach-of-contract damages claims. Run them with a robotic, AI-driven aging-management programme at a fraction of today's cost. Own the spent fuel as a strategic feedstock for recycling and advanced-fuel developers.
what_it_owns: The NRC Part 50/72 licences for the ISFSIs (permission), the canisters and their contents (the physical asset: fuel with ~95% recoverable uranium plus plutonium/minor actinides), the right to DOE judgment-fund recoveries (contracted cash flow), and the aging-management evidence base for welded stainless canisters (P9 evidence that lets it renew licences and extend intervals as its own approver under the licence).
wedge_first_revenue: Buy ISFSI-only sites from decommissioned plant owners and decommissioners (Yankee Rowe, Connecticut Yankee, Maine Yankee, Zion, La Crosse, Humboldt Bay, Rancho Seco, Kewaunee, Vermont Yankee, Pilgrim, Indian Point and others, est. ~20+ stranded sites). Sellers want to exit a perpetual liability with security, staffing and licence obligations. They pay Custody a lump sum and/or the stream of future DOE damages. First revenue is the assigned DOE damages (recent settlement: $145M across the three Yankees) plus seller exit fees. Margin comes from cutting site O&M with remote monitoring, robotic canister inspection and shared security.
ladder: 1) Own and operate 3-5 standalone ISFSIs, collecting DOE damages. 2) Roll up to 20+ sites, pooling security, monitoring and licensing (P3 multiplexing). 3) Become the default custodian for every reactor at shutdown, taking the ISFSI at final shutdown. 4) Fuel-as-asset: contract supply of recovered material to recyclers (Oklo, Curio, SHINE) and to fast-reactor developers, or own a recycling front end. The tens of thousands of tonnes of US SNF become a domestic fissile reserve. 5) If federal consolidated storage or a repository arrives, Custody is the owner and operator the DOE contracts with to package and transport.
numbers: DOE has paid $11.1B from the Judgment Fund through FY2024 for failing to take spent fuel, and its remaining liability is in the tens of billions (https://wyoleg.gov/InterimCommittee/2025/09-2025072914-02USDOEPresentation.pdf; https://exchangemonitor.com/federal-price-tag-spent-fuel-disposal-delay-hits-7-4-billion). Recent example: $145M paid to the three Yankee operators (https://exchangemonitor.com/feds-will-pay-145m-to-ex-yankee-operators-in-latest-lawsuit-over-spent-fuel). Payout pace is ~$0.8-1B/yr nationally (est. from the cumulative trend). Dry-storage cask market: ~$4.5B globally in 2024, rising to ~$6B by 2030, with the US at ~$1.2B (market-research estimate, https://www.giiresearch.com/report/go1799205-spent-nuclear-fuel-snf-dry-storage-casks.html). 58 ISFSIs and 1,600+ casks loaded (older, https://enr.com/articles/4251-u-s-nuclear-plants-provide-market-niche-for-waste-disposal-system-providers). Per-site economics (est.): standalone ISFSI O&M of ~$8-12M/yr, recoverable from DOE. Cutting cost by 40-50% gives Custody the spread, ~$4-6M/yr per site, so 20 sites is ~$100M+/yr of largely government-backed cash flow. Capital: low for the asset (sellers often pay you), but licence-transfer approval and financial assurance need ~$20-50M of balance sheet (est.). Time to $100M revenue: ~5-7 years (est.). Ceiling comparables: Holtec targeted a ~$9.4-10.2B IPO valuation in Sep 2026, built heavily on decommissioning and spent-fuel storage (https://www.renaissancecapital.com/IPO-Center/News/121530/nuclear-plant-equipment-provider-holtec-nuclear-sets-terms-for-825-million); EnergySolutions (PE).
ai_role: AI fixes per-unit labour and paperwork, which here is most of the cost. Robotic crawler inspection of canisters for chloride-induced stress corrosion cracking, with ML-read ultrasound and eddy-current data. Fleet-wide thermal, radiation and intrusion sensing replaces guard-heavy security models (subject to NRC security rules). Physics-informed degradation models support licence renewals and longer inspection intervals under the licensee's own aging-management programme. LLMs automate licence-renewal applications, DOE damages claims accounting and litigation evidence, which are document-heavy and recur every few years. AI also models each canister's inventory (burnup, isotopics) to value the fuel for recyclers.
main_killer: Regulatory and political. NRC licence transfers and security rules, state and local opposition, and the open question of whether the government will challenge assignment of the DOE damages claims. The recycling upside depends on unproven economics, and ISFSI O&M may be too small a business without it.
ai_answer_to_killer: Licence transfers of shutdown sites are a well-trodden NRC path (Holtec, NorthStar and EnergySolutions have done whole plants), and this is a narrower transfer, so it rides precedent rather than a new queue. Damages flow through the licensee and the owner of the contract with DOE (the Standard Contract), so buy the entity holding the contract rather than assigning the claim. The cost cut comes from evidence and automation inside the licensee's own programme, where the licensee is its own approver. The business is profitable on DOE damages alone (a floor). Recycling and fissile-reserve value is the optional ceiling, and AI-based isotopic inventory turns it into a priced asset that can be pre-sold to recyclers.
competitors: Holtec International (HI-STORM, HI-STORE CISF, decommissioning, IPO target ~$10B); Orano TN; NAC International; Westinghouse ISFSI services (https://westinghousenuclear.com/data-sheet-library/dry-cask-storage-isfsi-services/); NorthStar/Orano (decommissioning); EnergySolutions; Deep Fission/Deep Isolation (disposal concepts); Interim Storage Partners (WCS, Texas). None focuses on rolling up standalone ISFSIs as an owner with AI-run operations.
principles_used: P14 (gate inside the licensee), P9 (operating evidence for aging management), P3 (pooling across sites), P10 (contracted cash flow as financing), P12 (value goes to the owner of the asset and liability, not the service vendor).

score.name: Custody (owner of the stranded spent-fuel ISFSIs and the fuel as a future asset)
score.rationale: Note: the web search budget for this turn ran out before any query ran, so these scores rely on prior knowledge and the cited sources. The core spread does not exist. DOE Standard Contract damages pay back costs actually incurred, they are not a fixed fee. Cut site O&M by 40-50% and the DOE recovery falls by the same amount, so no $4-6M/yr per-site margin is left. What remains is seller exit fees and maybe a performance-based fee. Many of the named sites are already owned by funded decommissioners: Holtec has Pilgrim, Indian Point and Oyster Creek; NorthStar has Vermont Yankee; EnergySolutions has Zion, La Crosse and Kewaunee. That fits the law that the first rungs are already held. Even with ~20 sites at ~$8-12M/yr O&M, the total pool is ~$200M/yr, which is a small ceiling. The billion-dollar case rests on recycling economics that are unproven, and on a repository or consolidated-storage contract that is political. AI-driven inspection and paperwork automation is plausible and does sit inside the licensee's own aging-management programme. Licence transfer has precedent. Defensibility comes from the licences plus the evidence base, but Holtec and Orano already hold both.
score.biggest_risk: DOE damages are cost reimbursement, so cutting cost shrinks revenue, and the stranded-site pool is small and mostly already owned by Holtec, NorthStar and EnergySolutions.

name: Munitions Reserve Utility: an owned, AI-surveilled stockpile sold as surge capacity
sector: Defence munitions: stockpile life extension, reserve inventory and availability contracts
one_liner: Buy aged, near-demil and allied-excess munitions and rocket motors at scrap value, then recertify them with AI non-destructive surveillance and aging models. Hold them in owned, instrumented magazines, and sell allied governments 'rounds-on-call' availability contracts, a capacity market for munitions, the way generators sell MW-days.
what_it_owns: The physical inventory (title to the rounds, motors and components), the instrumented magazine sites, and the per-round aging and surveillance evidence library (a fleet-wide reliability case, the munitions equivalent of ETOPS). Also the recertification line and its approvals, and long-dated availability contracts priced on that evidence. Low-variance evidence lowers its cost of capital (P10).
wedge_first_revenue: 1) Take custody of munitions slated for demilitarization. DoD pays to demil and faces a 'storage capacity crisis' (Army JMC), so inventory can come in at negative or zero cost. Harvest and recertify serviceable rounds and components for sale through FMS/DCS to partner nations, and as targets, test assets and training rounds. 2) A performance-based recertification contract on one legacy family, modelled on the Stinger SLEP at McAlester: about 2,700 unserviceable missiles were evaluated and about 70% returned to inventory. First revenue $5-30M (est.).
ladder: 1) Demil-feedstock recertify and resell (training, targets, FMS). 2) Contractor-run surveillance and SLEP under the Army Stockpile Reliability Program, building the evidence history. 3) Own magazines and hold allied reserve stocks on its own balance sheet, with annual availability fees plus a strike price per round drawn: a 'strategic munitions reserve as a service' for NATO and Indo-Pacific partners who lack storage and surge lines. 4) Securitise the availability-contract book once 24-36 months of aging data cut the spread. 5) Become the swing supplier, the 'United Rentals plus PJM capacity owner' of munitions, with warm lines attached.
numbers: Excess stockpile: about 375,000 short tons awaiting demil in 2020, cut by about 48k short tons/yr. DoD forecast 582,789 tons of additions FY16-20, and JMC warns of a 'storage capacity crisis' (https://www.army.mil/article/284293/jmc_commander_discusses_future_of_ammunition_industrial_base ; https://govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GAOREPORTS-GAO-01-372/pdf/GAOREPORTS-GAO-01-372.pdf). Life extension works: average missile shelf life was raised from 7.9 to 22.6 years through SRP (https://www.army.mil/article/156942). Stinger: about 2,700 unserviceable rounds evaluated, about 70% returned to inventory (https://www.army.mil/article/273140/peo_missiles_and_space_teams_with_mcalester_army_depot_to_revive_stinger_inventory). Demand: 155mm output is 36k/month against a 100k goal (https://www.defensenews.com/news/your-military/2026/07/14/manufacturing-woes-hamper-us-155-mm-ammo-production/), and the PAC-3 objective went from 3,376 to 13,773 (https://breakingdefense.com/2026/01/fy26-defense-bill-boosts-budget-by-8b-largely-bypassing-last-minute-28b-munitions-request/). Unit economics: a recertified round at 20-40% of new-build cost (est., by analogy to the resurrection-fleet turbine ratio), plus availability fees of 3-8% of round value a year (est.). Capital: $50-150M for magazines and the recert line, then inventory financing (est.). Time to $100M revenue: 4-5 years (est.). Comparables: United Rentals ($16.1B revenue, owned fleet), HEICO for approval-backed aftermarket, and GE Vernova LTSA economics for availability contracts.
ai_role: (a) Vision models read CT, X-ray, ultrasound and shearography of motors and warheads to find grain cracks, debonds and propellant aging per round, turning sampled surveillance into 100% per-unit evidence (P4, P9). (b) Physics-informed aging models pool data across lots and heterogeneous storage histories. The temperature and humidity telemetry from instrumented magazines is the 'operating hours', which attacks the small-n problem. (c) Reverse-engineering and TDP generation for replacement aging components (seals, batteries, igniters, electronics) (P12). (d) AI drafts the recertification packages, hazard classifications and transfer paperwork. (e) Inventory optimisation decides which lots to recertify, harvest or demil.
main_killer: The government is the owner and the approver. Title to US munitions rarely transfers, the program office alone certifies serviceability, and export of recertified rounds needs State Department approval. Allies may refuse to let a private company hold their war reserve.
ai_answer_to_killer: 1) Start where title does transfer: allied and partner excess (Eastern European and Gulf stocks), commercial-origin motors, and demil-designated material DoD would pay to destroy. 2) Earn approval through the existing Stockpile Reliability Program as a contractor, so per-round AI surveillance becomes the accepted evidence over 2-3 years. Each recertified lot builds the operating-evidence record, the ETOPS pattern (P9). 3) For allies, the company holds inventory in allied-sovereign sites under government oversight. It owns the inventory and data, but the state keeps release authority, which matches existing GOCO norms. 4) Being the holder of risk and evidence, with the lowest cost of capital (P10), is a moat the OEMs, who want to sell new rounds, will not copy.
competitors: Government depots (McAlester, Anniston, Tooele, Letterkenny), Nammo Demil, General Dynamics OTS, American Ordnance, BAE (SLEP work), Rheinmetall (allied ammo stocks), demil contractors (Kinetic Global, Day & Zimmermann), and allied state arsenals.
principles_used: P9 (operating evidence as certificate), P10 (recurring availability revenue as financing), P4 (delta qualification of aged rounds), P12 (reverse-engineer replacement components), P3 (owned pooled surge capacity)

score.name: Munitions Reserve Utility: an owned, AI-surveilled stockpile sold as surge capacity
score.rationale: Note: no web search ran (turn budget used up); scored from prior knowledge and the cited sources. The government owns, certifies and releases these munitions. The killer is title, release authority and export control (State Department/ITAR), and AI does not touch any of that: it is a gatekeeper queue, which AI does not fix. Demil stock is mostly obsolete or unserviceable by design. Allied excess, mostly Soviet-calibre, has largely gone to Ukraine already. The early rungs are SLEP and recertification contracting, which is a service (close to the rule line). Unit economics rest on an analogy to turbines, not on munitions data. Private holding of allied war reserves is unprecedented, so the availability-contract market may never form. AI non-destructive surveillance is plausible and useful (Stinger SLEP precedent), but it speeds up evidence, not permission.
score.biggest_risk: Governments will not transfer title or delegate release and serviceability authority to a private holder, so the owned-inventory model never forms and the company becomes a SLEP contractor.

name: Horsepower Utility (AWS for locomotive traction)
sector: Rail - mainline and short-line locomotives
one_liner: Buy the thousands of stored, out-of-favour diesel-electric locomotives at near-scrap prices, bring them back to life and re-certify them in-house with an AI-built parts and control library, and sell 'certified horsepower-hours' (power by the hour, with uptime guaranteed) to short lines, industrial railroads and Class Is in surge periods.
what_it_owns: A fleet of locomotives the company owns outright, 4,000-6,000 hp, eventually 500-2,000 units. Its own EPA remanufacture-system certificates under 40 CFR 1033, so it is its own emissions approver, and its own Part 229 inspection and maintenance program. A reverse-engineered parts and repair library for EMD 645/710 and GE FDL/7FDL engines, traction motors and controls. Its own retrofit control stack (update authority over the fleet). A telemetry and reliability record it uses to borrow against the fleet more cheaply.
wedge_first_revenue: Month 0-6: buy 10-20 stored SD40-2/SD70/Dash-9 class units from Class I surplus sales or brokers. Restore them with AI-generated work packages and reverse-engineered parts, then lease them to short lines (about 600 US short lines run many 40-60-year-old units) at a per-day rate with an uptime guarantee. First revenue comes from short-term horsepower leases during harvest and grain or peak season, when lease locomotives are scarce. Locomotives need no FRA type certificate: the owner or operator performs its own Part 229 periodic inspections, so the gate already sits with the operator.
ladder: 1) Short-line and industrial leases of restored units, priced per day or per MWh-equivalent of traction. 2) Fleet-wide AI control retrofit (P8): fuel-trim, adhesion and AESS (automatic engine start-stop) logic written by the company, aiming at 5-10% fuel savings and better tractive effort. The company keeps the uplift because it owns the units. 3) Hold its own EPA remanufacture certifications, so units come back at Tier 0+/1+/2+ and later battery-hybrid repowers; the certificates become the permission moat (P2, P14). 4) Securitise lease cash flows once there are 24-36 months of history (P10), which lowers cost of capital below Class I captive shops. 5) Surge capacity contracts with Class Is: guaranteed horsepower on call, on the AWS reserved-instance model. 6) Battery and hydrogen repower kits on its own frames, giving a zero-emission horsepower utility for yards and ports.
numbers: Market: US Class I fleet about 23,000-25,000 locomotives (AAR, est.); PSR left several thousand units stored in 2019-2023 (est. 3,000-5,000 at peak). New Tier 4 road locomotives cost about $3-4M each (est.), and Wabtec modernisations about $2-2.5M (est.). Stored or used SD70/Dash-9 units are est. $150-600k depending on condition. Wabtec 2024 revenue about $10.4B, of which Freight about $7.3B (est., Wabtec 10-K). Progress Rail (Caterpillar) is the other OEM. Unit economics (est.): $400k acquisition plus $350k restoration gives $750k all-in, against $3.5M new. A lease at about $450-700/day x 300 days is $135-210k/yr per unit, an 18-28% gross yield before maintenance. 1,000 units x $180k is about $180M/yr lease revenue, plus fuel-savings sharing and repower margins. Capital: about $15M for a first 20 units, then asset-backed lines of credit. Time to $100M revenue: est. 6-8 years (about 550 units on lease). Ceiling comparables: GATX (railcar and locomotive lessor, market cap est. $5-6B); Genesee & Wyoming taken private by Brookfield/GIC for about $8.4B in 2019; Wabtec market cap est. $30B+. Note: live web search was unavailable in this run (shared search budget exhausted), so the figures are from prior knowledge and marked est.; verify them before the YC application.
ai_role: (1) Reverse compilation: scans, metallurgy and legacy EMD/GE manuals become technical data packages for obsolete parts. It turns per-part engineering cost from about $50k into about $5k, so the long tail of the parts list becomes economic. (2) AI-generated work packages and inspection records make a restoration a repeatable process rather than artisanal shop work. (3) ML control retrofit gives each unit its own tuning for adhesion, fuel and engine life (P8). (4) Fleet telemetry and failure models cut the variance of availability, which lowers the cost of debt (P9, P10). (5) AI drafts the EPA certification test plans and the paperwork.
main_killer: Demand and price ceiling. Class Is now run fewer, larger trains (PSR) and dump surplus units, so used horsepower is cheap for everyone, which caps lease rates. Wabtec and Progress Rail also lease and modernise themselves. On top of that, EPA remanufacture rules (40 CFR 1033) and possible future California or state rules could strand old Tier 0 units.
ai_answer_to_killer: Turn the cheap supply into the advantage: the company is the low-cost owner of the oversupplied asset (the resurrection-fleet logic moved to rail) and sells uptime, not the iron. AI keeps per-unit restoration and parts cost below what the OEMs charge to modernise. The emissions killer becomes the moat: the company holds its own EPA remanufacture certificates and builds battery-hybrid repower kits, with AI-drafted certification packages and in-house test cells. A stored Tier 0 frame becomes a certified low-emission unit at a fraction of the price of a new Tier 4. The demand ceiling is lifted by moving up into surge contracts with Class Is and electrified yard power, where scarcity is real.
competitors: Wabtec (modernisations, leasing), Progress Rail/Caterpillar (EMD, Progress Rail leasing), GATX, Helm Financial/Motive Power (est.), CIT/Wells Fargo Rail (now part of GATX/other lessors, est.), NRE/National Railway Equipment (rebuilds and gensets), MotivePower, Knoxville Locomotive Works, and new zero-emission entrants (Wabtec FLXdrive, Progress Rail battery EMD Joule). Most rebuild for a fee or lease without owning certifications plus AI control retrofits as a fleet operator.

score.name: Horsepower Utility (AWS for locomotive traction)
score.rationale: The web search budget was exhausted; figures are from prior knowledge. Locomotive leasing already exists as a mature, competitive business: Progress Rail leasing, Motive Power/Helm, NRE, and Class I surplus sales. Precision scheduled railroading (PSR) left the market oversupplied, so the lease rate of $450-700/day is optimistic. N is 3 because the asset is cheap but yields are capped. T is 2: about 550 units on lease for $100M takes 6-8+ years, at the outer edge or beyond. C is 3: the total US locomotive lease pool is a sub-$1B revenue market. The GATX and G&W comparables are railcar fleets and railroads, not locomotive horsepower, so $1B+ needs the battery repower rung to work. A is 3: AI lowers per-part reverse-engineering cost, and ML control retrofits are plausible. But the killer is demand and price ceiling, which AI does not change. D is 2: EPA 40 CFR 1033 remanufacture certificates and Part 229 programmes are routinely held by existing rebuilders, so they are not a scarce permission moat, and Wabtec and Progress Rail can match on parts and modernisation.
score.biggest_risk: Structural oversupply of used horsepower after PSR caps lease rates and utilisation. The 'scarce capacity' premise behind an AWS-style utility does not hold in this market.
